# The Elderly Digital Divide: Age Is Just a Number, and So Is Your Smartphone Password

Aging has its benefits: senior discounts, rambunctious grandchildren, peaceful retirement, and hopefully a heap of wisdom. But many who enter into their so-called golden years also face challenges when it comes to staying connected and socially engaged with friends, family, and the world around them. Making these challenges even harder is the existence of an elderly digital divide. As human interaction becomes increasingly reliant on digital technology, older adults are especially likely to encounter challenges that block them from the benefits of connection in the digital world.

To understand how seniors are impacted by the digital divide, it’s necessary to grasp the broader issues of loneliness for older adults and the effects of ageism. And while there are certainly barriers blocking greater digital engagement for seniors, there are also promising [solutions](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8570906). As the world grappled with the difficulties of the COVID-19 Pandemic, the importance of those solutions became apparent.

## How the Digital Divide Is Isolating the Elderly

Older adults already experience isolation, but because so much social interaction now occurs online, overcoming that isolation has become even harder.

### Loneliness As a Broader Issue

The consensus—which has drawn increased attention in recent years—is that many older adults are at risk of experiencing social isolation and loneliness. The CDC reports that a third of adults in the United States over age forty-five report loneliness, and one in four adults over sixty-five are socially isolated.

Americans over sixty, according to [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2019/07/03/on-average-older-adults-spend-over-half-their-waking-hours-alone/), spend on average seven hours alone per day. In the United Kingdom, more than [one million](https://www.nhs.uk/mental-health/feelings-symptoms-behaviours/feelings-and-symptoms/loneliness-in-older-people/) of those over seventy-five report not having spoken to a friend, neighbor, or family member for at least a month.

To be sure, social isolation and loneliness are [distinct](https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/loneliness-and-social-isolation-tips-staying-connected). Isolation describes the absence of social contact, while loneliness is a negative emotion caused by feelings of disconnection and aloneness. To be clear, you can be socially isolated and not feel alone, or you can feel lonely even when surrounded by many people. And of course, social isolation makes loneliness much more likely.

It’s also important to note that loneliness is more than just a negative emotion. Dr. Steve Cole, from the University of California, Los Angeles, [calls](https://www.nia.nih.gov/news/social-isolation-loneliness-older-people-pose-health-risks) loneliness a “fertilizer for other diseases” that can contribute to plaque buildup, cancer spread, and inflammation. The [CDC](https://www.cdc.gov/aging/publications/features/lonely-older-adults.html) notes that social isolation can increase the chance of premature death, dementia, stroke, and heart disease. Loneliness is serious, which makes its relationship with the elderly digital divide even more important.

### Digital Exclusion Leads to Social Isolation

The digitally connected world spends a lot of time online. More than four in five Americans report going online every day, and [31 percent](https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2021/03/26/about-three-in-ten-u-s-adults-say-they-are-almost-constantly-online/) report going “almost constantly” online. Many of those who access the internet use social media to connect with friends and family and add new people to their universe. In the United States, [72 percent](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/fact-sheet/social-media/) of adults regularly visit at least one social media site.

But the data show that older adults are less connected to the digital world. One in four adults over sixty-five doesn’t use the internet, and more than 35 percent lack a home broadband connection. According to Pew Research Center, about one-third of those over sixty-five years of age report using social networking.

As their friends and family communicate online, seniors without access—whether for lack of technology, digital literacy, desire, or broadband—are left out of the loop. They miss the laughter, the family updates, the shared empathy, the intellectual stimulation—all those intangibles that make human interaction so vital to the mind and soul. [They also miss](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23969758/) the greater independence that an internet connection can bring, and the sea of information online that can contribute to higher quality of life. While the data can be mixed, many [studies](https://bmcmedinformdecismak.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12911-021-01500-2) point to mental, physical, and emotional benefits for older adults who use the internet.

Greater digital inclusion helps older Americans and older adults around the world fight back against isolation and loneliness.

### COVID-19 Pandemic Emphasizes Digital Divide

The negative consequences of exclusion from technology and connection to the digital world were very evident during the pandemic, especially for older adults. As the world entered lockdown to combat the virus, real-life activities like grocery shopping and visiting the doctor transitioned to the digital world. Vaccine information and appointments often required internet access. The [Stanford Center on Longevity](https://longevity.stanford.edu/the-pandemic-has-accelerated-the-need-to-close-the-digital-divide-for-older-adults/) points out that libraries and community centers, which once served as alternative ways to meet people and go online, were also shut down.

The pandemic tested the limits of social isolation for seniors, leading proponents of closing the elderly digital divide to double down on their drumbeat of advocacy. The president of the American Association of Retired Persons called for closing the digital divide as a matter of [equity](https://generations.asaging.org/digital-equity-human-right-whose-time-has-come).

## Impact of Ageism on the Digital Divide

While lack of access to technology may contribute to the digital exclusion of older adults, ageism also plays a role in [elderly technology adoption](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2017/05/17/technology-use-among-seniors/).

### Ageism Defined

The World Health Organization [defines](https://www.who.int/news-room/q-a-detail/ageing-ageism) ageism as “stereotypes…prejudice…and discrimination toward others or oneself based on age.” Anyone at any age can experience ageism, but age discrimination becomes especially relevant for the older population. A large majority of older Americans report regularly encountering [at least one](https://healthblog.uofmhealth.org/lifestyle/most-adults-say-theyve-experienced-ageism-but-majority-still-hold-positive-attitudes) “day-to-day” experience of ageism. Age discrimination is particularly relevant in employment decisions, where [studies show](https://academic.oup.com/esr/article/37/1/49/5900768) that age matters to hiring managers.

### How Ageism Holds Back Digital Engagement

Discriminatory policies and practices can certainly hinder digital inclusion for older adults. A lost job or a discriminatory experience in the healthcare industry may, for instance, affect income, well-being, and ultimately the capacity to use digital technology. Missing infrastructure, a lack of technology, or inadequate digital literacy training makes digital inclusion very difficult. But equally important to these external constraints is an internal one: the perceived ageism that leads many in the older population to opt out of crossing the digital divide.

Some older adults with the opportunity to use digital technology and access the internet may choose not to because they’ve internalized ageist rhetoric. Many seniors hear from younger adults or society that an older person lacks the digital skills and competence needed to use technology and navigate the internet.

A [scholar](https://www.heraldopenaccess.us/openaccess/the-effect-of-ageism-on-the-digital-divide-among-older-adults) at the University of Massachusetts Lowell suggests that lower self-efficacy and fear and anxiety created by this rhetoric can depress technology and internet adoption. Ageist messaging may also lead seniors to “underestimate the usefulness of the internet.” Another [study](https://academic.oup.com/gerontologist/article-abstract/60/7/1213/5857601?redirectedFrom=fulltext) showed that women with perceptions of aging that were more negative were less likely to use the internet. Men also saw lower levels of internet use in response to age discrimination.

Messaging during the COVID-19 pandemic brought age further into the spotlight. Because the virus posed a greater threat to older adults, many viewed COVID as “[an older person problem](https://academic.oup.com/ageing/article/49/5/692/5831206).”

## Barriers to Narrowing the Digital Divide for the Elderly

From ageism to technology to digital literacy, many barriers prevent bridging the digital divide for older adults.

### Lack of Access

The growing pace of technological change [enhances](https://www.comsoc.org/publications/ctn/digital-divide-humanitys-greatest-challenge) social inequality and societal challenges that already exist. That’s why for many seniors, digital engagement begins and ends with a lack of digital technology or broadband access. As mentioned above, Pew survey data indicate that older Americans lag younger Americans in smartphone ownership, home broadband, internet access, tablet ownership, and social media use.

The same lines of digital exclusion that broadly cut through society also map to the older adult population. One [study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23639979/) of disabled and homebound older adults revealed startlingly low levels of internet use (17 percent for those above sixty). Black and Hispanic adults and those with lower incomes were most likely to be among those who never use the internet. In general, older adults face increasing [economic and health inequalities](https://www.un.org/development/desa/ageing/briefings-series.html), and lack of income or capacity can be key drivers in preventing digital engagement.

### The Catch-up Curve

But even if seniors can access the digital world, they face a catch-up curve as they work toward equal digital footing. Because technology has developed so quickly, many older adults never had the opportunity to practice and gain basic digital literacy. In Europe, only [25 percent](https://unece.org/digitalization/press/ageing-digital-era-unece-highlights-key-actions-ensure-digital-inclusion-older) of older adults possess “basic or above basic digital skills,” according to the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe.

Feeling behind leads to apprehension about what it takes to catch up. One [focus group](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2017.01687/full) of older tablet users expressed negative perceptions of digital technology like “lack of instructions,” “lack of…confidence,” “too complex technology,” and feelings of comparison and inadequacy. To catch up—which for some means gaining literacy in a few decades-worth of technological change—can seem daunting.

### Additional Reasons for Digital Disengagement

The Centre for Ageing Better points out other [perceptions](https://www.ageing-better.org.uk/blogs/how-digital-divide-affects-older-adults-use-technology-during-covid-19) that play a role in technological adoption among older populations. For some, cultural differences and preferences discourage use. The way people communicate, or sometimes fail to communicate, by way of Twitter or Facebook is quite different from the lunch counter conversations of the 1940s. And social capital matters, too, because going online, having people to talk to, and staying connected sometimes requires support from family and friends.

Even for an older person who wants to opt-in, [physical barriers and accessibility](https://www.aarpinternational.org/the-journal/current-edition/journal-articles-blog/2020/10/bryant_david) can prevent digital inclusion. User experience, which includes the use of fonts and colors to the buttons and accessories that power the technology, can challenge adults with physical disabilities. Concerns about privacy or the complication of installation can also discourage adoption.

## Strategies to Bridge the Digital Divide among the Elderly

Despite the barriers to helping older adults experience digital inclusion, several strategies and resources offer promise to overcome the digital divide for seniors.

### Helping Seniors Go Online

The broader effort to help individuals join the digital world is particularly meaningful for older adults. In the United States, government-funded [discounts](https://www.fcc.gov/lifeline-consumers) can help older Americans afford broadband internet access. The European Union has a long-running focus on [digital inclusion](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en). [Digital literacy](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/9417139) training that is accessible to older adults also matters.

New technology, especially the Internet of Things (IoT), can also benefit seniors without requiring adoption. The [integrated future of IoT](https://futurenetworks.ieee.org/topics/charting-an-integrated-future-iot-and-5g-research-papers) innovations that will improve smart home capability, healthcare technology, and transportation will benefit older adults significantly.

### Accessibility in Design Is Key

Building digital technology and experiences that are accessible to older adults, a population with a [higher incidence](https://www.un.org/development/desa/disabilities/disability-and-ageing.html) of disabilities, is critical to bridging the divide.

Some researchers have advanced a concept known as “Universal Design,” which is a model that would account for the needs of all users in the design of products. This means thinking about flexibility of use, tolerance for error, physical effort required, size and space requirements for devices, and intuitiveness of use. The web development community is also increasingly focused on [accessibility](https://www.w3.org/standards/webdesign/accessibility)—say goodbye to tiny font size and poor color contrast that challenge even the sharpest of eyes.

### Older Adults as Full Participants

But designing technology well requires input from those who will use it, which includes older adults. Scholars [emphasize](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6801827/) the importance of “co-design,” which means proactive and ethical inclusion of older users during research and development. Companies and brands also have an opportunity to adapt their digital offerings to include seniors and thereby expand their brand reach.

## Closing the Elderly Digital Divide

Digital equity, which is when older adults have full access to the economic, personal, and civic benefits of digital access, is within reach. Even though the elderly digital divide looks wide, strategies and resources exist for seniors to make their golden years even brighter with help from the digital world.

args.summary:
This article from IEEE's CTU initiative examines the elderly digital divide—the gap in digital access, literacy, and engagement affecting older adults. Key points include:

**Isolation and Loneliness:** The CDC reports one in three US adults over 45 experience loneliness, and one in four over 65 are socially isolated. In the UK, over one million people over 75 haven't spoken to a friend or family member in at least a month. Loneliness is described as a "fertilizer for other diseases," contributing to plaque buildup, cancer, inflammation, and increased risk of premature death, dementia, stroke, and heart disease.

**Digital Exclusion:** One in four adults over 65 doesn't use the internet; over 35% lack home broadband; only about one-third use social media. This excludes seniors from family updates, intellectual stimulation, and the independence that internet access can bring.

**COVID-19 Impact:** The pandemic highlighted the digital divide as healthcare, grocery shopping, and vaccine appointments moved online, while libraries and community centers (alternative access points) were shut down.

**Role of Ageism:** Ageism—stereotypes, prejudice, and discrimination based on age—contributes to the digital divide. Internalized ageist rhetoric leads seniors to lower self-efficacy, fear, anxiety, and underestimation of the internet's usefulness. The WHO defines ageism, and studies show negative perceptions of aging correlate with lower internet use.

**Barriers:** Include lack of access (technology/broadband), the "catch-up curve" (only 25% of older Europeans have basic or above basic digital skills), physical barriers, accessibility issues, privacy concerns, and cultural preferences.

**Solutions:** Government-funded broadband discounts (e.g., FCC Lifeline), digital literacy training, IoT innovations (smart home, healthcare tech), Universal Design principles for accessibility, and co-design processes that include older adults in technology development.

The article concludes that digital equity for seniors is achievable through available strategies and resources.

# Senior Citizens and Technology: Closing the Digital Divide

Are you a senior citizen struggling to keep up with the fast-paced world of technology? You’re not alone. With advancements in technology happening daily, it can be overwhelming for older adults to stay up to date. This article will explore the importance of bridging the digital divide for senior citizens and provide tips on navigating the digital world with ease.

## **What is the Digital Divide?**

The term “digital divide” refers to the disparity between individuals who have access to information and communication technology and those who do not. This divide includes discrepancies in internet accessibility, computer availability, and technological literacy.

For senior citizens, this gap can impede their ability to participate in online activities, access necessary services, and stay connected with others. By implementing educational programs and improving access, we can bridge this divide and enhance the quality of life for seniors.

### **How Does the Digital Divide Affect Senior Citizens?**

* Senior citizens can be greatly impacted by the digital divide, which can result in:
* Lack of access to information and services, limiting their ability to engage in online activities and access essential resources.
* Reduced social connectivity, leading to feelings of isolation and loneliness due to the inability to communicate with family and friends through digital means.
* Limited opportunities for learning and skill development, affecting their ability to adapt to the digital age and access online educational resources.
* Challenges in utilizing telehealth services, resulting in barriers to accessing remote medical assistance and healthcare information.

## **Why is it Important to Close the Digital Divide for Senior Citizens?**

Closing the digital divide for senior citizens is important for several reasons. It ensures that they have access to essential services, can stay connected with their loved ones, and have opportunities for lifelong learning. It also promotes social inclusion, mental well-being, and independence, allowing them to navigate the modern world effectively.

To bridge this gap, it is crucial to provide tailored technology training, create user-friendly devices and interfaces, and offer affordable internet access. Additionally, fostering intergenerational connections can greatly enhance seniors’ digital literacy.

### **What Are the Benefits of Technology for Senior Citizens?**

Technology offers numerous benefits for senior citizens, such as enhancing communication through video calls, promoting mental stimulation with brain-training apps, and providing access to online health resources. It also provides convenience through online shopping and transportation services, promoting independence and social engagement. Studies have shown that technology can improve cognitive functions and reduce feelings of isolation among older adults.

## **What Are the Barriers for Senior Citizens to Access Technology?**

Despite the increasing prevalence and importance of technology in our daily lives, many senior citizens still face barriers to accessing and utilizing it effectively. In this section, we will discuss the various obstacles that senior citizens may encounter when trying to use technology. From physical limitations to financial constraints, these barriers can make it challenging for older adults to fully participate in the digital world. By recognizing and addressing these barriers, we can work towards closing the digital divide for senior citizens.

### **1. Physical Barriers**

* **Assess physical limitations:** Identify specific challenges such as vision impairments, limited dexterity, or mobility issues.
* **Adaptation of devices:** Customize technology tools to accommodate physical barriers, for instance, using larger font sizes or voice-command features.
* **Accessible technology:** Introduce senior-friendly devices like easy-to-use smartphones, tablets with touchscreen features, or specialized keyboards and mice.

### **2. Technological Barriers**

* 1. Lack of Familiarity: Seniors may struggle due to limited exposure to technology, leading to a lack of confidence in using devices.
* 2. Accessibility Issues: Physical limitations can hinder the use of devices, necessitating adaptive technology.
* 3. Complexity: Complicated interfaces and fast-paced technological changes may pose challenges for seniors.

Overcoming the technological barriers, seniors are now embracing technology through personalized training programs, simplified user interfaces, and the development of user-friendly devices, fostering greater digital inclusion.

### **3. Financial Barriers**

1. Identify potential funding sources for technology access programs aimed at senior citizens.
2. Offer subsidies or discounts for technology devices and internet services to senior citizens facing financial barriers.
3. Partner with government and non-profit organizations to establish financial assistance programs for senior citizens to obtain and sustain access to technology.
4. Provide financial literacy and budgeting workshops specifically designed for senior citizens to assist them in effectively managing technology-related expenses.

### **4. Attitudinal Barriers**

* Encourage a positive outlook towards technology by highlighting its advantages for senior citizens and addressing any attitudinal barriers.
* Offer mentoring programs and peer support groups to help seniors overcome any apprehensions or fears about using technology.
* Organize workshops and seminars focusing on the ease of use and benefits of technology, to shift negative attitudes towards a more optimistic view.
* Promote intergenerational activities that foster a culture of learning and sharing technology knowledge, breaking down any resistance or skepticism.

## **How Can We Close the Digital Divide for Senior Citizens?**

As technology continues to advance and become an integral part of daily life, there is a growing concern over the digital divide among senior citizens. Many older adults face barriers to accessing and utilizing technology, which can lead to feelings of isolation and exclusion from the modern world. In this section, we will discuss actionable steps that can be taken to close the digital divide for senior citizens. These include providing access to technology, offering training and support, addressing affordability issues, and promoting a positive attitude towards technology. By implementing these strategies, we can ensure that seniors are not left behind in the digital age.

### **1. Providing Access to Technology**

* Establish community technology centers with internet access for seniors.
* Provide affordable or free devices, such as tablets or smartphones, specifically designed for seniors’ needs.
* Collaborate with libraries or senior centers to offer technology borrowing programs.
* Implement government initiatives to subsidize technology costs for senior citizens.

### **2. Offering Technology Training and Support**

* Conduct digital literacy workshops to educate seniors about basic technology use.
* Provide one-on-one training sessions tailored to the specific needs and pace of each senior.
* Establish tech support hotlines or online resources offering guidance for common tech issues.
* Collaborate with local community centers to set up technology help desks for seniors.

### **3. Addressing Affordability Issues**

* Discover government programs that offer subsidies for technology purchases.
* Partner with technology companies to offer senior-friendly devices at discounted prices.
* Implement community initiatives for device donation and recycling to ensure accessibility for all seniors.
* Advocate for policy changes to reduce taxes or provide exemptions for technology products specifically for seniors.

### **4. Promoting a Positive Attitude towards Technology**

* Educate seniors about the benefits of technology, emphasizing how it can enhance their lives and promoting a positive attitude towards its use.
* Offer workshops and seminars to familiarize seniors with technology, addressing their fears and concerns and promoting a positive attitude towards learning and using new technology.
* Provide ongoing support and encouragement as seniors navigate the digital world, promoting a positive attitude towards technology and its capabilities.
* Showcase success stories of seniors who have embraced technology to inspire a positive outlook and promote a positive attitude towards technology.

## **Success Stories of Closing the Digital Divide for Senior Citizens**

Senior citizens have experienced success stories in bridging the digital divide through various programs and initiatives. For example, community centers in Sarasota, Florida, have implemented technology classes specifically designed for seniors, leading to increased digital literacy and confidence. Furthermore, volunteer-led workshops and one-on-one coaching sessions have empowered older adults to effectively navigate digital tools and platforms.

#### News | August 23, 2022

Contact

***What is the digital divide?*** *Simply put, it’s the divide between those who have access to the internet and those who do not. Potential barriers to digital access include installation, knowledge, and trust.*

The NCIOM [Healthy Aging Task Force](https://nciom.org/task-force-on-healthy-aging/) focuses on social isolation, nutrition, mobility, and falls prevention; the effects of the digital divide on these Task Force priorities are important to consider. [Digital technology has been shown](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30974780/) to help foster independence, increase quality of life, and improve mental and physical health. For older adults, digital technology has the potential to help overcome some of the challenges of aging. Social isolation can be decreased through networking online and video calls with family and friends. Virtual exercise regimens can increase physical function. [Internet use has also been shown](https://www.jmir.org/2021/2/e26145/) to reduce the likelihood of depression and loneliness in older adults, and allows access to information and services within their communities.

While the age gap in owning digital technology is beginning to close, the disparities that remain are important ones. Part of the problem is the mismatch between what older adults need from digital technology and what is available. Barriers include physical challenges; the size of the buttons, font size, and dexterity all have the potential to make using a digital device more difficult. Vision or hearing impairment can also affect the use of digital services. The top-down strategy of companies attempting to adapt technologies after a product has been developed has not always been successful, sparking concerns about ageism in technology development.

In addition, digital literacy is a challenge for many older adults, particularly those who were introduced to digital technology after their working years, leaving them to adapt to these changes without much support. This can affect older adults in myriad ways. A key issue is the lack of confidence in the ability to adopt new technologies. This lack of confidence can cause barriers to successful adaptation, impacting an older adult’s ability to uptake new information. An obstacle to confidence may also be the negative stereotype typically associated with older adults’ ability to use digital technology.

The digital divide also affects access to health care and other important services. For those able to take advantage of telehealth, digital platforms can provide access to remote medical health or education, help manage nutrition, and manage illness. [This](https://nciom.org/covid-19-and-the-digital-divide/) previous NCIOM blog post highlights the importance of telehealth at the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly for high-risk groups such as older adults. Yet, [studies have shown](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11606-021-06629-4) that there are widening digital access gaps for those with serious illness; this demographic has shown static digital technology ownership while those without serious illness face increasing ownership.

The [North Carolina Digital Equity and Inclusion Collaborative](https://www.ncbroadband.gov/digital-divide/digital-equity-collaborative) (NCDEIC) is part of Gov. Roy Cooper’s plan to close the digital divide with nearly $1 billion in federal American Rescue Plan funds as well as $30 million in state funds. This will be spent by the end of 2026 with the aim to build internet infrastructure and support digital literacy training.

# What Is the Digital Divide? Meaning, Causes & Impact

What Is the Digital Divide? Meaning, Causes & Impact

## **Key Takeaways**

* **The digital divide describes gaps in who can access, use, and benefit from digital technology.**
* **Economic factors, geography, education, and age all contribute to technology inequality.**
* **Digital gaps affect education, employment, healthcare access, and social participation.**

Your daughter’s teacher emails an assignment at 8 p.m. Your doctor’s office only schedules appointments online. Your employer expects you to complete training modules from home. The government portal requires digital verification for benefits.

For millions of people, these everyday expectations create impossible barriers. Not everyone has reliable internet, a working device, or the skills to use digital systems confidently.

The modern world runs on digital tools: for learning, working, accessing healthcare, and staying connected. Yet despite this reliance, benefits don’t reach everyone equally. Some communities thrive with high-speed internet and cutting-edge devices, while others struggle with spotty connections and outdated equipment.

This uneven access creates real challenges. Understanding the digital divide, what it is, why it exists, and how it affects daily life, is the first step toward building a more inclusive digital future.

## **What Is the Digital Divide?**

The digital divide refers to the gap between people who have meaningful access to digital technology and those who don’t. It’s not just about owning a smartphone or having an internet connection; it’s about the quality of that access, the skills to use it effectively, and the ability to benefit from digital opportunities.

This divide appears at every level: globally between developed and developing nations, nationally between urban and rural areas, and locally between neighborhoods just miles apart. A family with fiber-optic internet and multiple laptops experiences technology differently from a household sharing one smartphone with unreliable mobile data.

The gap affects specific groups more severely. Low-income communities often can’t afford devices or monthly internet bills. Rural areas lack the infrastructure for high-speed connections. Older adults may have access but lack confidence using digital tools.

According to the [Pew Research Center](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/fact-sheet/internet-broadband/), as of 2025, 4% of U.S. adults don’t use the internet at all, and this rises to 10% among those 65 and older.

## **Types of Digital Divide**

Digital inequality operates on multiple levels. Understanding these distinctions helps explain why simply providing internet access doesn’t solve the problem.

### Access divide

The access divide describes disparities in who can connect to the internet and own digital devices. Rural communities face significant infrastructure gaps because installing broadband in sparsely populated areas costs more per household, making it less profitable for internet providers.

Even in areas with available service, cost creates barriers. Households earning less annually are more likely to lack home internet compared to higher-income households. Some families can only afford [**mobile-only internet**](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2024/01/31/americans-use-of-mobile-technology-and-home-broadband/) plans, which limit what activities are practical. For example, filling out job applications or completing homework becomes frustrating on a small screen with data caps.

Device ownership matters too. When multiple family members need devices simultaneously for school and work, someone gets left out.

### Skills divide

The skills divide refers to differences in digital literacy: the ability to navigate technology effectively, safely, and productively. Having access to the internet means little if you don’t know how to use it or feel intimidated by digital tools.

Digital literacy includes practical skills like using email, searching for information online, recognizing phishing scams, managing privacy settings, and completing online forms. It also encompasses critical evaluation, distinguishing reliable sources from [**misinformation**](https://ischool.syracuse.edu/what-is-misinformation/) and protecting personal information.

Many people struggle to feel confident using modern technology. According to [**AARP research**](https://www.aarp.org/pri/topics/technology/internet-media-devices/2024-technology-trends-older-adults/), 64% of adults over 50 feel that technology is not designed with their age group in mind.

Students from well-resourced schools often receive regular technology training, while students in under-resourced districts may have limited exposure beyond basic tasks. This creates workforce readiness gaps that extend long after graduation.

### Usage divide

The usage divide describes how people use digital technology differently based on their socioeconomic status and education. Not all internet use creates equal opportunities.

Some people primarily use technology for entertainment, such as streaming videos, gaming, or social media. Others use it for education, career advancement, financial management, and civic participation. [**Research shows that**](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/46541612_Digital_Distinction_Status-Specific_Types_of_Internet_Usage) higher-income users engage in more “capital-enhancing” activities like online courses and job networking, while lower-income users often engage in more passive consumption.

The usage divide also relates to device type. Try writing a resume or navigating complex government forms on a smartphone. It’s technically possible but frustrating, which discourages people from completing important tasks.

## **Causes of the Digital Divide**

Digital inequality results from multiple overlapping factors:

* **Economic factors:** A new laptop costs several hundred dollars, and monthly internet bills ranging from $50 to $100 add up to $600 to $1,200 annually. These cumulative costs put consistent digital access out of reach for millions of households.
* **Geographic limitations:** [**Recent data**](https://www.usda.gov/sustainability/infrastructure/broadband) confirms that rural Americans are close to 20 times more likely than urban residents to lack access to fixed broadband service.
* **Educational factors:** Schools in lower-income districts often have outdated equipment and less robust tech curricula. Students graduate without the digital skills their peers from better-resourced schools take for granted.
* **Age-related gaps:** Older adults often lack confidence using technology and feel excluded from systems that assume digital fluency.
* **Infrastructure limitations:** Some areas still rely on aging copper telephone lines or satellite connections. Infrastructure upgrades require massive investments that many communities can’t fund independently.
* **Policy or regulatory barriers:** When digital access isn’t treated as essential infrastructure, investment remains fragmented and uneven.

Understanding [**digital transformation**](https://ischool.syracuse.edu/what-is-digital-transformation/) helps contextualize why these barriers matter. As more systems become digital-first, limited access to technology can quickly turn into fewer opportunities.

## **Effects of the Digital Divide**

The digital divide affects learning, work, healthcare, and participation in society, often making existing gaps even wider.

### Education

The digital divide limits students’ ability to complete homework, access online resources, and participate in remote learning. Students without home internet struggle to access learning management systems, submit digital assignments, or conduct online research. The educational impact compounds over time, as students who fall behind often struggle throughout their academic careers.

### Employment

Most employers now require online applications. [**U.S. Census Bureau**](https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2025/01/work-from-home-inequalities.html) data shows that higher-wage workers were significantly more likely to work remotely, while lower-wage workers couldn’t. This wage gap often correlates with digital access.

Career training increasingly happens online. Workers without digital access to skill-building courses and certifications can’t stay competitive. The shift toward remote work models further disadvantages people without quality home internet setups.

### Healthcare

According to the [**American Medical Association**](https://www.aha.org/fact-sheets/2025-02-07-fact-sheet-telehealth), approximately 80% of healthcare providers offered telehealth in 2022, but significant disparities exist in who can access these services. Older adults, rural residents, and low-income patients face the greatest barriers.

Healthcare systems increasingly rely on patient portals for appointments, test results, and prescription refills. Patients without digital access must call during business hours, often missing time-sensitive medical information.

### Social participation

The [**National Digital Inclusion Alliance**](https://www.digitalinclusion.org/) reports that citizens without digital access face significant barriers to accessing public services and engaging with elected representatives. Government services from tax filing to benefit applications have moved online.

Banking has shifted digital, too. People without digital banking access pay more in fees for check cashing and money orders. The shift toward digital civic participation means residents without access have less ability to influence decisions affecting their communities.

## **Examples of the Digital Divide**

The digital divide affects people differently based on where they live, their income, their age, and the technology available to them. The examples below show how limited digital access can create real challenges in everyday life.

* **Rural student:** A girl lives 45 minutes from her high school in a rural area. Her family can’t afford satellite internet, so she completes all homework at school or the public library. When assignments are posted after hours, Maria falls behind.
* **Low-income family:** A family shares one smartphone among five people. When both parents need to search for jobs online and two kids have homework, decisions get made about whose needs take priority.
* **Older adult:** A person is 72 and recently widowed. His doctor’s office switched to an online patient portal. He has a computer but feels overwhelmed creating accounts. He avoids the system and waits weeks for appointments.
* **Limited infrastructure:** A town of 3,000 residents has one provider offering 10 Mbps maximum speeds. Students struggle with online learning platforms, and local businesses can’t compete because they lack bandwidth for modern systems.

## **How to Bridge the Digital Divide**

Closing the digital divide requires coordinated efforts that address access, skills, and long-term support. Bridging this gap is not about a single solution, but about combining infrastructure development, education, policy action, and cross-sector collaboration to ensure that digital access becomes more equitable and sustainable.

### Expanding infrastructure

Infrastructure investment forms the foundation of digital inclusion. Federal and state broadband initiatives now focus on expanding affordable internet access through large-scale infrastructure funding, including nationwide broadband deployment programs and state-managed subsidy efforts. State and local governments also support broadband expansion through public–private partnerships aimed at reaching underserved communities.

At the local level, libraries, schools, and community centers provide essential access by offering free Wi-Fi, computers, and basic technology support. Device donation programs collect used laptops, refurbish them, and distribute them to students and low-income families.

### Improving digital literacy

Schools integrate digital skills throughout the curriculum. Libraries offer free digital literacy workshops for adults, covering basics like email, online safety, and job searching. Community organizations target specific populations with tailored training: programs for older adults move at a comfortable pace, while programs for immigrants offer multilingual instruction.

### Policy solutions

Federal programs like the [**Broadband Equity Access and Deployment Program**](https://broadbandusa.ntia.gov/funding-programs/broadband-equity-access-and-deployment-bead-program) allocate billions to expand broadband in underserved areas. Subsidy programs reduce cost barriers, and school districts receive E-Rate funding for internet access and technology.

Digital inclusion is advanced through education at institutions like Syracuse University’s [**Innovation, Society, & Technology Bachelor’s Degree**](https://ischool.syracuse.edu/academics/innovation-society-and-technology-bachelors-degree/) program, which prepares students to address technology’s societal impacts.

### Support from private and nonprofit sectors

Tech companies donate devices and fund digital literacy programs. [**Microsoft’s Airband Initiative**](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/corporate-responsibility/airband-initiative) and [**Google’s Project Connect**](https://sites.google.com/view/project-connects/home) work to expand broadband in underserved communities. Nonprofits like EveryoneOn connect families to affordable internet, while PCs for People refurbishes and distributes computers.

Progress is often strongest when different groups work together. Partnerships between schools and local businesses, libraries and internet providers, or nonprofits and government agencies allow resources and expertise to be shared, leading to solutions that no single organization could create on its own.

## **Moving Toward Digital Equity**

Digital equity requires ongoing effort from many groups. Understanding the digital divide shows the size of the problem, but real progress happens when people and institutions take action. This includes schools improving technology access for students, libraries expanding community services, businesses investing in inclusive infrastructure, and governments treating digital access as essential.

Communities that prioritize digital inclusion see clear outcomes, including students completing their education, workers accessing employment, and patients managing their health more effectively. Over time, these individual gains contribute to broader community improvement.

Everyone has a role to play. Educators, voters, volunteers, and professionals all influence how digital access is expanded and supported. For those interested in contributing through education and policy, [**Syracuse University offers programs**](https://ischool.syracuse.edu/academics/) that examine technology’s societal impact and prepare students to address complex challenges related to equity and access.

## **Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)**

### What is the main cause of the digital divide?

There’s no single cause; multiple overlapping factors create digital inequality. Economic barriers (cost of devices and service), geographic limitations (lack of rural infrastructure), educational gaps (limited digital literacy), age-related differences, and policy shortcomings all contribute.

### How does the digital divide affect students?

Students without reliable internet and devices struggle to complete homework, access online resources, and participate in virtual learning. These gaps create long-term educational disadvantages that affect college readiness and career prospects.

### Who is most affected by the digital divide?

Low-income households, rural residents, older adults, people with disabilities, and some racial and ethnic minorities experience the most significant barriers.

### How does the digital divide impact daily life?

Digital inequality affects education (completing homework, accessing courses), employment (job applications, remote work), healthcare (telehealth appointments, patient portals), and social participation (staying connected, accessing government services). As more essential services move online, the divide increasingly determines who can participate fully in modern society.

## What Is the Digital Divide? Meaning, Causes & Impact

This page from Syracuse University's iSchool provides a comprehensive overview of the digital divide—the gap between people who have meaningful access to digital technology and those who don't. It goes beyond device ownership to include quality of access, skills to use technology effectively, and ability to benefit from digital opportunities.

### Key Takeaways
- The digital divide describes gaps in who can access, use, and benefit from digital technology
- Economic factors, geography, education, and age all contribute to technology inequality
- Digital gaps affect education, employment, healthcare access, and social participation

### Types of Digital Divide
1. **Access Divide**: Disparities in who can connect to the internet and own devices. Rural communities face infrastructure gaps; cost is a major barrier (monthly bills of $50–$100). Some families rely on mobile-only internet.
2. **Skills Divide**: Differences in digital literacy—navigating technology effectively, safely, and productively. According to AARP research, 64% of adults over 50 feel technology is not designed with their age group in mind.
3. **Usage Divide**: How people use technology differently based on socioeconomic status. Higher-income users engage in more "capital-enhancing" activities; lower-income users often engage in more passive consumption.

### Causes
- **Economic factors**: Device costs ($200+) plus annual internet bills ($600–$1,200)
- **Geographic limitations**: Rural Americans are nearly 20 times more likely than urban residents to lack fixed broadband (USDA data)
- **Educational factors**: Under-resourced schools have outdated equipment and weaker tech curricula
- **Age-related gaps**: Older adults often lack confidence with digital tools
- **Infrastructure and policy limitations**

### Effects
- **Education**: Students without home internet struggle with homework, online resources, and remote learning
- **Employment**: Higher-wage workers are more likely to work remotely; lower-wage workers cannot (U.S. Census Bureau data)
- **Healthcare**: ~80% of providers offered telehealth in 2022, but older adults, rural residents, and low-income patients face greatest barriers (AMA)
- **Social participation**: Citizens without digital access face barriers to government services, banking, and civic engagement

### Bridging the Divide
Solutions include expanding broadband infrastructure (federal programs like BEAD), improving digital literacy through schools and libraries, policy solutions (subsidy programs, E-Rate funding), and support from private/nonprofit sectors (Microsoft's Airband Initiative, Google's Project Connect, EveryoneOn, PCs for People).

The page concludes that digital equity requires ongoing effort from schools, libraries, businesses, and governments, and that communities prioritizing digital inclusion see clear outcomes in education, employment, and healthcare.

# ‘We wanted to find new friends’: See how older Californians are proving that senior isolation isn’t inevitable

COVID-19 isolated many older Californians. Now, some are building new relationships with help from local senior centers.

![](https://calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/IsadoraKosofsky-300-200x200.jpg?crop=1)![](https://calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/Jenny-Jacklin-Stratton-200x200.jpg?crop=1)  by [Isadora Kosofsky](https://calmatters.org/author/isadora-kosofsky/) and [Jenny Jacklin-Stratton](https://calmatters.org/author/jenny-jacklin-stratton/)

### Share this:

* [Share on X (Opens in new window) X](https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2026/02/look-inside-los-angeles-senior-centers/?share=x&nb=1)
* [Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook](https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2026/02/look-inside-los-angeles-senior-centers/?share=facebook&nb=1)
* [Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp](https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2026/02/look-inside-los-angeles-senior-centers/?share=jetpack-whatsapp&nb=1)

Older adults are among the fastest-growing populations in California. By 2030, residents over 65 are expected to outnumber those under 18, signaling a major demographic shift. Recognized as community focal points under the 1965 [Older Americans Act,](http://acl.gov/about-acl/authorizing-statutes/older-americans-act) more than 11,000 [senior centers operate nationwide](https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2026/02/senior-centers-aging-health/), offering different services such as meals, wellness classes, and spaces that foster social bonds.

[Research shows](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf) social isolation poses serious risks to older adults’ mental and physical health. As people age, many face compounding health needs, fixed incomes, transportation challenges, and the loss of spouses, housing, mobility, or independence. [Senior centers provide](https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2026/02/senior-centers-what-we-learned/) community support, yet despite their significant role, both older adults and the programs that serve them largely remain underrepresented in media.

In this photo essay, Los Angeles–based photojournalist and filmmaker Isadora Kosofsky documents the long-term impact of COVID-19-related senior center closures, many of which were the first communal spaces to shut down and the last to reopen, tracing their gradual return to the present day. Her work spans multiple years and communities including Tehachapi, Lincoln Heights, Westchester, Watts, and Culver City.

“I have seen very little in-depth storytelling about senior centers,” she says. “They exist in nearly every ZIP code, yet we know so little about these spaces and the people who gather within them.”

The intimate photographs reflect moments of solitude and connection, illuminating senior centers as daily spaces for kinship and community. “Ultimately, the project is about belonging,” Kosofsky says. “In our unprecedented aging world, it is vital that we report on how older adults seek meaning and build new relationships.

![An older adult with white hair walks along a quiet, tree-lined sidewalk at dusk while another older adult wearing a face mask sits on a walker nearby, with parked cars and buildings lining the street.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-02.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

People socially distance themselves outside subsidized senior housing in Santa Monica, in 2020. A 2024 University of Colorado Boulder study revealed that more than half of older adults still spend more time at home and less time socializing in public than they did prior to the pandemic. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![A handwritten note taped to a wall reads, “A Father is someone who keeps pictures of his family in his wallet where the money used to be,” beside a wooden cabinet topped with small figurines.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-03.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Edgar Burns, 93, lived in the Westchester neighborhood of Los Angeles. For over 10 years, he lived alone in the home he once shared with his wife and where he raised his three children. A former Mattel toy inventor, he continued to create toys well after retirement. He kept in touch with members of the Westchester Senior Center by phone, including the director. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![An older adult lies on a bed with a patterned gray-and-white cover, one hand resting on a tablet while a TV remote, a used tissue, and a face mask sit nearby.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-04.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Shane Shabad, 90, who lives in affordable senior housing in Santa Monica, relies on his iPad for information. His vision loss makes it challenging for Shane to watch television, so he listens to the local Iranian radio. “Since nobody is talking to me during the day, I have noise.”  Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![Several deer lie partially hidden in tall, dry grass on a sloping hillside, their ears and heads visible above the straw-colored vegetation.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-05.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Older adults in rural areas, like Tehachapi in the Mojave Desert, face additional risks of social isolation. They face multiple barriers to connecting with others, such as transportation challenges, more limited economic resources, and more restricted access to health care, especially mental health care. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 

Sandie Shultis, 76, sits in her home in Tehachapi. She served on the board of the Tehachapi Senior Center but has not returned since the shutdown. “I’m such a homebody,” she shared. Sandie has lived alone with her four dogs since her husband, Ray, passed away. In 2025, Sandie moved from Tehachapi to Bakersfield to be closer to medical services. Photos by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![At dusk, an older adult sits at a desk inside a softly lit room, seen through a window from outside, reading papers while the exterior of the house remains in shadow.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-08.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Edgar Burns, 93, uses his computer to video chat with his grandchildren. Edgar was an active member of the Westchester Senior Center near his home for over a decade. He joined the community after his wife passed away. During the pandemic, he filled his time with socially distanced meals with his family, gardening, and used Portal, which his grandson set up for him. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![An older adult wearing a face mask reclines on the grass in a shaded yard while another masked person crouches several feet away holding a bag, with leafy plants and houses in the background.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-09.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Burns, and granddaughter, Lianna Levine, 16, sit on the front lawn of his home. “Sure, I would like to do more things with my grandkids, but I can’t, so I don’t,” he said in 2020. “It’s just a few more months.” Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![An older adult wearing a protective face mask and cap stands indoors behind a screen door, one hand resting near their chest as they look outward.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-10.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Burns stands in the doorway of his home. He immediately returned to the Westchester Senior Center upon its reopening in 2022. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

  

Shane Shabad, 90,  is a former ice cream store owner who emigrated to the US from Iran in the 1970s. In 2021, his son, who was his primary support person, died suddenly. Shabad faced increased isolation thereafter, relying on his daughter and granddaughter for support to purchase groceries. Photos by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![Low sun shines over a fenced backyard with overgrown grass, trees, and power lines, creating lens flare across the scene.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-13.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Burns, 93, dug holes for a week in the backyard of his home of 50 years. Edgar planted two different kinds of tomatoes in his garden, as COVID-19 cases rose in LA County. After preparing the soil in the yard at high noon, he walked for a mile daily. He picked blueberries off of an overgrowing plant beside his home. “Busy keeps me happy,” Edgar said in 2020. “Due to the coronavirus, all these things become important because you can’t do anything else.” Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![Two older adults sit on a bench along a hallway wall displaying framed documents, lit by a patch of sunlight, while another older adult wearing a cap stands nearby facing them.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-14.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Members gather in the main hallway at the Culver City Senior Center in 2025. “Even those that are recluse, all of us have a longing, different degrees of longing to belong and to be connected,” said Elena Portacolone, professor of sociology at the Institute for Health and Aging at UCSF. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![An older adult stands behind a pass-through counter in a community room kitchen, surrounded by coffee makers, snacks, and paper goods, while a television plays on a small table nearby.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-15.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

A member gathers food at the Watts Senior Center in Los Angeles in November 2025. “They have their homes. And our senior citizen centers are the second home,” said Leslie Richter, former supervisor for the Department of Recreation and Parks through the City of Los Angeles, which operates 29 senior centers in the city. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![An older adult wearing a knit cap stands between parked cars in a sunlit lot, smiling while holding a small paddle and keys beside an open car door.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-16.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Gina Clewly, 85, stands next to her car with a ping pong paddle at the Culver City Senior Center. Gina drives from Beverly Hills to Culver City multiple times per week to play ping pong. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![Four older adults sit around a table playing a tile game inside a community room while another older adult stands outside the window with a walker, looking in.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-17.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Macau Chen, 87, arrives in the morning to play Maj-Jong at the Culver City Senior Center. Macau speaks Cantonese only and has found community amongst the Maj-Jong players who sometimes spent eight hours at the senior center playing with other members in the hallways. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

  

**First:** Manon Levenberg, 85, attends a yoga class at the Culver City Senior Center. Manon has been practicing yoga for 30 years. “The yoga classes that are not in a senior citizens center are geared to a different demographic. The younger groups are just not a fit for me,” said Manon. “I think people are much more aware of fitness and moving. The pandemic has just changed a lot for people. I think a lot has been positive.” She cites loneliness and loss of friends as reasons that pushed her to seek out the center. **Last:** Rosalie Ranola, 79, participates in a Tai-Chi class. Photos by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![Two older adults sit closely together at a table in a community room, smiling and leaning in as one wraps an arm around the other’s shoulder, while several others sit nearby with trays of food and drinks.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-20.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Members of the Westchester Senior Center interact during lunch in Los Angeles. “We wanted to find new friends,” said Andrew Wong, 86, who became a member after the pandemic. Andrew and his wife attend both the Westchester Senior Center and the Culver City Senior Center. He was motivated to join, so he could also take an iPhone education class. “At my age, it’s hard to learn.” Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![Several handwritten name tags in plastic sleeves are arranged on a wooden surface, labeled with names such as Petra, Martin, Carolina, Pat, Nena, Lisa, Tony, and Leila.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-21.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Name tags at the Tehachapi Senior Center in Tehachapi. “It gives people something to do. A lot of seniors here have lost loved ones,” said Lewis Brown, who has been the center director since 2014. “Their kids don’t live in Tehachapi. You come here to socialize. And exercise and have a hot lunch.” Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![A handler wearing a glove steadies a large hawk as it flaps its wings near their face, while a smiling older adult in a sun hat watches closely. A crowd of adults and children stands nearby observing the demonstration outside a building.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-22.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Edgar Burns, 96, attends a fair at the Getty Center in Los Angeles in 2023 during the first outing with the Westchester Senior Center since the pandemic shutdown. For some older adults, transportation to and from the center to cultural and artistic events allows them to get out of their home with support. He continued to attend the senior center until his death in January 2025. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

  

**First:** Leonard Yee, 66, a member, sings karaoke at the Westchester Senior Center in Los Angeles. **Last:** Burns paints during a watercolor class. Senior centers offer a myriad of class and social programs, including art-making, music and current events. They also provide grief support groups. Photos by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![A group of older adults seated in a circle raise their arms overhead during a chair exercise class, while a pair of outstretched arms in the foreground frames the scene.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-25.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Members of the Tehachapi Senior Center stretch during a chair exercise class. Surveys reveal that more older adults are coming to senior centers for fitness classes since they reopened.  The volunteer run center of 200 members offers exercise, Scottish dance, line dancing, and support groups. “We are self-sufficient,” said Lewis Brown. While they use a city building, the members pay utilities and insurance through fundraiser dinners and member donations.  Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![Older adults dance and socialize in a community hall decorated with orange balloons, ghost cutouts, and Halloween banners while a DJ plays music on a small stage.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-26.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Chris Garcia, 78, dances with Eva De La Torre, 75, alongside other members of the Lincoln Heights Senior Center during a Halloween party. “I have no money, I live from Social Security” said Carmen Guerrero, 69, who became an active member of the center after she closed down her salon during the pandemic. “I want to be happy. Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

  

**First:** Laura Shroder, 89, embraces another member during karaoke at the Culver City Senior Center. “We have a bunch of people who want to get up and sing, whether they can or not. It is a way to go ahead and have the spotlight on you,” said Lee Karol, 69, a member and volunteer who has run karaoke since the center reopened. **Last:** A memorial wall for past members of the Watts Senior Center. Photos by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

  

**First:** Julie and Ed Bilow leave a Valentine’s Day party at the Culver City Senior Center in 2026. **Last:** A staff member of the Watts Senior Center decorated the main room for Christmas last year. Some older adults have limited support networks; senior centers mark holidays and allow members to celebrate their birthdays. “If it wasn’t for this place, I’d be falling apart,” said Sue Bennett during her 94th birthday party in the dining room at the Culver City Senior Center. “I have a support system here. I live alone.” Photos by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

 ![In warm sunset light, a smiling person in glasses and a scarf is blurred in the foreground while another person crosses a parking lot in the distance pulling a small rolling suitcase and carrying a tote bag.](https://i0.wp.com/calmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/NOT4FILE-021326-LA-SENIOR-PHOTO-ESSAY-IK-CM-30.jpg?resize=780%2C520&ssl=1)

Amy Valesco, 92, who lives alone, waits for her caregiver to pick her up the Culver City Senior Center after playing mahjong; another member is seen walking away in November 2025. “We are here from 9-4,” Ms. Valesco said. “This is like a second home…I’ve made a lot of friends here. It’s like a second family.” Photo by Isadora Kosofsky for CatchLight/CalMatters

args.summary: This CalMatters photo essay documents the long-term impact of COVID-19 on senior isolation in California and the vital role senior centers play in rebuilding social connections among older adults. By 2030, residents over 65 in California are expected to outnumber those under 18. Research shows social isolation poses serious risks to older adults' mental and physical health, comparable to smoking 15 cigarettes a day. The story follows Los Angeles-based photojournalist Isadora Kosofsky's multi-year documentation spanning communities including Tehachapi, Lincoln Heights, Westchester, Watts, and Culver City. Key individuals featured include Shane Shabad (90, living alone with macular degeneration in Santa Monica), Edgar Burns (93, former Mattel toy inventor who lived alone after his wife's death and returned to the Westchester Senior Center upon reopening in 2022), Sandie Shultis (76, who moved from Tehachapi to Bakersfield for medical care), and Andrew Wong (86, who joined senior centers after the pandemic to find new friends). Senior centers offer meals, wellness classes, fitness programs, grief support groups, and social spaces. The essay highlights that over 11,000 senior centers operate nationwide under the Older Americans Act, yet both older adults and the programs serving them remain underrepresented in media. The piece emphasizes that senior centers serve as "second homes" for many, with members describing them as "like a second family" and a vital support system for those who live alone.

# How did the Sudden Closures of Adult Day Services During COVID-19 Impact Dementia Care Dyads?

### Laura M Girling

### Regina L Hrybyk

Correspondence concerning this article should be addressed to Laura M. Girling, Department of Health Sciences, Towson University, 8000 York Rd., Towson, MD 21252, Lgirling@towson.edu

Issue date 2025 Oct.

## Abstract

The COVID-19 pandemic significantly disrupted daily routines across all age groups. However, the impact of the enforced closures of Adult Day Services (ADS) on dementia care dyads has received limited qualitative attention. To address this gap, data from a National Institute of Health (NIH) study (N=43) were analyzed to explore how COVID-19 impacted community-dwelling persons with dementia and their caregivers. Analyses were conducted on the subsample of caregivers (n=13) who supported a community-dwelling person with dementia who attended an ADS program at the onset of COVID-19. Findings indicate four central themes: (a) struggle to meet the needs of the person with dementia, (b) physical and cognitive decline of the person with dementia, (c) lack of time for self-care, and (d) adaptations by ADS and caregivers. This study posits that the mandated closure of ADS sites due to COVID-19 exacerbated both caregiving burden and deterioration in individuals with dementia.

## Introduction

Adult Day Services (ADS), designed for community-dwelling adults who require assistance due to disability or disease, offers a structured environment where individuals can receive medical care and engage in meaningful activities. Amid the unprecedented challenges posed by the COVID-19 pandemic, ADS sites were classified as non-essential and consequently mandated to close ([Parker, et al., 2021](#R30)). While the repercussions of these closures, on various populations, have been documented ([Sadarangani, et al., 2021](#R34); [Sadarangani, et al., 2022](#R35); [Parker, et al., 2021](#R30); [Vervaecke, et al., 2021](#R39)); there remains a paucity of information regarding the impact of ADS closures on the unique group of ADS participants diagnosed with dementia and their caregivers. Studying dementia caregivers specifically is important as challenges they face are often more intense and unique compared to those of general caregivers ([Queluz et al., 2020](#R31)). To explore how dementia dyads were impacted by ADS closures, data were drawn from an interview-based study that investigated experiences of dementia caregivers during the COVID-19 pandemic. Data were filtered by the subsample of informal caregivers who provided care to an individual with dementia who was attending an ADS program at the onset of COVID-19. Drawing on the experiences of informal caregivers, this study builds on the literature depicting the detrimental effects suspending ADS support has on the specific caregiving population of persons with dementia.

## Literature Review

### ADS & Dementia

ADS “is a system of professionally delivered, integrated, home-and community-based, therapeutic, social and health-related services provided to individuals to sustain living within the community” ([NADSA, 2024](#R25)). Data from the National Center for Health Statistics indicate that nearly one third of ADS participants have a formal diagnosis of dementia ([Harris-Kojetin et al., 2016](#R12); [Lendon & Singh, 2021](#R19)). The [National Adult Day Services Association (2024)](#R27) indicates that approximately 90% of ADS centers offer cognitive stimulation programs, and nearly 80% offer memory training. Beyond cognitive stimulation, ADS programs can offer persons with dementia a sense of belonging, providing opportunities to connect with peers and reduce social isolation.

In addition to providing support to persons with dementia, ADS programs also provide unique support to dementia caregivers. It is suggested that a major benefit of ADS programs is reducing caregivers’ exposure to care-related stressors, including behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (e.g., depression, agitation, etc.) (Bangerter et al., 2021). Likewise, utilizing ADS has been shown to improve cortisol regulation among dementia caregivers ([Klein et al., 2016](#R17)). Although findings are mixed ([Femia, et al., 2007](#R5); [Gitlin, et al., 2006](#R10); [Zarit, et al., 2001](#R42); [Parker, et al., 2021](#R30)), ADS may be most beneficial for dementia caregivers who use the services regularly and for greater durations ([Du Preez et al., 2018](#R4); [Gaugler et al., 2003](#R6)). For instance, in a recent study, regular daily ADS use appeared to benefit sleep health for older dementia care dyads by encouraging earlier and more regular sleep timing ([Liu, et al., 2022](#R22)). Similarly, when compared to a control group, caregivers who regularly used ADS for at least three months showed lower worry, strain, depressive symptoms, and anger ([Zarit, et al., 1998](#R43)). A recent randomized trial showed that when integrating an evidenced-based caregiver support programs, ADS Plus (which included dementia education, referrals, strategies for care challenges, etc.), within existing adult day programs, caregiver mood improved and increased ADS utilization by about 60% ([Reever, et al., 2024](#R32); [Gitlin, et al., 2019](#R9)).

### ADS & COVID-19

Due to COVID-19, ADS facilities throughout the country were forced to shut down abruptly, leaving families to cope with the sudden cessation of in-person services. Mandatory closures of ADS centers deprived participants of daily assistance and available amenities (e.g., meals preparation, health surveillance, social interaction), while concurrently leaving caregivers devoid of respite.

Despite closures, many ADS sites delivered or prepared food for clients (36.4%), provided telephone support (100%), offered virtual medical check-ins with a nurse or social worker (40.1%), and shared virtual activities (63.6%) ([Parker et al., 2021](#R30)). As [Sadarangani and colleagues (2022)](#R35) point out, studies that have evaluated ADS closures on older adults and their caregivers consistently show “1.) exacerbated isolation and caregiver strain, 2.) accelerated cognitive and functional declines, 3.) unsafe behaviors, 4.) increased use of care in higher-cost settings (e.g., emergency rooms and skilled nursing facilities, and 5.) limited opportunities for productive engagement among the older adults they serve.”

While these studies have provided valuable insights into the impact of ADS closures, qualitative studies have largely focused on the perspectives of formal providers including ADS staff ([Sadarangani et al., 2021](#R34)), ADS directors ([Vervaecke et al., 2021](#R39)), or groups of informal care partners supporting general populations of older adults such as those broadly categorized as having a disability ([Lightfoot et al., 2021](#R20); Naruse, 2021; [Parker et al., 2021](#R30)). Little attention has been given to dementia care dyads and how they were impacted by ADS closures. The primary purpose of this study is to expand upon the limited, qualitative inquiry in this area to explore how COVID-induced ADS closures impacted dementia dyads.

## Methods

### Sampling & Data Collection

Data for this study were drawn from an NIH-funded interview-based investigation that explored how COVID-19 impacted community-dwelling persons with dementia and their informal and formal caregivers (N=43). Participants were recruited through community outreach in a mid-Atlantic region of the United States. Eligibility criteria were: English speaking, age 18 or older, and provided either ongoing formal care (paid) or informal support to a person with dementia. Informal caregivers were defined as an unpaid person with whom the person with dementia had contact weekly and relied on for assistance in daily activities. Interviewers conducted a single tape-recorded, in-depth interview with each informant. Interviews averaged 90 minutes. Informants received a $50 honorarium for their participation.

To explore the impact of ADS closures on dementia dyads, caregivers whose dementia care recipients was not attending an ADS site at the onset of COVID-19 (n=30) were excluded. This resulted in a subsample of thirteen informal dementia caregivers whose care recipient was attending ADS at the onset of COVID-19. Sample characteristics including age, number of years the informant provided dementia care to the person with dementia (PwD), sex, race/ethnicity, and the informant’s relationship to the PwD, can be found in [Table 1](#T1).
