Specifically, the excess risk of all CVD events decreased by 29% (for loneliness) and 15% (for social isolation). The excess risk of CVD mortality decreased by 25% (for loneliness) and 52% (for social isolation), respectively., Lower baseline levels of loneliness and social isolation were associated with lower obesity-related excess risk of CVD events. Our findings call for the integration of community engagement and social support networks into existing intervention programmes to provide more effective cardiovascular care for obese individuals., Our study found that, in predicting all CVD events, loneliness ranked fourth, following closely behind BMI, HbA1c, and smoking status., Obese people face much higher degrees of loneliness and social isolation than non-obese people, owing to worries about discrimination from social prejudice and the mobility inconvenience caused by large body size., Nearly 90% of our study participants were White, which necessitates caution when generalising our findings to other ethnic groups.
args.summary:
This is a prospective cohort study published in the Journal of Global Health (2025) examining the association between loneliness/social isolation and excess cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk in people with obesity, using UK Biobank data from 432,767 participants (100,947 obese; 331,820 non-obese) followed for a median of 12.48 years.

**Key Findings:**
- Among obese individuals, 67.7% had no loneliness, 26.3% mild, and 6.1% severe loneliness; 48.9% had no social isolation, 40.6% mild, and 10.5% severe.
- A total of 29,767 non-obese and 14,312 obese participants developed CVD outcomes during follow-up.
- Obese individuals with the lowest vs. highest baseline loneliness had 29% lower excess CVD risk and 25% lower CVD mortality risk.
- Those with the lowest vs. highest baseline social isolation had 15% lower excess CVD risk and 52% lower CVD mortality risk.
- When loneliness and social isolation were at their lowest, the risk of stroke among obese individuals was not statistically significantly different from non-obese individuals.
- Among traditional risk factors for predicting CVD in obese individuals, loneliness ranked 4th (behind BMI, HbA1c, and smoking status) and social isolation ranked 8th.

**Methods:** Loneliness was assessed via a 2-item scale (index 0-2) and social isolation via a 3-item scale (index 0-3). Outcomes included coronary heart disease, stroke, heart failure, and CVD mortality. Multiple adjustments were made for sociodemographic factors, lifestyle, and health conditions.

**Conclusions:** Lower baseline loneliness and social isolation were associated with reduced obesity-related excess CVD risk. The authors call for integrating community engagement and social support networks into intervention programs for obese individuals. Limitations include the UK Biobank's healthier sample, predominantly White participants (90%), brief self-reported measures, and the inability to establish causality.

### About Risk of Social Isolation - Age 65+

**Top State(s):** Utah: 1

**Bottom State(s):** Mississippi: 100

**Definition:** Index of social isolation risk factors (living in poverty; living alone; being divorced, separated or widowed; having never married; having a disability; and having independent living difficulty) among adults age 65 and older; normalized values are 1 to 100, with a higher value indicating greater risk

**Data Source and Years(s):** U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey, 5-Year Dataset, 2020-2024

**Suggested Citation:** America's Health Rankings analysis of U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey, 5-Year Dataset, United Health Foundation, AmericasHealthRankings.org, accessed 2026.

Across the United States, nearly a [quarter](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557972/) of adults age 65 and older are at risk for social isolation. [Social isolation](https://www.cdc.gov/social-connectedness/risk-factors/index.html) is generally described as the absence of social relationships. Social isolation differs from [loneliness](https://www.cdc.gov/social-connectedness/risk-factors/index.html), which is the feeling of lacking meaningful social relationships, while social isolation addresses the objective lack of social relationships. An individual can be socially isolated and not lonely or feel lonely and not be socially isolated.

Life events such as retirement, loss of loved ones, and age-related mental and physical decline can make it difficult for older adults to [maintain social connectedness](https://www.nia.nih.gov/news/social-isolation-loneliness-older-people-pose-health-risks). Strong social networks have been shown to improve [physical](https://doi.org/10.17226/25663) and [cognitive health](https://nap.nationalacademies.org/read/25663/chapter/5#52) as well as [self-management of chronic illness](https://doi.org/10.1177%2F1090198102251030). However, many older adults go through the stressful life events common to aging without the [benefits of social support](https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/aarp_foundation/2012_PDFs/AARP-Foundation-Isolation-Framework-Report.pdf#page=21). Further [negative impacts](https://www.nia.nih.gov/news/social-isolation-loneliness-older-people-pose-health-risks) on physical health and mental well-being associated with social isolation include [increased risk](https://www.doi.org/10.1177/1745691614568352) of [mortality](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40520-024-02925-1) and higher rates of [dementia](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroscience.2025.04.019), [coronary heart disease and stroke](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.socscimed.2025.117701).

The health care costs of social isolation are comparable to those of some chronic illnesses, accounting for an estimated [$6.7 billion](https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/ppi/2017/10/medicare-spends-more-on-socially-isolated-older-adults.pdf#page=5) in Medicare expenditures annually.

[Factors that influence social isolation](https://uploads.prod01.oregon.platform-os.com/instances/542/assets/documents/Aging%20In%20The%20Shadows%202017.pdf?updated=1557158117#page=9) include race/ethnicity, immigration status, level of English proficiency, sexual orientation, gender identity, and family and community support. Older adults at greater [risk of experiencing social isolation](https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/aarp_foundation/2012_PDFs/AARP-Foundation-Isolation-Framework-Report.pdf#page=16) include:

* Those who live alone. Although not everyone who lives alone is isolated, living alone is a well-documented [risk factor](http://doi.org/10.1177/1745691614568352) for social isolation. Older adults who are divorced, widowed or separated, as well as those who never married, are therefore more vulnerable to isolation.
* Those with a disability and those who are homebound. [Physical and mobility impairments](https://www.aarp.org/content/dam/aarp/aarp_foundation/2012_PDFs/AARP-Foundation-Isolation-Framework-Report.pdf#page=16) may limit older adults’ ability to attend events or participate in activities, leading to fewer social contacts and greater loneliness.
* Those living in poverty. The effects of economic hardship on one’s time, resources and safety can pose [complex barriers](https://uploads.prod01.oregon.platform-os.com/instances/542/assets/documents/Aging%20In%20The%20Shadows%202017.pdf?updated=1557158117#page=9) to social engagement, leading to isolation.

[Interventions](https://www.maturitas.org/article/S0378-5122(18)30163-4/fulltext) to reduce social isolation among older adults are [most successful](https://doi.org/10.3390/geriatrics6030082) when they directly involve older adults rather than simply providing services or training.

* Although not appropriate for all older adults, [technology-based interventions](https://doi.org/10.2196/jmir.4596) have been used internationally to enhance communication and connectedness, particularly among those with geographical or mobility barriers.
* [Expanded collaboration](https://nationalcenterformobilitymanagement.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/FINAL_CONDENSED_SOCIAL-ISOLATION-RESEARCH-PAPER.pdf#page=15) between public transportation and public health at the community level can reduce geographical and mobility barriers for older adults.
* [Service-provision](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.maturitas.2018.04.014) interventions where volunteers act as intermediaries between older adults may help sustain short- and long-term social connectedness.

args.summary:
This webpage from America's Health Rankings presents data on "Risk of Social Isolation - Age 65+" in the United States, based on U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey data (2020-2024). The measure is an index of social isolation risk factors among adults 65+ including living in poverty, living alone, being divorced/separated/widowed, never having married, having a disability, and having independent living difficulty.

Key data points:
- The national average for independent living difficulty among adults 65+ is 13.2%.
- **Top states (lowest risk):** South Dakota (9.6%), Vermont (9.6%), Maine (9.7%), North Dakota (9.8%), New Hampshire (9.9%).
- **Bottom states (highest risk):** Mississippi (16.2%), California (16.1%), Hawaii (15.4%), Alabama (15.4%), New York (15.1%).
- The overall index range: Utah (best) at 1, Mississippi (worst) at 100.

Nearly a quarter of U.S. adults 65+ are at risk for social isolation. Social isolation differs from loneliness—it is the objective absence of social relationships rather than the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connections.

**Health impacts:** Social isolation increases risk of mortality, dementia, coronary heart disease, and stroke. Healthcare costs of social isolation account for an estimated $6.7 billion in Medicare expenditures annually.

**Risk factors include:** living alone, having a disability or being homebound, living in poverty, race/ethnicity, immigration status, English proficiency, sexual orientation/gender identity.

**Interventions:** Technology-based interventions, expanded public transportation and public health collaboration, service-provision with volunteer intermediaries, and Medicare Advantage supplemental benefits (home-delivered meals, ride-sharing, companionship). Senior and community centers are highlighted as important for group interactions.

The data appears in America's Health Rankings Senior Report (published May 2026).

# The global prevalence and associated factors of loneliness in older adults: a systematic review and meta-analysis

* [Nader Salari](#auth-Nader-Salari-Aff1)[1](#Aff1),
* [Hadi Najafi](#auth-Hadi-Najafi-Aff2)[2](#Aff2),

## Abstract

Loneliness in older adults is a major health concern in today’s world. As a phenomenon that can significantly impact the well-being and quality of individuals’ lives, the issue has received limited attention to date. This systematic review and meta-analysis aim to summarize the findings on the prevalence of loneliness and its related factors. This study is a systematic review and meta-analysis. A comprehensive literature search covering Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, EMBASE, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar was conducted from inception to March 2025. I2 statistic was employed to assess the presence of statistical heterogeneity among the studies using a random-effects model. A total of 126 studies comprising 1,250,322 older adults were included in this review. The meta-analysis found that the prevalence of loneliness among this population was 27.6%. The highest prevalence of loneliness among older adults is observed in North America, with a prevalence rate of 30.5% (95% CI: 24.7–37); older women (30.9%) and institutionalized older adults (50.7%) had the highest prevalence of loneliness. The review of 189 papers revealed important factors that were related to loneliness. In general, the findings of this research showed that almost one out of every four older people in the world feels lonely, which highlights a considerable statistic. In light of the association of loneliness with various health, clinical, and social factors, including depression, suicidal ideation, and mortality, and the anticipated rise in the older population, mental health practitioners and policymakers must develop and implement interventions aimed at alleviating loneliness among older adults.

## Background

As the number of senior citizens worldwide has increased in recent years (Najafi et al. [2024](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR179 "Najafi H, Hosseinnataj A, Esmailpour Moalem A, Ilali ES, Papi S (2024) Cross-cultural adaptation and psychometric properties of the Persian version of the Geriatric Sleep Questionnaire (P-GSQ). CRANIO® 1-11")), mental health practitioners and policymakers have given greater consideration to the concept of active and successful aging in many countries (Foster and Walker [2015](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR65 "Foster L, Walker A (2015) Active and successful aging: A European policy perspective. Gerontologist 55:183–190")). However, failing to address the needs of this population, particularly their psychological and social requirements, might jeopardize their ability to age healthily and actively by causing social isolation and loneliness (Leigh-Hunt et al. [2017](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR138 "Leigh-Hunt N, Bagguley D, Bash K, Turner V, Turnbull S, Valtorta N, Caan W (2017) An overview of systematic reviews on the public health consequences of social isolation and loneliness. Public Health 152:157–171")). Despite the significance of loneliness in old age, one of the major health issues that older people in today’s world must deal with, has received insufficient attention to date (Ogrin et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR185 "Ogrin R, Cyarto EV, Harrington KD, Haslam C, Lim MH, Golenko X, Bush M, Vadasz D, Johnstone G, Lowthian JA (2021) Loneliness in older age: What is it, why is it happening and what should we do about it in Australia? Australas J Ageing 40:2202–2207")).

According to definitions, loneliness is “the uncomfortable experience that arises when a person’s network of social relations is inadequate in a significant manner, either qualitatively or quantitatively” (Perlman and Peplau [1982](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR197 "Perlman D, Peplau LA (1982) Theoretical approaches to loneliness. Loneliness: A sourcebook of current theory. Res Ther 36:123–134")). In other words, loneliness can be described as a person’s cognitive awareness of weakness in their personal and social relationships, which might result in feelings of sadness, emptiness, or regret (Asher and Paquette [2003](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR6 "Asher SR, Paquette JA (2003) Loneliness and peer relations in childhood. Curr Dir Psychol Sci 12:375–378")). Simply put, loneliness can be defined as the inability to build and sustain fulfilling relationships with people, which leads to a sense of deprivation. Emotional and social loneliness are the two categories of loneliness. Emotional loneliness was coined by Weiss (Weiss [1975](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR257 "Weiss R (1975) Loneliness: The experience of emotional and social isolation. MIT press")) and describes a state in which individuals lack at least one social contact with whom they can share their innermost thoughts and feelings. Social loneliness is accompanied by a sense of rejection and emptiness. Certain individuals have a heightened susceptibility to emotional loneliness, while others are more susceptible to social loneliness depending on their personality traits and life circumstances. However, it is the convergence of emotional and social loneliness that results in to the most profound sensations of loneliness (Weiss [1975](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR257 "Weiss R (1975) Loneliness: The experience of emotional and social isolation. MIT press")).

Loneliness occurs in all age groups. Older adults, however, are more likely to experience it due to a variety of circumstances, including experiencing traumatic events (e.g., bereavement), retirement, loss of mobility, and suffering from physical and mental diseases (Forbes [1996](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR63 "Forbes A (1996) Caring for older people: Loneliness. BMJ 313:7053352–7053354")). While studies report that 25 to 50 per cent of individuals over 65 experience loneliness (Holt-Lunstad et al. [2015](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR97 "Holt-Lunstad J, Smith TB, Baker M, Harris T, Stephenson D (2015) Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: a meta-analytic review. Perspect Psychol Sci 10:2227–2237")), other research suggests the prevalence may exceed 70%, especially under certain conditions (Molas Tuneu et al. [2023](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR168 "Molas Tuneu M, Jerez Roig J, Minobes Molina E, Coll Planas L, Escribà i Salvans A, Farrés Godayol P, Yildirim M, Rierola Fochs S, Goutan Roura E, Bezerra de Souza DL (2023) Social and Emotional Loneliness among older people living in Nursing Homes in Spain: a cross-sectional study")). This may be attributed to a number of chronic or acute health conditions among older individuals, along with factors related to their living and housing circumstances (e.g., assisted living, nursing homes, retirement communities, living at home as a community dweller, etc.).

Loneliness can cause a range of issues, including poor general health, mental and physical issues, development of diseases, social isolation, and suicidal thoughts. Among these, depression and anxiety are two disorders that are commonly associated with chronic loneliness. Compared to their non-lonely peers, lonely older adults are 1.9 times more likely to be depressed, 1.2 times more likely to have generalized anxiety, and 1.4 times more likely to express suicidal thoughts (Theeke [2009](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR237 "Theeke LA (2009) Predictors of loneliness in US adults over age sixty-five. Arch Psychiatr Nurs 23:5387–5396")). In addition, loneliness has been linked to a drop in mobility, a decrease in the ability to handle daily living activities, and a rise in the rates of cognitive decline in older adults (Boss et al. [2015](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR17 "Boss L, Kang D-H, Branson S (2015) Loneliness and cognitive function in the older adult: a systematic review. Int Psychogeriatr 27:4541–4553")). As a general rule, feelings of emptiness, sadness, and a loss of belonging are experienced by lonely individuals. Such feelings have varying effects on social interactions, lifestyle, and overall health (Wong et al. [2016](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR262 "Wong NM, Liu H-L, Lin C, Huang C-M, Wai Y-Y, Lee S-H, Lee TM (2016) Loneliness in late-life depression: structural and functional connectivity during affective processing. Psychol Med 46:122485–122499")).

Given the different prevalence reports of loneliness in diverse studies (ranging from 25% to 70%) among older adults and the evidence that loneliness adversely affects the overall health of older adults, performing a systematic review would be beneficial. Currently, no comprehensive reviews of published research have been found on the global prevalence of loneliness and its associated factors among older adults. The existing review studies are either regional or limited (Surkalim et al. [2022](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR229 "Surkalim DL, Luo M, Eres R, Gebel K, Van Buskirk J, Bauman A, Ding D (2022) The prevalence of loneliness across 113 countries: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ 376")), such as Chawla et al.‘s study, which estimates the prevalence of loneliness among older adults in high-income countries (Chawla et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR28 "Chawla K, Kunonga TP, Stow D, Barker R, Craig D, Hanratty B (2021) Prevalence of loneliness amongst older people in high-income countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One 16:7e0255088")). As a result, this systematic review and meta-analysis aims to summarize the findings on the prevalence of loneliness and its related factors to estimate the global prevalence of loneliness in older adults.

## Methods

This study is conducted according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statements (Page et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR188 "Page MJ, McKenzie JE, Bossuyt PM, Boutron I, Hoffmann TC, Mulrow CD, Shamseer L, Tetzlaff JM, Akl EA, Brennan SE (2021) The PRISMA 2020 statement: an updated guideline for reporting systematic reviews. BMJ 372")). Accordingly, the following steps were implemented: (a) systematic search of six databases; (b) organization of articles; (c) selection of articles in line with our study’s inclusion criteria; (d) data extraction; (e) data analysis; and (f) reporting the results.

### Search strategy

Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, EMBASE, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar were the six databases selected for scientific literature searches from inception to March 2025. Free words, Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms, and the keyword sections of relevant studies (original and review papers) were searched and examined by a researcher to ensure that all the necessary keywords were included. A different search strategy was applied for each database, tailored to their specific requirements. A combination of keywords including prevalence, outbreak, burden, epidemiology, loneliness, lonely, older adults, old men, old women, aged, and elderly with or without a question mark is used in this study. Keywords were combined using Boolean operators of (AND) and (OR). Furthermore, relevant reference list and citations were examined and hand-searched for any further studies. Table [1](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#Tab1) displays the specific search strategy utilized for every database.

**Table 1 Search strategy for selected databases.**

### Inclusion and exclusion criteria

The inclusion criteria for this study were as follows: research with participants aged 60 years and older; no restrictions were considered for the settings of older adults (living at home as a community dweller or being institutionalized); observational studies (longitudinal and cross-sectional studies) that reported the prevalence of loneliness or investigated factors related to loneliness in older adults; and only articles published in English were included in this study.

The exclusion criteria were case-control studies, interventional studies, review studies, brief reports, mixed-methods studies, duplicate articles, studies that did not provide the required and sufficient data, and studies without full text availability.

### Study selection and quality assessment

Initially, a researcher using Endnote X20 software generated a list of all the article titles and abstracts from specified databases. After eliminating duplicates, papers were independently screened by two researchers as the second phase of article selection. In this step, the researchers identified two key points: (a) all articles based on data from COVID-19 pandemic period were excluded to avoid bias in calculating the prevalence of loneliness; (b) some studies considered old age to begin at age 50 or 55, however the World Health Organization (WHO) states that old age begins at age 65 in developed countries and at age 60 in developing countries (Gorman [2017](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR78 "Gorman M (2017) Development and the rights of older people. In The ageing and development report pp 3-21 Routledge")). Therefore, we eliminated any research that defined the onset of old age as occurring before the age of 60. Using the STROBE checklist, two researchers assessed the quality of observational studies in selected articles. The STROBE guidelines consist of 22 checklist items. All three observational designs—cohort, cross-sectional, and case-control studies—share eighteen items. But, depending on the study design, the other four checklist items—items 6, 12, 14, and 15—have particular differences. It should be noted that case-control studies were not included in this analysis. We utilized a quantitative scoring method for the STROBE checklist according to Limaye et al.‘s study (Limaye et al. [2018](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR146 "Limaye D, Limaye V, Pitani RS, Fortwengel G, Sydymanov A, Otzipka C, Ziesenis P (2018) Development of a quantitative scoring method for STROBE checklist")). Every item had three quality score options: 0 (not fulfilled), 1 (fulfilled), and NA (not applicable). The maximum achievable STROBE scores were 77 and 84 for cross-sectional and cohort studies, respectively.

The adherence percentage was used as the proxy for assessing study quality, as determined by the formula:

$${Adherence\; percentage}=\frac{{Total\; STROBE\; score}}{{Maximum\; achivable\; score}}\times 100$$

Based on the resulting quality score, studies were classified into four categories: excellent (a score of greater than 85%), good (a score between 70% and 85%), fair (a score between 50% and 70%), and poor (a score less than 50%). Articles classified as “poor” were eliminated. Selected articles were entered into the data extraction process.

### Data extraction

We selected studies that provided data on the percentage or number of individuals reporting experiences of “loneliness,” irrespective of the specific scale used to measure this construct. While the method of measuring loneliness varied across studies, it was commonly reported as the frequency with which individuals experienced loneliness. Data were gathered from the selected studies on several key variables, including the country of research, year of data collection, participants’ age or age range, sample size, gender distribution, database location, number of individuals identified as “lonely”, and the various types of questionnaires used to assess loneliness. Importantly, missing values were accounted for when extracting the prevalence of loneliness in each study (the precise numbers of respondents were utilized). This review focused on studies that examined factors associated with loneliness and reported odds ratios, regression coefficients, or correlation coefficients.

### Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed using Comprehensive Meta-Analysis (Version 2) software. I2 statistic was employed to evaluate statistical heterogeneity among the studies and subsequently employed a random-effects model. The primary outcomes focused on the aggregate prevalence and 95% confidence interval (CI) of loneliness in older adults. The assessment of publication bias was conducted using Begg and Mazumdar correlation test, and funnel plots were created.

### Characteristics of articles included in meta-analysis

The quality assessment scores of the studies ranged from 50% adherence (fair quality) to higher than 85% adherence (excellent quality). 8 studies classified as “poor” with scores of below 50% were excluded. The participants, aged 60 and above, made up a total sample of 1,250,322 from studies conducted between the years 1979 and 2024. This study analyzed data on older adults across six continents, with most participants (488,811) residing in Asia and North America (482,421). The studies were conducted in 62 countries, with the United States contributing the highest number of studies (*n* = 18), followed by China (*n* = 15), and the Netherlands (*n* = 8). Five studies yielded prevalence estimates for an enormous area of Europe. Nearly all articles evaluated community-dwelling older adults, with the exception of 8 studies, which considered institutionalized older adults in settings such as nursing homes, elderly villages, and prisons. Among the total number of publications reviewed, 13 were identified as cohort studies, while the remaining were cross-sectional. ### The overall prevalence of loneliness

The review of 126 studies involving a total of 1,250,322 older individuals revealed a high level of heterogeneity (I2: 99.8) as determined by the I2 heterogeneity test. The assessment of publication bias, given the large participants sample size, was carried out using the Begg and Mazumdar correlation test. The results showed no presence of publication bias in the studies (*p* = 0.499) (Fig. [2](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#Fig2)). Consequently, the results were analyzed using the random-effects model. The meta-analysis found that the overall prevalence of loneliness in older adults was 27.6% (95% CI: 25.5–29.8) (Fig. [3](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#Fig3)). In Fig. [2](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#Fig2), based on the reported funnel, the effect size (logit event rate) is on the horizontal axis and the standard error is on the vertical axis. In meta-analyses without publication bias, the funnel plot resembles a funnel with the effect size of studies with small sample sizes and high variance at the large end. Also, the effect size of studies with large sample sizes and more minor variance at the small end of this funnel. In the middle of this funnel are studies with medium effect sizes. The symmetry of the left and right sides of the funnel plot indicates the absence of publication bias. In Fig. [3](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#Fig3) and its explanation, it should be noted that the black square in each study shows the reported prevalence of loneliness in the elderly, and the length of the line segment on which the square is located is the 95% confidence interval for the reported prevalence in each study. The diamond symbol at the end of Fig. [3](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#Fig3) also shows the prevalence worldwide for all studies.

### Factors associated with loneliness

The review of 189 papers identified key factors that were associated with loneliness (Table [6](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#Tab6)). Odds ratios, regression coefficients, and correlation coefficients between loneliness and the investigated key variables were reported by the studies. The related factors identified from the studies reviewed were categorized into the following major groups:

**Table 6 Factors associated with loneliness.**

[Full size table](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x/tables/6)

Of the one hundred and eighty-nine studies, fifty-two reported a positive and significant relationship between depressive symptoms and loneliness. In terms of marital status, twenty-four studies found significant associations between loneliness and different marital statuses. Specifically, not having a partner in three studies, widowhood in nine studies, being unmarried or single in seven studies, being divorced in three studies, and being married in one study were the associated factors. Nineteen studies indicated a significant link between living alone and loneliness. Seventeen studies suggested that poor mental or physical health/well-being status was associated with feelings of loneliness. Loneliness was significantly related to different types of frailty, including social frailty (as reported in one study), cognitive frailty (as reported in one study), and overall frailty (as reported in eight studies). With respect to gender differences, four studies identified that being female correlated with an increased risk of loneliness, whereas in two studies a positive association between being male and elevated odds of experiencing loneliness was reported. Cognitive impairment or decline (three studies) and cognitive difficulty (one study) were both associated with loneliness. Institutionalization was found to be a significant factor in three studies, indicating that greater institutionalization correlates with higher levels of loneliness. Additional associated factors included hearing impairment (three studies), anxiety (three studies), death wishes (two studies), insufficient sleep or sleep difficulty (two studies), social isolation (two studies), individualism (two studies), pain (two studies), falls and fear of falling (two studies), etc (Table [6](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#Tab6)). Thirteen articles indicated a significant correlation between health-related or overall quality of life and feelings of loneliness. Fourteen studies found that mental or physical health/well-being status was inversely related to loneliness. A cross-sectional study found that there was a negative relationship between hearing impairment and loneliness; as hearing impairment increased, loneliness decreased. The likelihood of maintaining high cognitive functioning (one study), recall and recognition (one study), and cognitive function (four studies) were associated with feelings of loneliness. According to three studies, a correlation was observed between subjective sleep quality, sleep satisfaction, and loneliness. One study found an inverse correlation between the male and an increased risk of loneliness. Four articles reported a correlation between being married and loneliness (Table [6](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#Tab6)).

## Discussion

Given the significant adverse effect of loneliness on the health and well-being of older individuals, there is an increasing number of studies suggesting that prioritizing the address of loneliness is essential for public health (Jeste et al. [2020](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR109 "Jeste DV, Lee EE, Cacioppo S (2020) Battling the modern behavioral epidemic of loneliness: suggestions for research and interventions. JAMA Psychiatry 77:6553–6554")). Based on the results of the meta-analysis in this study, the global prevalence of loneliness in older adults in the age range of 60 to 110 was reported to be 27.6%, suggesting that approximately one in four older people experience feelings of loneliness. The findings of Chawla et al.‘s study revealed that the pooled prevalence rate of loneliness among older adults in high-income countries was 28.5%, which is consistent with our findings (Chawla et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR28 "Chawla K, Kunonga TP, Stow D, Barker R, Craig D, Hanratty B (2021) Prevalence of loneliness amongst older people in high-income countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One 16:7e0255088")).

Based on the results of the meta-analysis conducted in this study, it was reported that the highest prevalence of loneliness among older adults was in North America at a rate of 30.5%, and Africa recorded the lowest prevalence of loneliness at 15.3%. In the explanation of this report, the most likely issue is social life in Africa in the form of different ethnicities increasing urbanization and the development of activity on social networks in North America.

Surkalim et al. conducted research to ascertain the prevalence of loneliness in various age groups (14). The prevalence of loneliness was reported to be 5.3% for young adults (18-29 years) and 6.9% for middle aged adults (30-59 years). Young and middle-aged adults had a reduced prevalence rate compared to older adults in our analysis. This can be attributed to the likelihood that older people are more prone to develop physical and mental diseases as a result of age-related changes and restrictions. For instance, Activities of Daily Living (ADL) are established indicators of functional limitations in older individuals. A study conducted by Liu et al. demonstrated that older adults with restricted ADL had a higher likelihood of experiencing depressive symptoms, even when confounding variables were taken into account (H. Liu et al. [2023](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR153 "Liu Y, Xu Y, Yang X, Miao G, Wu Y, Yang S (2023) The prevalence of anxiety and its key influencing factors among the elderly in China. Front Psychiatry 14:1038049")). It appears that relying on others to meet one’s basic needs may contribute to mental health issues, such as feelings of loneliness (Hacihasanoğlu et al. [2012](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR85 "Hacihasanoğlu R, Yildirim A, Karakurt P (2012) Loneliness in elderly individuals, level of dependence in activities of daily living (ADL) and influential factors. Arch Gerontol Geriatr 54:161–166")).

The results of the present study suggested that women had a higher prevalence of loneliness compared to men. Consistent with our findings, previous research revealed that compared to men, women have significantly more chronic diseases (Marengoni et al. [2008](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR160 "Marengoni A, Winblad B, Karp A, Fratiglioni L (2008) Prevalence of chronic diseases and multimorbidity among the elderly population in Sweden. Am J Public Health 98:71198–71200")) and are more at risk of suffering from disorders such as loneliness (Musich et al. [2015](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR176 "Musich S, Wang SS, Hawkins K, Yeh CS (2015) The impact of loneliness on quality of life and patient satisfaction among older, sicker adults. Gerontol Geriatr Med 1:2333721415582119")) and depression (Van de Velde et al. [2010](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR247 "Van de Velde S, Bracke P, Levecque K (2010) Gender differences in depression in 23 European countries. Cross-national variation in the gender gap in depression. Soc Sci Med 71:2305–2313")), resulting in a lower quality of life (K. H. Lee et al. [2020](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR135 "Lee KH, Xu H, Wu B (2020) Gender differences in quality of life among community-dwelling older adults in low-and middle-income countries: results from the Study on global AGEing and adult health (SAGE). BMC Public Health 20:1–10")). According to the results of this study, the prevalence of loneliness among elderly women is 30.9%, compared to the prevalence of loneliness in men, which is 24.2%. This increase can be explained by the expansion of gender role expectations in women, their increased activities as head of the family, increased occupational activities, and as a result, their socialization, as well as experiences related to married life and the increase in divorce or widowhood rates.

Loneliness can occur at any time during old age and is often associated with a range of losses, such as transitioning to long-term care facilities like nursing homes (Molas Tuneu et al. [2023](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR168 "Molas Tuneu M, Jerez Roig J, Minobes Molina E, Coll Planas L, Escribà i Salvans A, Farrés Godayol P, Yildirim M, Rierola Fochs S, Goutan Roura E, Bezerra de Souza DL (2023) Social and Emotional Loneliness among older people living in Nursing Homes in Spain: a cross-sectional study")). Loneliness has been frequently identified as a common concern in long-term care settings, according to numerous studies (Golden, Conroy, & Lawlor [2009](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR77 "Golden J, Conroy RM, Lawlor BA (2009) Social support network structure in older people: Underlying dimensions and association with psychological and physical health. Psychol Health Med 14:3280–3290"); Slettebø [2008](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR219 "Slettebø Å (2008) Safe, but lonely: Living in a nursing home. V ård i Nord 28:122–125")). Furthermore, research indicates that, compared to older adults who live in communities, those who are institutionalized have a higher prevalence of loneliness (Nägga et al. [2012](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR178 "Nägga K, Dong H-J, Marcusson J, Skoglund SO, Wressle E (2012) Health-related factors associated with hospitalization for old people: comparisons of elderly aged 85 in a population cohort study. Arch Gerontol Geriatr 54:2391–2397"); Prieto-Flores et al. [2011](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR202 "Prieto-Flores M-E, Forjaz MJ, Fernandez-Mayoralas G, Rojo-Perez F, Martinez-Martin P (2011) Factors associated with loneliness of noninstitutionalized and institutionalized older adults. J Aging Health 23:1177–1194")), which is in line with our results. One possible explanation is that older people may be affected by changes in their daily lives when they enter a long-term care facility, potentially leading to mental disorders such as feelings of loneliness, depression, and anxiety (Vasilopoulos et al. [2018](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR248 "Vasilopoulos A, Marinou S, Rammou M, Sotiropoulou P, Roupa Z, Siamaga E (2018) A research on anxiety and depression of the elderly in the community. HJNS 11:359–366")). For instance, a reduced frequency of communication with loved ones, as well as the feeling of being forced to share a room with other older adults, could affect one’s level of closeness and intensify the feelings of loneliness (Trybusińska and Saracen [2019](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR242 "Trybusińska D, Saracen A (2019) Loneliness in the context of quality of life of nursing home residents. Open Med 14:1354–1361")).

According to the findings of Chawla et al.‘s study, the prevalence of loneliness among older people was highest in Eastern Europe and Mediterranean countries and lowest in Northern European countries (Chawla et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR28 "Chawla K, Kunonga TP, Stow D, Barker R, Craig D, Hanratty B (2021) Prevalence of loneliness amongst older people in high-income countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis. PLoS One 16:7e0255088")). Similarly, Surkalim et al. found that, among 40 countries under review, the lowest pooled prevalence of loneliness was found in northern European countries (5.2%), followed by western Europe (8.7%), and southern Europe (15.7%), while eastern European countries had the highest prevalence of loneliness (21.3%) (Surkalim et al. [2022](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR229 "Surkalim DL, Luo M, Eres R, Gebel K, Van Buskirk J, Bauman A, Ding D (2022) The prevalence of loneliness across 113 countries: systematic review and meta-analysis. BMJ 376")). On the other hand, our findings showed that North America exhibited the highest prevalence of loneliness among older individuals (30.5%), followed by Asia (27.9%), Europe (27.2%), and Oceania (25.7%). Africa had the lowest prevalence rate (15.3%). The prevalence disparities in the studies can be attributed to several factors, such as the inclusion of different studies and the utilization of diverse scales to measure loneliness across the studies.

### Factors associated with loneliness

A variety of associated factors were identified, with the most important ones summarized below:

### Depression

The association between depression and loneliness is well-documented. Lee et al. conducted a longitudinal study by collecting data from older individuals in the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing (ELSA) over 13 years, from 2004 to 2017. The data was collected in seven waves, each occurring every two years (Lee et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR136 "Lee SL, Pearce E, Ajnakina O, Johnson S, Lewis G, Mann F, Pitman A, Solmi F, Sommerlad A, Steptoe A (2021) The association between loneliness and depressive symptoms among adults aged 50 years and older: a 12-year population-based cohort study. Lancet Psychiatry 8:148–157")). There was a positive correlation between a one-point increase in the loneliness score and a 0.16 increase in the severity of depressive symptoms. Depression has been linked to the formation of negative self-beliefs, which can lead to loneliness. In addition, experiences including companionship, a sense of belonging, and meaningful communication are satisfying. Conversely, a decrease in experiencing those satisfactions has been linked to depression (Lewis et al. [2017](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR139 "Lewis G, Kounali DZ, Button K, Duffy L, Wiles N, Munafò M, Harmer C, Lewis G (2017) Variation in the recall of socially rewarding information and depressive symptom severity: a prospective cohort study. Acta Psychiatr Scand 135:5489–5498")). As a result, interventions aimed at mitigating loneliness may be able to prevent or lessen depression in older persons, which is a global public health concern. Also, the results of a study conducted by Erzen et al. on loneliness and depression show that loneliness has a moderate effect on depression, and it can be said that loneliness is a significant variable affecting depression (282).

### Cognitive decline and dementia

The chronic feelings of loneliness could pose a danger to the development of neurocognitive dysfunction. Both temporary and chronic loneliness could lead to cognitive decline, according to several Chinese studies, while the effects of chronic loneliness are more significant (Zhong et al. [2016](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR277 "Zhong B-L, Chen S-L, Conwell Y (2016) Effects of transient versus chronic loneliness on cognitive function in older adults: Findings from the Chinese Longitudinal Healthy Longevity Survey. Am J Geriatr Psychiatry 24:5389–5398")). The association could be elucidated by variations in neurobiological mechanisms among those populations. Numerous studies are currently exploring and uncovering novel facets of the correlation between loneliness and dementia. There is currently no conclusive evidence on whether loneliness affects dementia or vice versa. Neurobiological and molecular investigations are essential for a more comprehensive understanding of the complex mechanisms connecting loneliness and dementia.

### Quality of Life

It is well known that loneliness has a negative impact on older adults’ mental and physical well-being (Williams‐Farrelly et al. [2024](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR261 "Williams‐Farrelly MM, Schroeder MW, Li C, Perkins AJ, Bakas T, Head KJ, Boustani M, Fowler NR (2024) Loneliness in older primary care patients and its relationship to physical and mental health‐related quality of life. J Am Geriatr Soc 72:3811–3821")). Individuals experiencing loneliness are more likely to engage in behaviors that lead to negative health consequences. All these issues have the potential to contribute to and diminish the quality of life for older people.

### Gender

Scholars have long debated which gender experiences more loneliness, with contrasting findings. Nevertheless, it appears that the prevailing evidence suggests a higher prevalence among females. Among the studies examined in this review, three studies identified a link between being male and experiencing loneliness (Barreto et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR11 "Barreto M, Victor C, Hammond C, Eccles A, Richins MT, Qualter P (2021) Loneliness around the world: Age, gender, and cultural differences in loneliness. Pers Individ Differ 169:110066"); Dahlberg and McKee [2014](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR42 "Dahlberg L, McKee KJ (2014) Correlates of social and emotional loneliness in older people: evidence from an English community study. Aging Ment Health 18:4504–4514"); P.-H. Huang et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR102 "Huang AR, Deal JA, Rebok GW, Pinto JM, Waite L, Lin FR (2021) Hearing impairment and loneliness in older adults in the United States. J Appl Gerontol 40:101366–101371")). On the other hand, four studies indicated that females were more susceptible to feelings of loneliness (Cohen-Mansfield et al. [2009](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR36 "Cohen-Mansfield J, Shmotkin D, Goldberg S (2009) Loneliness in old age: longitudinal changes and their determinants in an Israeli sample. Int Psychogeriatr 21:61160–61170"); Gale et al. [2018](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR68 "Gale CR, Westbury L, Cooper C (2018) Social isolation and loneliness as risk factors for the progression of frailty: the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing. Age Ageing 47:3392–3397"); Gao et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR71 "Gao Q, Prina AM, Prince M, Acosta D, Luisa Sosa A, Guerra M, Huang Y, Jimenez-Velazquez IZ, Llibre Rodriguez JJ, Salas A (2021) Loneliness among older adults in Latin America, China, and India: prevalence, correlates and association with mortality. [2015](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR176 "Musich S, Wang SS, Hawkins K, Yeh CS (2015) The impact of loneliness on quality of life and patient satisfaction among older, sicker adults. Gerontol Geriatr Med 1:2333721415582119")). As discussed earlier in the third paragraph, given the greater prevalence of chronic diseases and mental disorders among women, it is anticipated that the experience of loneliness, which is a factor contributing to individuals’ mental state, is also more prevalent among women compared to men. This is while Maes et al. report in their study that loneliness is a universal phenomenon and their results show that men and women are very similar in terms of average levels of loneliness across a wide range of different contexts (283).

### Marital status

In this review, twenty-eight studies evaluated loneliness by marital status. Except for one study, the findings of the rest indicated that being in a relationship, being married, or not being single, divorced, or widowed was associated with lower loneliness. However, the results of Hajek et al.’s study indicated that being married was positively correlated with loneliness, which is unexpected and contradicts earlier research (Hajek, Zwar, et al. [2024](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR88 "Hajek A, Zwar L, Gyasi RM, Kretzler B, König H-H (2024) Prevalence and determinants of loneliness among the oldest old living in institutionalized settings: Study findings from a representative survey. Z Gerontol Geriatr 57:3214–3219")). According to Jones et al.‘s study loneliness is most prevalent in subjects who had experienced widowhood, relatively less common in single people, and much less common in married people (Jones et al. [1985](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR111 "Jones DA, Victor CR, Vetter NJ (1985) The problem of loneliness in the elderly in the community: characteristics of those who are lonely and the factors related to loneliness. Br J Gen Pr 35:272136–272139")).

### Age

Several studies indicated a direct correlation between age and loneliness (Jia and Yuan [2020](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR110 "Jia G, Yuan P (2020) The association between sleep quality and loneliness in rural older individuals: a cross-sectional study in Shandong Province, China. BMC Geriatr 20:1–12"); Joseph et al. [2020](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR113 "Joseph L, Nalini S, Santhi V (2020) Prevalence of loneliness and depression among elderly in South India. Indian J Public Health Res Dev 11:11361–11366"); Tijhuis et al. [1999](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR239 "Tijhuis M, De Jong-Gierveld J, Feskens E, Kromhout D (1999) Changes in and factors related to loneliness in older men. The Zutphen Elderly Study. Age Ageing 28:5491–5495")), meaning that as age increases, so does loneliness; however, other studies have documented contradictory findings, indicating that age is inversely correlated with loneliness (Barreto et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR11 "Barreto M, Victor C, Hammond C, Eccles A, Richins MT, Qualter P (2021) Loneliness around the world: Age, gender, and cultural differences in loneliness. Pers Individ Differ 169:110066"); Liu et al. [2020](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR151 "Liu T, Lu S, Leung DK, Sze LC, Kwok WW, Tang JY, Luo H, Lum TY, Wong GH (2020) Adapting the UCLA 3-item loneliness scale for community-based depressive symptoms screening interview among older Chinese: a cross-sectional study. BMJ Open 10:12e041921")). Accordingly, a study by Yang et al. reports that while loneliness is widely seen as a problem of old age, there is some evidence that adolescence is the peak age for experiencing loneliness, and there are also differences between countries in reported levels of loneliness. The study reports that the prevalence of loneliness increases with age for the combined sample. However, the country in which a person lives may have a greater influence than age on reported levels of loneliness, with Russia and Eastern European countries having the highest proportions of lonely people and Northern European countries having the lowest proportions (284).

Thus, the results are inconsistent, necessitating more research with a larger sample size. Nevertheless, it makes sense to believe that loneliness may be more closely linked to aging, given the numerous adverse changes that occur with ageing, such as losing source of income, being apart from children, and losing friends and loved ones to death (Hazer and Boylu [2010](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR91 "Hazer O, Boylu AA (2010) The examination of the factors affecting the feeling of loneliness of the elderly. Procedia Soc Behav Sci 9:2083–2089")).

A significant finding was that while research indicates that there is a positive correlation between hearing complaints or impairments and feelings of loneliness (A. R. Huang et al. [2021](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR102 "Huang AR, Deal JA, Rebok GW, Pinto JM, Waite L, Lin FR (2021) Hearing impairment and loneliness in older adults in the United States. J Appl Gerontol 40:101366–101371")), a study conducted by van Blijswijket al. presents contrary results. Their findings show that hearing problems were correlated with a reduced sense of loneliness (van Blijswijk et al. [2015](/articles/s41599-025-05304-x#ref-CR246 "van Blijswijk SC, Chan OYA, van Houwelingen AH, Gussekloo J, den Elzen WP, Blom JW (2015) Self-reported hindering health complaints of community-dwelling older persons: a cross-sectional study. PLoS One 10:11e0142416")). The authors explained that this was the result of multiple tests leading to coincidental findings.

### Limitations

We might have overlooked some relevant studies due to our inclusion criteria, which restricted the review to only English-language publications. However, the findings are not expected to be significantly altered, given the substantial number of articles included in the meta-analysis. This study exclusively examined literature regarding the presence or absence of loneliness in older adults, while it remained unclear how intensely they experienced loneliness. Due to the time frame used to review studies and collect them from the reviewed databases, it was not possible to include newer studies based on this time limit. This study reports that 67 studies used a single-item questionnaire to investigate the prevalence of loneliness in the elderly, while other studies used a multi-item questionnaire. This is another limitation of this study that could affect the prevalence results and needs to be addressed in future studies. Therefore, it is suggested that future research in this field should focus more on cultural aspects and the effectiveness of cultural and social interventions in reducing feelings of loneliness in the elderly.

args.summary:
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (April 2025) examining the global prevalence and associated factors of loneliness in older adults. A comprehensive search of six databases (Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, EMBASE, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar) from inception to March 2025 identified 126 studies involving 1,250,322 older adults (aged 60+).

**Key Findings:**
- **Global prevalence of loneliness: 27.6%** (95% CI: 25.5–29.8) — approximately one in four older adults
- **By continent:** North America highest (30.5%), followed by Asia (27.9%), Europe (27.2%), Oceania (25.7%), and Africa lowest (15.3%)
- **By gender:** Women (30.9%) had higher prevalence than men (24.2%)
- **By setting:** Institutionalized older adults (nursing homes, etc.) had 50.7% prevalence vs. community-dwelling
- Studies from 62 countries; US (18 studies), China (15), and Netherlands (8) contributed most
- Most common measurement tools: single-item questionnaire (67 studies), UCLA Loneliness Scale (35 studies), De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale (13 studies)

**Associated Factors (from 189 papers):**
- Strong positive associations: depression (52 studies), widowhood/being unmarried/divorced (24 studies), living alone (19 studies), poor health/well-being (17 studies), frailty (10 studies)
- Additional factors: cognitive impairment, institutionalization, hearing impairment, anxiety, sleep difficulties, social isolation, pain, falls
- Inverse associations: good quality of life, being married, higher cognitive function, better sleep quality

The authors note that loneliness is linked to depression, suicidal ideation, and mortality, and recommend that policymakers develop interventions to alleviate loneliness among older adults. Study limitations include restriction to English-language publications and reliance on single-item questionnaires in many studies.

![Image 2: out the window woman staring ](https://www.michiganmedicine.org/sites/default/files/styles/article_main_image/public/2024-12/woman-staring-out-window.jpg.jpg?h=f0fb51a5&itok=jCESOEyk)

Getty Images

Loneliness and isolation among older Americans have mostly returned to pre-pandemic rates, but that still means[more than one third of people age 50 to 80 feel lonely, and nearly as many feel isolated](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/10.1001/jama.2024.23213?guestAccessKey=6cc10a4c-125a-45c4-aef8-6869c2776dd6&utm_source=For_The_Media&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=ftm_links&utm_content=tfl&utm_term=120924), a national study shows.

And some older adults – especially those dealing with major physical health or mental health issues – still have much higher rates of loneliness and social isolation than others.

The findings, from a review of six years of data from the[National Poll on Healthy Aging](https://www.healthyagingpoll.org/), are published in _JAMA_ by a team from the University of Michigan[Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation](https://ihpi.umich.edu/).

Starting in 2018, and most recently earlier this year, the poll asked older adults nationwide how often they’d felt they lacked companionship (the subjective feeling of being alone, or loneliness), and felt isolated from others (the experience of social isolation).

The poll is supported by AARP and Michigan Medicine, U-M’s academic medical center.

The latest data show that in 2024, 33% of older adults felt lonely some of the time or often in the past year, about the same as the rate in 2018 (34%).

During the years in between, as many as 42% of older adults had this level of loneliness.

Similarly, 29% of older adults said they felt isolated some of the time or often in 2024, just above the rate of 27% seen in 2018.

During the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, 56% of older adults said they had experienced this level of isolation, but the rate has declined each year since.

![Image 3: in the past year feeling of loneliness were higher among adults age 50-80 reporting fair or poor health and those not working or on disability infographic moving](https://www.michiganmedicine.org/sites/default/files/2024-12/infographic_loneliness-among-groups.gif)

 Credit: IHPI 

“At the surface, this might seem like great news, that we’re back to where we were before COVID-19 struck. But that baseline was not good, and it was especially bad for some groups of older adults, who continue to have very high rates of loneliness and social isolation,” said Preeti Malani, M.D., MSJ, the study’s lead author and a professor of internal medicine at the U-M Medical School.

“One of the biggest differences now is that we have greater recognition of the impact of loneliness and isolation on health especially as we age.”

Malani serves as senior advisor to the poll, which she directed from 2017 to 2022.

The groups of older adults with the highest rates of loneliness in 2024 were:

*   Those who said their mental health is fair or poor: 75% (in 2018, it was 74%)
*   Those who said their physical health is fair or poor: 53% (up from 50% in 2018)
*   Those who were not working or received disability income (does not include retirees): 52% (up from 38% in 2018)

The groups with the highest rates of social isolation in 2024 were:

*   Those who said their mental health is fair or poor: 77% (up slightly from 79% in 2018)
*   Those who said their physical health is fair or poor: 52% (up from 43% in 2018)
*   Those who were not working or received disability income (does not include retirees): 50% (up from 36% in 2018)

These rates for 2024 are double, or even more, the rates of loneliness and isolation seen among older adults who said their physical health or mental health were excellent, very good or good, or those who were working or retired.

![Image 4: changes in feelings of social isolation among adults age 50-80, 2018-2024 moving infographic](https://www.michiganmedicine.org/sites/default/files/2024-12/trends-in-isolation_moving_infographic.gif)

 Credit: IHPI 

“These trends make it clear: clinicians should see loneliness and isolation as a key factor in their patients’ lives, especially those with serious physical or mental health conditions,” said poll director Jeffrey Kullgren, M.D., M.P.H., M.S., an associate professor of internal medicine at U-M and primary care clinician at the VA Ann Arbor Healthcare System.

“We should consider screening our patients for these issues and connecting them with resources in their communities, whether that’s a senior center, Veterans’ groups, volunteering opportunities, or services offered by an Area Agency on Aging or other community organizations,” he said.

### **Other key findings**

In general, adults age 50 to 64 were more likely than those age 65 to 80 to say they felt lonely or isolated across all poll years, and rates had not dropped back to pre-pandemic rates for those age 50 to 64 in 2024.

Similarly, those with household incomes below $60,000, and those who live alone, were more likely to say they sometimes or often felt lonely or isolated than those with higher incomes or those living with others, a finding that was consistent across most years.

However, rates in 2024 for those who live alone were lower than for those who live with others.

### **More about loneliness and isolation in older adults**

The new study builds upon the evidence collected by United States Surgeon General Vivek Murthy, M.D., M.B.A. and his team and published in an[official advisory](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf) in May 2023.

The AARP Foundation has created an initiative called [Connect2Affect](https://connect2affect.org/), offering resources to help older adults combat social isolation and loneliness for themselves and others.

Malani and colleagues published a [Patient Page in _JAMA_ on social isolation](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/10.1001/jama.2024.23213) in May 2024; it’s available for free and is designed for clinicians to share with patients.

### **About the poll**

The data in the _JAMA_ paper come from six fieldings of the NPHA from 2018 to 2024, most of which asked older adults to report how often they felt a lack of companionship or felt isolated from others in the past year. The poll fielded in June 2020 asked participants to reflect on the past three months. The poll is not longitudinal – each fielding’s sample was unique. poll sample ranged in size from 2,033 to 2,563 and the organization that administers the poll changed once, beginning in 2022. Get more details about [NPHA methodology.](https://www.healthyagingpoll.org/survey-methods)

Read NPHA reports on [loneliness and isolation among older adults](https://www.healthyagingpoll.org/national-reports).

In addition to Malani and Kullgren, the authors of the new JAMA research letter are poll team members Erica Solway, Ph.D., M.S.W., M.P.H., Matthias Kirch, M.S., Dianne Singer, M.P.H., and J. Scott Roberts, Ph.D.

**Funding/disclosures:**Malani is a deputy editor at JAMA but was not involved in the review process for the article.

**Paper cited:** “Loneliness and Social Isolation Among US Older Adults, 2018-2024,” _JAMA._[DOI:10.1001/jama.2024.23213](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2819153?guestAccessKey=6cc10a4c-125a-45c4-aef8-6869c2776dd6&utm_source=For_The_Media&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=ftm_links&utm_content=tfl&utm_term=120924)

# How the U.S. — and the World — Can Help Address Loneliness and Mental Health of Older People

![Elderly man drinking from coffee cup staring out kitchen window](/sites/default/files/styles/hero_image_desktop/public/Gunja_Mental%20Health%20Older%20Adults_2191899199_3x2.png?h=4362216e&itok=dktK-kyu)

An elderly resident at home in Chatham, N.H., a small farming community on the edge of the White Mountain National Forest, December 5, 2024. Older adults in the U.S. reported the highest rates of diagnosed mental health conditions, nearly one of five, compared to one of 20 in the Netherlands. Photo: Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images

An elderly resident at home in Chatham, N.H., a small farming community on the edge of the White Mountain National Forest, December 5, 2024. Older adults in the U.S. reported the highest rates of diagnosed mental health conditions, nearly one of five, compared to one of 20 in the Netherlands. Photo: Andrew Lichtenstein/Corbis via Getty Images

![Arnav Shah](/sites/default/files/styles/bio_photo_thumb_160x160_/public/AS_670x670.jpg?itok=LWblq_Tz)

Researcher, Programs, The Commonwealth Fund

![Munira Z. Gunja](/sites/default/files/styles/bio_photo_thumb_160x160_/public/MG_670x670.jpg?itok=53NN7JXB)

Senior Researcher, Promoting International Learning and Exchange, The Commonwealth Fund

![Reggie Williams](/sites/default/files/styles/bio_photo_thumb_160x160_/public/20250917_cmwf_Reggie%20Williams%20-5-Edit-2.jpg?itok=8wGmfbek)

Senior Vice President, Promoting International Learning and Exchange; Special Advisor, Values, The Commonwealth Fund

![Arnav Shah](/sites/default/files/styles/bio_photo_thumb_160x160_/public/AS_670x670.jpg?itok=LWblq_Tz)

![Munira Z. Gunja](/sites/default/files/styles/bio_photo_thumb_160x160_/public/MG_670x670.jpg?itok=53NN7JXB)

Senior Researcher, Promoting International Learning and Exchange, The Commonwealth Fund

![Reggie Williams](/sites/default/files/styles/bio_photo_thumb_160x160_/public/20250917_cmwf_Reggie%20Williams%20-5-Edit-2.jpg?itok=8wGmfbek)

Senior Vice President, Promoting International Learning and Exchange; Special Advisor, Values, The Commonwealth Fund

New survey research shows that most older adults with an untreated mental health issue said they did not want or need mental health care, possibly indicating that stigma is an obstacle to seeking treatment

The Netherlands and the U.K. are among the countries addressing the loneliness many older people experience through home visits, staffed telephone lines, and referrals to community supports

As people get older, issues like physical frailty, cognitive decline, grief, and loneliness [can take a serious toll](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2827710?guestAccessKey=6cc10a4c-125a-45c4-aef8-6869c2776dd6&utm_source=For_The_Media&utm_medium=referral&utm_campaign=ftm_links&utm_content=tfl&utm_term=120924) on their mental health. Around the world, it is important for countries to monitor and support the emotional, psychological, and social well-being of their aging populations. New survey research from the Commonwealth Fund, looking at adults age 65 and older in the United States and nine other countries, examines why people do not get the mental health care they need.[1](#footnote1)

![chart visualization](https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/22570379/thumbnail)
![Shah_loneliness_mental_health_older_people_Exhibit_01](/sites/default/files/Shah_loneliness_mental_health_older_people_Exhibit_01.png)

The survey asked questions about mental health and specifically about diagnosed medical conditions, emotional distress, and self-reported isolation. Older adults in Australia, France, the U.S., and Canada reported the highest rates of having at least one mental health concern, with a quarter or more of people in each of these countries reporting this concern. Older adults in the U.S. reported the highest rates of diagnosed mental health conditions, nearly one of five, compared to one of 20 in the Netherlands.

Rates of self-reported emotional distress, defined as having anxiety or great sadness that it is difficult to cope with by yourself, were highest among older adults in France (25%) and Australia (24%).

Older adults are also more likely to report [loneliness and social isolation](https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/loneliness-and-social-isolation/loneliness-and-social-isolation-tips-staying-connected), which can negatively affect their [mental health and well-being](https://www.commonwealthfund.org/blog/2022/more-covid-19-fallout-social-isolation-associated-poor-health-and-emotional-distress). Around one of 20 older adults in the U.S. said they often felt isolated from others. Rates of self-reported isolation among older adults were highest in Australia (10%) and lowest in Switzerland (2%).

![scatter visualization](https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/22606369/thumbnail)
![Shah_loneliness_mental_health_older_people_Exhibit_02](/sites/default/files/Shah_loneliness_mental_health_older_people_Exhibit_02.png)

Older adults with a mental health care issue, including a diagnosed mental health condition, self-reported emotional distress, or feeling isolated from others, were asked why they did not receive mental health treatment or counseling. The most common reason — cited by more than six of 10 older adults in all surveyed countries — was not wanting or needing a health care professional, which could indicate a hesitation to seek treatment or a belief that their mental health condition did not require a health care intervention. Previous research has found that [stigma is a major obstacle](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2875324/) among older adults seeking mental health services.

In the U.S., 13 percent of older adults reported not getting mental health either because they could not afford the cost, could not find an appropriate provider, didn’t know how to find the treatment they needed, or the wait to see a professional was too long. Fewer than one of 10 older adults in all countries cited affordability and accessibility as main reasons for not receiving care.

## How Are Countries Addressing Mental Health and Loneliness in Older Adults?

For older adults, loneliness and social isolation [can increase risks](https://www.nia.nih.gov/news/social-isolation-loneliness-older-people-pose-health-risks) for both physical and mental health needs. In recent years, adults age 75 and older had the [highest suicide rate](https://www.healthaffairs.org/content/forefront/suicide-rates-high-and-rising-among-older-adults-us) among all age groups in the U.S.

Yet, many older adults with mental health issues are not seeing mental health providers because they believe they do not want or need to do so. While this could indicate that their mental health is not detracting from day-to-day well-being, these results could reveal a hesitancy to seek treatment because of ongoing stigma.

Other countries have taken a variety of approaches to address older adults’ mental health. For example:

## Using the Medicare Program to Help Older Adults’ Mental Health

Medicare, the federal program that provides health insurance for adults age 65 and older in the U.S. and younger adults with significant disabilities, [covers both outpatient and inpatient](https://www.medicare.gov/providers-services/original-medicare) mental health services as well as prescription drugs that treat mental illness. The program also covers annual depression and substance use screenings; some Medicare Advantage plans [cover additional services](https://www.kff.org/medicare/issue-brief/faqs-on-mental-health-and-substance-use-disorder-coverage-in-medicare/) like grief counseling.

Medicare payment reforms finalized for 2024 [aimed to expand access](https://www.commonwealthfund.org/blog/2024/medicare-reforms-support-behavioral-health-expanding-access-peer-support-specialists-and) to different types of behavioral health care providers. The goal of these reforms was to allow more flexibility in the types of providers that are eligible to be reimbursed and support community-based care.

However, there are still [gaps in Medicare mental health coverage](https://www.commonwealthfund.org/publications/explainer/2023/mar/medicare-mental-health-coverage-included-changed-gaps-remain). These include inpatient day limits that can impact beneficiaries with chronic mental illness, limited mental health provider networks, and a lack of coverage for serious mental health needs like psychiatric rehabilitation. Medicare beneficiaries experiencing loneliness or isolation [are more likely to report](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39892526/) poor patient–provider communication, including listening to patients, showing respect, and spending sufficient time with patients. Improving such communication could help connect people with needed mental health services.

Across countries, nearly one of five older adults, or more, reported at least one mental health issue. Without policies aimed at addressing mental health, this problem will only grow as the age-65-and-older population gets larger and is compounded for their [family members and caregivers](https://lemonadamedia.com/show/uncared-for/). Ultimately, collaborative learning among health leaders and policymakers is key to improving older adult behavioral health. We face a choice: investing in integrated care, leveraging technology, and bolstering the workforce to ensure timely, high-quality access to vital services across all settings, or failing to meet the critical needs of older adults.

A Commonwealth Fund blog post published April 16, 2025, examines mental health challenges among adults aged 65+ in the U.S. and nine other countries. Key findings from new survey research include: older adults in the U.S. reported the highest rates of diagnosed mental health conditions (nearly 1 in 5), compared to 1 in 20 in the Netherlands. Rates of self-reported emotional distress were highest in France (25%) and Australia (24%). Around 1 in 20 older adults in the U.S. said they often felt isolated. The most common reason for not seeking mental health care—cited by over 6 in 10 older adults across all surveyed countries—was not wanting or needing a healthcare professional, potentially reflecting stigma. In the U.S., 13% cited affordability or access barriers.

The article discusses how other countries address loneliness, including home visits, staffed telephone lines, and community referrals (e.g., Netherlands and U.K.). It reviews Medicare's mental health coverage, noting 2024 payment reforms aimed at expanding access to behavioral health providers, but also persistent gaps such as inpatient day limits, limited provider networks, and lack of coverage for psychiatric rehabilitation. The authors conclude that without targeted policies, the problem will grow as the 65+ population increases, and call for collaborative learning, investment in integrated care, technology, and workforce strengthening.
