# Older Americans Act Provides Assistance for Supportive Services

October 16, 2008

[Facebook](https://medicareadvocacy.org/#facebook "Facebook")[Twitter](https://medicareadvocacy.org/#twitter "Twitter")[LinkedIn](https://medicareadvocacy.org/#linkedin "LinkedIn")[Share](https://www.addtoany.com/share#url=https%3A%2F%2Fmedicareadvocacy.org%2Folder-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services%2F&title=Older%20Americans%20Act%20Provides%20Assistance%20for%20Supportive%20Services)

[![Image 1: Print Friendly, PDF & Email](https://cdn.printfriendly.com/buttons/printfriendly-pdf-email-button-notext.png)](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services# "Printer Friendly, PDF & Email")

## Introduction

Advocates assisting Medicare beneficiaries, including those who are dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid, should review the supportive services available under the Older Americans Act (OAA) for individuals in their homes or communities. The OAA includes a wide variety of services that may assist those receiving home health care under Medicare or Medicaid. In passing the OAA in 1965, Congress sought to provide assistance to older Americans through supportive social services while maintaining the participants' "maximum independence and dignity in a home environment."[[1]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn1 "Endnote") The OAA is administered nationally by the Assistant Secretary for Aging of the Department of Health and Human Services. The Assistant Secretary for Aging heads the office of the United States Administration on Aging. A major function of the Administration on Aging is to provide funds to designated State Units on Aging which in turn distribute funds to Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs). Together, State and Area Agencies on Aging develop and implement systems for the delivery of services. Each state is responsible for the creation of social services programs suited to its residents' needs.[[2]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn2 "Endnote") Because each state receives funding proportional to its population of older individuals,[[3]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn3 "Endnote") programs and services differ from state to state.

## Eligibility

To be eligible for services funded by the Older Americans Act, program participants must be 60 years old or older[[4]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn4 "Endnote") and must be in greatest social or economic need.[[5]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn5 "Endnote") These eligibility factors have been a source of confusion to programs. To address this confusion, Congress has clarified that while serving the general population of persons 60 years of age and older, OAA-funded programs have a mandate to identify and target low-income minority individuals suffering from physical and mental disabilities, language barriers, or those who are racially, ethnically, culturally, or geographically isolated.[[6]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn6 "Endnote")

Congress has clarified that the economic need aspect of eligibility is not defined by "means-testing." Rather, program participants may be encouraged to make voluntary contributions toward services and providers have the flexibility to suggest a non-prohibitive contribution amount. The Older Americans Act also does not use Social Security quarters of coverage requirements as an eligibility factor. OAA programs therefore have the potential to reach a segment of the population 60 and older that does not qualify for Medicare or Medicaid services. Moreover, because eligibility does not depend on work experience, seniors with little to no work experience are still eligible to receive the benefits.

Notably, immigrants otherwise made ineligible for federal and state public benefits by the Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act (PRWORA) are also eligible for in-home care, nutrition services, and other community programs under the Older Americans Act.[[7]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn7 "Endnote")

## Programs Funded under Title III of the OAA

Title III Programs are divided into four programs: Supportive Services, Nutrition and Meals Services, Disease Prevention and Health Promotion, and the National Family Caregiver Support Program.

A. Supportive Services (Title III-B) Certain services deemed "priority" services under the Act must be funded annually. These include:

*   Legal assistance;
*   Access to services (transportation, outreach, information and assistance, and case management services); and
*   In-home services (homemaker and home health aides, visiting and telephone reassurance, chore maintenance).[[8]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn8 "Endnote")

Consequently, these services are most prevalent. Other optional programs may be offered, including such services as health screening, education and training; transportation services; and minor residential repair and renovation projects designed to adapt homes to the needs of older individuals.[[9]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn9 "Endnote") Additionally, states may have programs providing advice on financial planning for retirement, programs designed to prevent institutionalization, and investigations into nursing home abuse.

Title III-B Supportive services also include special provisions for "Frail Older Americans" and their caregivers. These programs are designed to assist individuals who are unable to perform at least two activities of daily living (ADLs) without substantial human assistance[[10]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn10 "Endnote") Services may include chore maintenance and the assistance of homemakers or home health aides.[[11]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn11 "Endnote") Notably, older Americans with Alzheimer's disease and related neurological disorders are specifically mentioned as intended beneficiaries.

B. Nutrition and Meals Services (Title III-C)

State and local programs also receive funding under Title III-C to provide older Americans with Nutrition and Meals services. Title III-C requires that programs be established to deliver meals to adult day care centers and also to seniors residing at home.[[12]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn12 "Endnote") All state and local programs receiving funding are generally required to deliver at least one meal per day, five days a week to program participants.[[13]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn13 "Endnote")

The Nutrition programs are a valuable resource for several reasons. The programs reach a variety of people, many of whom may not be Medicare and/or Medicaid beneficiaries, thus widening the scope of people eligible to participate. Because states are permitted to arrange for the delivery of meals to "multigenerational meal sites," disabled individuals under 65 residing in housing primarily serving the elderly are eligible to participate in the meals programs.[[14]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn14 "Endnote") In addition, spouses of older Americans already participating in meals programs are themselves eligible to participate and receive home-delivered meals regardless of their age or condition.[[15]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn15 "Endnote") Finally, the meals programs ensure good nutrition. Title III requires that the meals meet federal dietary guidelines. Providers are encouraged to serve modified meals (low fat, low sodium, or low calorie) upon request to meet the needs of program participants,[[16]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn16 "Endnote") and many state and local programs offer nutritional education services or counseling.[[17]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn17 "Endnote")

C. Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (Title III-D)

The Older Americans Act also provides states with money to be used for disease prevention and health promotion. Specifically, state agencies and local organizations may use money from Title III-D grants for health screening, education and training, and individual health counseling. States are directed to provide these services at senior centers, in connection with meal delivery programs at congregate meal sites, or through the home delivery meal program.[[18]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn18 "Endnote") Because states must give first priority for such programs to areas that are medically underserved,[[19]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn19 "Endnote") these services may provide important health screening tools to older Americans who other wise lack access to services.

D. National Family Caregiver Support Program (Title III-E)

Title III-E of the OAA provides funding to state and local programs to assist caregivers of older Americans in many ways. Relatives of older Americans providing in-home care qualify for supportive services.[[20]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn20 "Endnote") State and local agencies may provide caregivers with information and assistance about available services for older Americans; individual counseling and training to assist caregivers in decision making; "respite care" to provide temporary relief to caregivers of their responsibilities; and supplemental services to supplement the caregiver's activities.[[21]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftn21 "Endnote")

## Conclusion:

The programs funded under the Older Americans Act represent an array of services that may fill unmet needs. Medicare participants may benefit from the additional services provided by Title III, and individuals ineligible for Medicare or Medicaid may find the programs especially useful. Information about local services can be found by contacting a local Area Agency on Aging or the State Office on Aging. Additional information about the OAA and its services and programs is available through the Administration on Aging, at[http://www.aoa.gov/](https://www.aoa.gov/). The national elder care locator, 1-800-677-1116, is an important resource for identifying and accessing local Title III supportive services.

* * *

[[1]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref1 "Endnote") Older Americans Act of 1965, Pub. L. No. 89-73, at 3021(a)(1)(A), (codified as 42 U.S.C. § 3001-3057(n)). [[2]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref2 "Endnote") See 42 U.S.C. § 3025(a).

[[3]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref3 "Endnote") See id. at § 3024.

[[4]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref4 "Endnote") Title III programs were intended to benefit "older individuals," originally defined as individuals over age 60. 42 U.S.C. § 3022(9).

[[5]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref5 "Endnote") See 42 U.S.C. 3025(a(2)(E).

[[6]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref6 "Endnote") 42 U.S.C. 3002(30).

[[7]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref7 "Endnote") Provisions of PRWORA bar the delivery of specific types of public benefits to certain aliens residing in the United States. See 8 U.S.C. §§ 1611; 1621 (2000). As a result, non-qualified aliens and non-immigrants are generally barred from securing public benefits falling within PRWORA's statutory definitions. However, certain types of public benefits are not contemplated by PRWORA. Additionally, exceptions within the Act itself and guidance from the United States Secretary of Health and Human Services indicate that PRWORA does not, and should not be interpreted as applying to all public benefits. See 8 U.S.C. § 1621; HHS Release, 63 Fed. Reg. 41658 (August 4, 1998). The programs funded by the Older Americans Act do not fall within PRWORA's exclusion and immigrants may therefore still benefit from OAA services. See Fed. Reg. 45256 (Aug. 26, 1997).

[[8]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref8 "Endnote") 42 U.S.C. § 3027(a). [](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref9 "Endnote")

[[9]](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref9 "Endnote") See 42U.S.C. § 3030d(a). [](https://medicareadvocacy.org/older-americans-act-provides-assistance-for-supportive-services#_ftnref10 "Endnote")

args.summary:
This article from the Center for Medicare Advocacy (dated October 16, 2008) outlines the supportive services available under the Older Americans Act (OAA) for individuals aged 60 and older, particularly those who may also be eligible for Medicare or Medicaid. The OAA, passed in 1965, aims to help older Americans maintain independence and dignity in a home environment. It is administered by the Administration on Aging, which funds State Units on Aging and Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) to deliver services tailored to each state's needs.

**Eligibility:** Participants must be 60+ and in greatest social or economic need. There is no means-testing; voluntary contributions are encouraged. Notably, immigrants ineligible for other federal benefits under PRWORA can still receive OAA services. Eligibility does not depend on work history or Social Security quarters.

**Title III Programs (the core of the article):**

- **Title III-B (Supportive Services):** Priority services include legal assistance, transportation, outreach, case management, and in-home services (homemaker/home health aides, chore maintenance). Special provisions exist for "Frail Older Americans" (those unable to perform 2+ ADLs) and those with Alzheimer's disease.
- **Title III-C (Nutrition/Meals):** Provides at least one meal per day, five days a week to senior centers and homes. Meals meet federal dietary guidelines, and modified meals (low-fat, low-sodium) are available. Spouses of participants and disabled individuals under 65 in senior housing are also eligible.
- **Title III-D (Disease Prevention & Health Promotion):** Funds health screening, education, and counseling at senior centers, congregate meal sites, or via home-delivered meals. Priority is given to medically underserved areas.
- **Title III-E (National Family Caregiver Support Program):** Provides caregivers with information, counseling, training, respite care, and supplemental services.

**Conclusion:** OAA programs can fill gaps for Medicare/Medicaid beneficiaries and those otherwise ineligible. Local services can be found by contacting a local AAA, State Office on Aging, or the national elder care locator (1-800-677-1116).

# Older Americans Act Services and Providers

## Home delivered meals, congregate meals, transportation services and more...

### Title III of the Older Americans Act provides funding for supportive services, nutrition services, and family caregiver support.

### Supportive Services (III B)

Supportive services provide a range of social services aimed at helping older adults remain independent in their own homes and communities. Funds must support access to services, in-home services, and legal assistance. The program may also support other services, such as care management, adult day services, and activities of senior centers.

### Nutrition Services (III C1, C2)

The [nutrition program](/programs-services/home-delivered-and-congregate-meals/ "Meal Services") provides meals and socialization to older adults in congregate settings such as senior centers, as well as meals to frail older adults in their homes. The purpose of the program is to reduce hunger and food insecurity, promote socialization and provide meals to the homebound.

### Family Caregiver Support (IIIE)

The [Family Caregiver Support Program (FCSP)](/programs-services/family-caregiver-support/ "Family Caregiver Support") recognizes the vital role performed by informal caregivers and is authorized by Title III-E of the Older Americans Act. Its intent is to directly benefit informal, unpaid caregivers with services consistent with the Act’s mandates through a statewide, easily identifiable program that supports the efforts of caregivers.

Unlike many other programs funded and managed by WRAAA, the family caregiver is the target of this program. These services aid family caregivers to better understand their role, learn when and how to access assistance and find the services/information needed to decrease stress and better care for their loved ones.

The webpage describes Older Americans Act (OAA) services and providers managed by the Western Reserve Area Agency on Aging (WRAAA), serving Cuyahoga, Geauga, Lake, Lorain, and Medina counties. Title III of the OAA funds three main program areas:

1. **Supportive Services (III B)** – Helps older adults remain independent through access to services, in-home services, legal assistance, care management, adult day services, and senior center activities.
2. **Nutrition Services (III C1, C2)** – Provides congregate meals in senior centers and home-delivered meals to homebound older adults to reduce hunger and food insecurity.
3. **Family Caregiver Support (III E)** – Supports informal, unpaid caregivers with services to help them understand their role, access assistance, and reduce stress.

A full list of OAA services includes Adult Day Health, Adult Guardianship, Transportation, Chore Services, Homemaking, Legal Assistance, Ombudsman, Personal Care, Restaurant Vouchers, Support Groups, and more. The page provides a link to the 2026 OAA Service Providers list (Offices on Aging and Senior Centers) and contact information (800-626-7277 or 216-621-0303).

AmeriCorps Seniors

| Agency overview |
| Jurisdiction | [Federal government of the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_government_of_the_United_States "Federal government of the United States") |
| Headquarters | * [Washington, D.C.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C.") |

**AmeriCorps Seniors** is a [United States government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_government "United States government") program run by the [Corporation for National and Community Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation_for_National_and_Community_Service "Corporation for National and Community Service"). The program engages volunteers aged 55 and older to serve their communities. There are over 200,000 volunteers nationwide.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

AmeriCorps Seniors is made up of seven constituent programs—State and National, VISTA, NCCC (National Civilian Community Corps), Foster Grandparents, Retired and Senior Volunteer Program (RSVP), Senior Companions and Volunteer in Community—which were brought together under one umbrella when the [Corporation for National and Community Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation_for_National_and_Community_Service "Corporation for National and Community Service") (CNCS) was formed by then-[president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_(government_title) "President (government title)") [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") in 1993. At that time, the three programs were collectively called Senior Corps.[[2]](#cite_note-2) On September 29, 2020, CNCS announced the agency was rebranding itself as AmeriCorps, and Senior Corps was being rebranded as AmeriCorps Seniors.[[3]](#cite_note-3)

Three of the programs have unique histories, and each was developed to meet a specific need. The Foster Grandparent Program was piloted on August 28, 1965, to entice low income people over 60 in community service. The Senior Companion Program began as part of the Department of Health, Education and Welfare and Administration on Aging in 1968, and before being legislated and signed into law under President [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon"). The Retired and Senior Volunteer Program (RSVP) began as an outgrowth by private groups and government agencies to create opportunities of engagement, activity, and growth for older Americans following the work of the [Community Service Society of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_Service_Society_of_New_York "Community Service Society of New York") on [Staten Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island "Staten Island") beginning in 1965; the Society's success led the [Older Americans Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Older_Americans_Act "Older Americans Act") being amended to create RSVP as a nationwide program in 1969.

## History

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AmeriCorps_Seniors&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

Senior Corps was formed from a merge of its constituent programs: Foster Grandparents, Retired and Senior Volunteer Program (RSVP), and Senior Companions. The three were originally mandated under the [Domestic Volunteer Service Act of 1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestic_Volunteer_Service_Act_of_1973 "Domestic Volunteer Service Act of 1973") with similar aims. The three programs have unique histories, and each was developed to meet a specific need, but all were crafted on the same belief that older adults are valuable resources to their communities. When the [Corporation for National and Community Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corporation_for_National_and_Community_Service "Corporation for National and Community Service") was formed by then-[president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_(government_title) "President (government title)") [Bill Clinton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Clinton "Bill Clinton") in 1993, the three organizations were reformed into the single agency Senior Corps.

The Foster Grandparent Program was piloted on August 28, 1965, to attract low income individuals over 60 into community service. The program quickly revealed the positive impact these thriving older Americans have on exceptional and special needs children and grew in scope. In the 1980s, the Foster Grandparent Program was championed by First Lady [Nancy Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nancy_Reagan "Nancy Reagan"). She drew attention to the program and helped it grow as one of her pet projects.

In 1968, the Senior Companion Program began as part of the Department of Health, Education and Welfare and Administration on Aging. Five years later, President Richard Nixon asked Congress to expand the role of low-income older volunteers who provide personal services to others. Seven months later, the Senior Companion Program was signed into law.

RSVP began as an outgrowth by private groups and government agencies to create opportunities of engagement, activity, and growth for older Americans. One of the earliest programs, the [Community Service Society of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Community_Service_Society_of_New_York "Community Service Society of New York"), began in 1965 on [Staten Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Staten_Island "Staten Island"). The project involved a small group of volunteers who were dedicated to serving their communities in a variety of ways. It was due to the success of their efforts that led to an amendment to the [Older Americans Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Older_Americans_Act "Older Americans Act"), creating RSVP as a nationwide program in 1969.

## Programs

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AmeriCorps_Seniors&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Programs")]

Senior Corps is for [people age 55+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senior_citizen "Senior citizen") who want to share their experiences with others who are most in need of [mentors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentorship "Mentorship"), coaches, or a companion.

### Foster Grandparents

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AmeriCorps_Seniors&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Foster Grandparents")]

First operational on August 28, 1965, the Foster Grandparents program enables [seniors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senior_citizen "Senior citizen") to interact with and support young children, thus acting as [foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foster_care "Foster care") [grandparents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grandparents "Grandparents"). Open to seniors 55 and over, the program's goal is to provide "grandparents" who will give emotional support to victims of abuse and [tutor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tutor "Tutor"), [mentor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentorship "Mentorship"), and care for children with disabilities. The participants make a difference in the lives of these children, receive pre-service and monthly training sessions, transportation [reimbursement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reimbursement "Reimbursement"), an annual [physical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_examination "Physical examination"), and [accident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Accident_insurance "Accident insurance") and [liability insurance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liability_insurance "Liability insurance") while working with the child/children. Some Foster Grandparents also receive small tax-free [stipends](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stipend "Stipend") to offset costs incurred while participating in the program; eligibility for these stipends is based on income criteria.

### RSVP

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AmeriCorps_Seniors&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: RSVP")]

Much like the Foster Grandparents program, the Retired and Senior Volunteer Program (RSVP) seeks to provide a way in which senior citizens can give back to their community. Flexible in nature, RSVP allows participants to choose how and when they work. Open to seniors 55 and over, the program's goals are wide and varied, and include job training, tutoring children, building homes, helping [immunize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunization "Immunization") children, relief services, and aid to community organizations. Volunteers are given a pre-service orientation, on-the-job training from the placement agency or organization, and supplemental insurance while on duty. This program does not provide a stipend.

One of the more widespread RSVP programs is a telephone reassurance service; RSVP volunteers contact other seniors by phone to ensure their well-being and provide friendly chat.

### Senior Companions

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=AmeriCorps_Seniors&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Senior Companions")]

The Senior Companions program is aimed at helping citizens who need extra assistance to live independently, such as adults with disabilities or those with [terminal illnesses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_illness "Terminal illness") and their [caregivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caregiver "Caregiver"). Participants provide both emotional and physical support by assisting with simple house [chores](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_work "House work"), providing transportation, and offering companionship.

A senior companion must be 55 years of age and able to give between 5 and 40[[4]](#cite_note-4) hours of service per week. In addition to making a significant contribution to the lives of others, participants receive pre-service and monthly training, transportation reimbursement, an annual physical, and meals and accident and liability insurance while on duty. Income-eligible Senior Companions also receive a modest, tax-free stipend to offset the cost of volunteering.

args.summary:
**AmeriCorps Seniors** is a United States government program run by the Corporation for National and Community Service (CNCS) that engages volunteers aged 55 and older to serve their communities. The program has over 200,000 volunteers nationwide.

**History:** Originally called Senior Corps, the program was formed in 1993 under President Bill Clinton when three constituent programs—Foster Grandparents, RSVP (Retired and Senior Volunteer Program), and Senior Companions—were merged under CNCS. On September 29, 2020, CNCS rebranded itself as AmeriCorps, and Senior Corps was rebranded as AmeriCorps Seniors.

Each of the three main programs has a unique history:
- **Foster Grandparents Program:** Piloted on August 28, 1965, to attract low-income individuals over 60 into community service. In the 1980s, First Lady Nancy Reagan championed the program.
- **Senior Companion Program:** Began in 1968 under the Department of Health, Education and Welfare and Administration on Aging, signed into law under President Richard Nixon in 1973.
- **RSVP:** Originated from private groups and government agencies, including the Community Service Society of New York on Staten Island (1965). Success led to an amendment to the Older Americans Act creating RSVP as a nationwide program in 1969.

**Programs:**
- **Foster Grandparents (55+):** Seniors interact with and support young children, providing emotional support to abuse victims, tutoring, mentoring, and caring for children with disabilities. Benefits include pre-service training, transportation reimbursement, annual physical, accident/liability insurance, and some income-eligible participants receive tax-free stipends.
- **RSVP (55+):** Flexible program allowing seniors to choose how and when to volunteer. Activities include job training, tutoring, building homes, immunization help, relief services, and a widespread telephone reassurance service. No stipend provided.
- **Senior Companions (55+):** Helps adults with disabilities or terminal illnesses (and their caregivers) live independently. Provides emotional/physical support, house chores, transportation, and companionship. Requires 5–40 hours/week. Includes training, transportation reimbursement, annual physical, meals, insurance, and income-eligible tax-free stipends.

AmeriCorps, the federal agency that sponsors service, volunteering, and civic engagement provides funding and support for the 8 Maine AmeriCorps Seniors programs.

## child at table with adult helping with colors and turning pagesFoster Grandparent

Foster Grandparents devote their volunteer service entirely to disadvantaged or disabled youth. They are individuals age 55 and over who thrive on direct interaction with children and believe they can make a difference in their lives. Income-eligible Foster Grandparents receive a modest stipend to help offset the costs of volunteering.

In Maine, two programs cover the state. The Opportunity Alliance in Portland operates Foster Grandparents in York, Cumberland, and southern Oxford Counties. Penquis Community Action overs all remaining counties. Learn more about the opportunities to serve using the information below.

Penquis Foster Grandparent Program
:   **Counties served:** Androscoggin, Aroostook, Franklin, Hancock, Kennebec, Knox, Lincoln, Oxford, Penobscot, Piscataquis, Sagadahoc , Somerset , Waldo, Washington, and the town of Brunswick.

    **Primary Contact**: Maria Staples, Program Director

     262 Harlow Street, Bangor, ME 04401  
    **phone**: (207) 207-973-3611  
    **email**:mstaples@penquis.org  
    **web site**: [www.penquis.org](http://www.penquis.org/)

    The Foster Grandparent Program places volunteers 55 years of age or older in public or nonprofit settings such as schools, Head Start centers, correctional institutions, and child care centers, to serve as tutors and mentors to children and youth with special needs.  Among other activities, they review schoolwork, reinforce values, teach skills and care for infants and children with disabilities.

    Volunteers serve an average of 15-36 hours per week.  Benefits include a non-taxable stipend, mileage, paid time off, training, supervision and recognition.  Help to mobilize one of Maine's greatest resources - its seniors - to prepare our children and youth to be successful students and responsible citizens.

    For more information, contact mstaples@penquis.org or submit an inquiry on line through this [LINK](https://www.penquis.org/volunteer-opportunities/foster-grandparent-application/).

## AmeriCorps Seniors programs benefit the community, the organization, and the volunteer. Think of what you can do when you give your time to help your community.

#### Bring out the Best of America

AmeriCorps Seniors service provides tangible benefits for volunteers. The Foster Grandparent program offers modest stipends and other ways to help offset the costs of your involvement. The Retired Senior and Volunteer program offers a flexible schedule with unlimited opportunities. Other benefits include annual recognition, training, and liability insurance.

### Ready to volunteer?

## Call [(903) 813-3562](tel:903-813-3562 "If you're interested in being a part of our program or for more information, give us a call!")

![AmeriCorps Seniors](/wp-content/uploads/2017/11/senior-volunteer.png)

# Why volunteer?

* **Help your community**  
  Know that you are giving your time, talent, wisdom, and experience to your community and neighbors who need you.
* **Help yourself**  
  Through service, you can add to the quality and health of your life. Research indicates that volunteers enjoy better health, make new friendships, stay active and involved in the community, and learn new skills.
* **Make a difference**  
  Be part of a national movement to transform America through the involvement of its citizens.
* **Save money for the organizations you serve**

# AAA vs. ADRC vs. Eldercare Locator: Which to Use (2026)

Three federal front doors lead to help for an aging parent: the Eldercare Locator, your local Area Agency on Aging (AAA), and an Aging and Disability Resource Center (ADRC).

Brevy Care Team

8 min read · Published July 16, 2026 · Last verified July 16, 2026

Three federal front doors lead to help for an aging parent: the [Eldercare Locator](https://eldercare.acl.gov/home), your local [Area Agency on Aging](/caregiver/area-agencies-on-aging) (AAA), and an Aging and Disability Resource Center (ADRC). They overlap, they cost nothing to contact, and they are frequently the same phone call. If you don't know your local agency yet, start with the Eldercare Locator; connecting families to services in their community, including their local Area Agency on Aging, is exactly what it is there for.

## In This Guide

* [The Three Front Doors: Eldercare Locator, AAA, and ADRC](#the-three-front-doors-eldercare-locator-aaa-and-adrc)
* [When to Start With the Eldercare Locator](#when-to-start-with-the-eldercare-locator)
* [What Your Area Agency on Aging Actually Does](#what-your-area-agency-on-aging-actually-does)
* [What an ADRC Adds](#what-an-adrc-adds)
* [Which Door: AAA, ADRC, or Eldercare Locator?](#which-door-aaa-adrc-or-eldercare-locator)
* [Is It Free, and Who Qualifies?](#is-it-free-and-who-qualifies)
* [They're Often the Same Phone Call](#theyre-often-the-same-phone-call)
* [Frequently Asked Questions](#frequently-asked-questions)
* [Learn More](#learn-more)

## The Three Front Doors: Eldercare Locator, AAA, and ADRC

These three names get used interchangeably, but each does a distinct job. The Eldercare Locator is the national connector to services in your community. The Area Agency on Aging is the local agency that plans and delivers services. The ADRC is a state one-stop that screens you across aging and disability programs. Here is how they line up.

| Front door | What it is | Start here when | How to reach it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Eldercare Locator** | The free, nationwide public service of the [Administration for Community Living](https://acl.gov/) that connects older adults, families, and caregivers to services in their community, including the local AAA | You don't know your local aging agency and need a place to begin | Call 1-800-677-1116 (Mon to Fri, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. ET) or use eldercare.acl.gov |
| **Area Agency on Aging (AAA)** | Your state-designated local agency that plans and delivers [Older Americans Act](https://acl.gov/about-acl/authorizing-statutes/older-americans-act) services | You want the actual services: meals, transportation, a caregiver break, benefits counseling | Find yours through the Eldercare Locator or your state's aging office |
| **ADRC / No Wrong Door** | A state single entry point covering both aging and disability long-term services and supports, part of the federal [No Wrong Door](https://acl.gov/programs/connecting-people-services/aging-and-disability-resource-centers-programno-wrong-door) system | You are weighing long-term care or Medicaid options, or the person has a disability at any age | Ask for your state's ADRC, sometimes branded an "access point"; it is often the same office as your AAA |

## When to Start With the Eldercare Locator

The Eldercare Locator is the national entry point, and it is the right first call when you don't yet know which local agency serves your parent's address. It is a free, nationwide public service of the Administration for Community Living (ACL), the federal agency that funds the aging network,eldercare.acl.gov <https://eldercare.acl.gov/home> · Accessed Aug 7, 2026 and it is administered by USAging.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Area Agencies on Aging*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 13, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/area-agencies-aging> Trained staff answer at 1-800-677-1116, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern, and you can call or send a text. You can also email, use online chat, or search at eldercare.acl.gov.eldercare.acl.gov <https://eldercare.acl.gov/home> · Accessed Aug 7, 2026

Be precise about what the Locator is for, because that is this guide's whole question. It connects older adults, their families, and caregivers to services in their community: the local Area Agency on Aging, in-home help, transportation, and information about paying for care.eldercare.acl.gov <https://eldercare.acl.gov/home> · Accessed Aug 7, 2026,Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *ACL (Administration for Community Living) — What If I Suspect Abuse, Neglect, or Exploitation?*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 14, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/protection-and-advocacy-systems/what-if-i-suspect-abuse-neglect-or-exploitation> What it does not do is deliver any of them. It will not bring the meals, run a benefits screen, arrange a caregiver break, or manage a case; the local agencies it connects you to do that. The route to Older Americans Act services runs through your local Area Agency on Aging, and the Locator is how a family finds theirs.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Area Agencies on Aging*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 13, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/area-agencies-aging>

So use the Locator once, to get pointed to the right local number. After that, most of your contact is with the AAA or ADRC it sends you to.

## What Your Area Agency on Aging Actually Does

Your [Area Agency on Aging](/caregiver/area-agencies-on-aging) is where the services live. An AAA is a public or private nonprofit agency that its state designates to address the needs of older people at the regional and local level under the Older Americans Act. Each one covers a defined "planning and service area," which may be a single city, a county, or a multi-county district, and a state designates exactly one AAA per area.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Area Agencies on Aging*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/area-agencies-aging>

This is the agency that arranges home-delivered and congregate meals, rides to medical appointments, family caregiver support, and benefits counseling for your area. When a hospital discharge planner or a state hotline tells you to "call your AAA," this is the door they mean.

One thing worth knowing before you dial: "Area Agency on Aging" is a general term, and the names of local AAAs vary.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Area Agencies on Aging*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/area-agencies-aging> Yours may operate as a "Council on Aging," an "Aging and Disability Services" office, or a regional commission. That is exactly why the Eldercare Locator is useful; it finds your agency by address, whatever it happens to be called locally.

## What an ADRC Adds

An [Aging and Disability Resource Center](https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/aging-and-disability-resource-centers) (ADRC) is a single point of entry into the long-term services and supports system, and it is broader than the AAA in two ways. First, it serves older adults, people with disabilities, caregivers, veterans, and families, rather than only people 60 and over. Second, it serves people at all income levels, providing objective information, counseling, and help accessing both public and private programs.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Administration for Community Living (acl.gov) - Aging and Disability Resource Centers*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/aging-and-disability-resource-centers>

The ADRC is the door built for a screening conversation, especially when long-term care or Medicaid long-term services and supports may be in the picture. It is part of the federal No Wrong Door system, which is meant to make any entry point into the network lead to the same coordinated help.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Administration for Community Living (acl.gov) - Aging and Disability Resource Centers*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/aging-and-disability-resource-centers>

The brand maze applies here too. Some states call their ADRC an "access point" or a "no wrong door" system rather than an ADRC.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Administration for Community Living (acl.gov) - Aging and Disability Resource Centers*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/aging-and-disability-resource-centers> If a search for "ADRC" in your state turns up nothing, search your state's own aging or disability services page, or let the Eldercare Locator route you.

## Which Door: AAA, ADRC, or Eldercare Locator?

Match the door to your situation:

* **You don't know your local agency.** Start with the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116. It routes you to the right local office by address.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Area Agencies on Aging*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 13, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/area-agencies-aging>
* **You know you need services now,** like meals, transportation, or a break from caregiving. Your Area Agency on Aging is where those live. If you already have its number, call it directly and skip the Locator step.
* **You are weighing long-term care, Medicaid, or supports for a disability at any age.** Ask for your state's ADRC. It is the door built to screen you across aging and disability programs at all income levels.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Administration for Community Living (acl.gov) - Aging and Disability Resource Centers*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/aging-and-disability-resource-centers>

In many communities the AAA and the ADRC are the same organization, so one call often opens both. When in doubt, the Locator sends you to whichever office covers your parent's address, and that office sorts out the rest.

## Is It Free, and Who Qualifies?

Contacting any of these doors is free, and the baseline to qualify for Older Americans Act services is an age, not an income. The Act defines an "older individual" as someone 60 or older, and individuals 60 and over may receive OAA benefits.Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives. (n.d.). *42 U.S.C. 3002 - Definitions (Older Americans Act sec. 102)*. uscode.house.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-section3002&num=0&edition=prelim> The ADRC door is wider still, serving people with disabilities and people at all income levels.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Administration for Community Living (acl.gov) - Aging and Disability Resource Centers*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/aging-and-disability-resource-centers>

There is no means test. An AAA and its service providers may not means test for any service for which contributions are accepted, and may not deny services to an older adult or family caregiver who will not or cannot contribute.Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives. (n.d.). *42 U.S.C. 3030c-2 - Consumer contributions (Older Americans Act sec. 315)*. uscode.house.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-section3030c-2&num=0&edition=prelim> That said, "free" and "no bill in the mail" are not the same sentence. Voluntary contributions may be requested for OAA-funded services, and are encouraged for people whose self-declared income is at or above 185% of the federal poverty line. The request must be noncoercive, your assets are never counted, and refusing to contribute cannot cost you the service.Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives. (n.d.). *42 U.S.C. 3030c-2 - Consumer contributions (Older Americans Act sec. 315)*. uscode.house.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-section3030c-2&num=0&edition=prelim>

Free to qualify does not guarantee immediate service. Availability can vary by program and area, so ask your AAA directly about current wait times and openings when you call.

## They're Often the Same Phone Call

The most useful thing to understand is that these doors are complementary, not competing. The Eldercare Locator routes; the Area Agency on Aging delivers; the ADRC screens across aging and disability. In practice they connect to one another, and one office frequently plays more than one role. You do not have to pick the "correct" door and worry about getting it wrong. Any of the three will move you toward the same local network, and the person who answers can hand you off to the right desk.

If you are just beginning, our guide to [getting started as a caregiver](/caregiver/getting-started) walks through the first week, and the [National Family Caregiver Support Program](/caregiver/national-family-caregiver-support-program) covers the specific help available to family caregivers through these same agencies.

## Frequently Asked Questions

 Is the Eldercare Locator the same as an Area Agency on Aging?

No. The Eldercare Locator is a single nationwide service that connects older adults, families, and caregivers to services in their community, including their local Area Agency on Aging.eldercare.acl.gov <https://eldercare.acl.gov/home> · Accessed Aug 7, 2026 The AAA is the local agency that actually plans and delivers those services in your area, and finding yours is one of the main things the Locator is used for.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Area Agencies on Aging*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 13, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/area-agencies-aging>

  Do I have to be low income to use these agencies?

No. Older Americans Act services carry no means test, and the baseline to qualify is age 60, not an income limit.Office of the Law Revision Counsel, U.S. House of Representatives. (n.d.). *42 U.S.C. 3030c-2 - Consumer contributions (Older Americans Act sec. 315)*. uscode.house.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://uscode.house.gov/view.xhtml?req=granuleid:USC-prelim-title42-section3030c-2&num=0&edition=prelim> An ADRC goes further and serves people at all income levels, including people with disabilities of any age.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Administration for Community Living (acl.gov) - Aging and Disability Resource Centers*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/aging-and-disability-resource-centers>

  What if my state doesn't seem to have an "ADRC"?

Some states brand their ADRC as an "access point" or a "no wrong door" system instead.Administration for Community Living. (n.d.). *Administration for Community Living (acl.gov) - Aging and Disability Resource Centers*. acl.gov. Retrieved Jul 15, 2026, from <https://acl.gov/programs/aging-and-disability-networks/aging-and-disability-resource-centers> If the term returns nothing, search your state's aging or disability services page, or call the Eldercare Locator and let it route you to the right office.

  Which number do I actually call first?

If you don't already have a local number, call the Eldercare Locator at 1-800-677-1116, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. Eastern.eldercare.acl.gov <https://eldercare.acl.gov/home> · Accessed Aug 7, 2026 If you already know your AAA or ADRC, call it directly.

This guide from Brevy (published July 16, 2026, last verified July 16, 2026) explains the three main federal "front doors" for getting help with an aging parent: the Eldercare Locator, the Area Agency on Aging (AAA), and the Aging and Disability Resource Center (ADRC). All three are free to contact and often overlap or are the same office.

**Eldercare Locator:** A nationwide public service of the Administration for Community Living (ACL) that connects families to their local aging services. It does NOT deliver services but routes callers to the right local agency. Reach it at 1-800-677-1116 (Mon-Fri, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. ET) or eldercare.acl.gov.

**Area Agency on Aging (AAA):** The local state-designated agency that actually delivers services under the Older Americans Act—meals, transportation, caregiver support, benefits counseling. Each state designates one AAA per planning and service area (city, county, or multi-county district). Local names vary (e.g., "Council on Aging").

**ADRC (Aging and Disability Resource Center):** A broader state single entry point serving older adults, people with disabilities (any age), veterans, and families at all income levels. It is part of the federal No Wrong Door system and is designed for screening conversations about long-term care and Medicaid.

**Which to use:**
- Don't know your local agency → Start with Eldercare Locator
- Need immediate services (meals, transport, caregiver break) → Call AAA directly
- Weighing long-term care, Medicaid, or disability supports → Ask for ADRC

**Eligibility & Cost:** Contacting any is free. Older Americans Act services require age 60+ (no income test/means test). ADRC serves all ages and income levels. Voluntary contributions may be requested but cannot be required, and services cannot be denied for refusal to contribute.

**Key takeaway:** The three doors are complementary, not competing. Any will move you toward the same local network. The FAQ section clarifies that the Eldercare Locator is not the same as an AAA, and that some states may brand ADRCs differently ("access point" or "no wrong door" system).

An area agency on aging (AAA) is a public or private nonprofit agency designated by a state to address the needs and concerns of all older persons at the regional and local levels. AAA is a general term — names of local AAAs may vary.

AAAs are primarily responsible for a geographic area, also known as a planning and service area (PSA), that is either a city, a single county, or a multi-county district. AAAs may be categorized as a county, city, regional planning council or council of governments, private, or nonprofit.

AAAs coordinate and offer services that help older adults remain in their homes, if that is their preference, aided by services such as home-delivered meals, homemaker assistance, and whatever else it may take to make independent living a viable option. By making a range of supports available, AAAs make it possible for older individuals to choose the services and living arrangements that suit them best.

Find your local AAA by visiting the [Eldercare Locator website](http://eldercare.acl.gov/)or calling 1-800-677-1116.

# Discover How Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) Support You

**What Is an Area Agency on Aging (AAA)?**  
 Area Agencies on Aging, or [**AAAs**](https://www.usaging.org/Files/USAging_Local%20Leaders%2023_508.pdf) as they are often called, are trusted local organizations dedicated to helping older adults live with independence and dignity in their homes and communities. Established under the Older Americans Act in 1973, AAAs coordinate a wide range of services that support aging well and help family caregivers manage the challenges of caregiving. There are more than 600 AAAs across the United States, each tailored to meet the specific needs of the older adults and families in their communities.

|  |
| --- |
| **Finding Your AAA**  Find your local AAA by using the Eldercare Locator, a national hotline and website. To speak with a specialist who will guide you to support and resources that are available near you:   * **Phone, text or video phone** (ASL direct video): [1-800-677-1116](tel:+18006771116). * **Email**: [eldercarelocator@usaging.org](mailto:eldercarelocator@usaging.org). * **[Start an o](https://home-c6.incontact.com/inContact/ChatClient/ChatClient.aspx?poc=9801c7c8-84a3-4269-8e5f-51dbf40f9ae9&bu=4593078)[nline chat](https://home-c6.incontact.com/inContact/ChatClient/ChatClient.aspx?poc=9801c7c8-84a3-4269-8e5f-51dbf40f9ae9&bu=4593078)**. * **Website**: [www.eldercare.acl.gov](https://www.eldercare.acl.gov). |

  
 **Why Would I Need to Reach Out to a AAA?**  
 There are so many different reasons that people reach out to their local AAA. Here are just a few examples:  

* You may have had a fall at home and are worried about it happening again. AAAs have fall prevention programs that can help you feel more safe living on your own.
* You may find that you are having difficulty doing simple tasks around your house, such as laundry, meal preparation or household chores. AAAs can provide you with assistance with these.
* You may have questions about Medicare or Medicaid. AAAs have experts on staff who can help you navigate these complicated programs.
* You may recently have had to stop driving. AAAs are transportation programs so that you can participate in senior center activities or get to crucial medical appointments.
* You might be caring for an elderly parent and find that you are having a hard time doing it by yourself. AAAs can offer respite services.

  
 Every AAA is different. Each one assesses the needs of its own individual community and then tailor services to meet those needs. However, there are some core services that every AAA provides.  
    
   
    
 **Services for Older Adults**  
 AAAs provide vital programs that promote health, safety and independence for older adults, including:  

* **In-Home Support Services:** Help with everyday tasks such as bathing, dressing and light housekeeping.
* **Transportation:** Rides to medical appointments, grocery stores and community activities.
* **Health and Wellness Programs:** Classes and workshops that promote physical activity, chronic disease management and fall prevention.
* **Benefits Counseling:** Assistance navigating Medicare, Medicaid and other public benefits.
* **Home-Delivered and Congregate Meals:** Nutritious meals delivered to your home or served in community settings.

  
 **Services for Caregivers**  
 Caring for a loved one can be rewarding but also overwhelming. AAAs offer support and relief for caregivers through:  

* **Respite Care:** Temporary relief services so caregivers can take a break.

Search results: 



--- SOURCE 1: Social Isolation and Loneliness in Older Adults ---
URL: https://www.nationalacademies.org/projects/HMD-HSP-17-25/publication/25663

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine webpage details a completed consensus study (2020) on the health impacts of social isolation and loneliness in adults aged 50 and older, particularly among low-income, underserved, and vulnerable populations. The study was sponsored by the AARP Foundation.

Key findings: Approximately one-quarter of community-dwelling Americans aged 65+ are socially isolated, and social isolation presents a major risk for premature mortality comparable to high blood pressure, smoking, or obesity.

The committee, chaired by Dan G. Blazer II, was tasked with: 1) examining evidence linking social isolation/loneliness to poor health outcomes; 2) exploring effects on healthcare access and utilization; 3) making evidence-based recommendations for healthcare system interventions; and 4) examining translation and dissemination of findings to healthcare practitioners.

--- SOURCE 1: Correlates of Loneliness and Social Isolation among Older Adults during the COVID-19 Outbreak: A Comprehensive Assessment from a National United States Sample ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2308-3417/9/4/96

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in Geriatrics (2024), examines correlates of loneliness and social isolation among U.S. older adults during the COVID-19 outbreak using data from the 2020 National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS), a nationally representative sample of 3,257 respondents aged 65+ (representing 26,229,876 older adults). The study used weighted multiple logistic regression models to analyze sociodemographic, health, social support, and community correlates of three outcomes: loneliness during COVID-19, higher loneliness compared to pre-pandemic, and social isolation.

Key findings: About 35.2% reported loneliness during the outbreak, 21.9% reported higher loneliness than before COVID-19, and 32.8% were socially isolated. 

**Loneliness correlates** (increased odds): female gender (86% higher), college education (82% higher), physical activity (53% higher), depression (187% higher), anxiety (173% higher), and functional limitations (66% higher). Protective factors: being married (49% lower odds), having one child (30% lower), good sleep quality (82% lower), and being Black (35% lower odds compared to White).

**Higher pandemic loneliness correlates** (increased odds): female (103% higher), college degree (148% higher), physical activity (38% higher), anxiety (92% higher), and virtual communication access (64% higher). Protective: being married (32% lower), having one child (37% lower), employment (52% lower), Black (35% lower), and good sleep quality (68% lower).

**Social isolation correlates** (increased odds): higher age (3% per year), Black (45% higher), Hispanic (76% higher), children in household (one child: 47% higher; two+: 148% higher), and metropolitan residence (42% higher). Protective: physical activity (37% lower), higher income (48% lower), virtual communication access (34% lower), and transportation access (65% lower).

The study found that many correlates for loneliness and social isolation were mutually exclusive or had opposing directional relationships, underscoring the need to examine both constructs separately. The authors recommend multifaceted interventions spanning individual, community, and societal levels to address the social disconnection epidemic among older adults.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a transcript of a webinar titled "Barriers to digital literacy for older adults: Bridging the Digital Divide," co-hosted by Elder Abuse Prevention Ontario and the Ontario Age-Friendly Communities Outreach Program on March 24, 2025.

**Presentations:**

**Dr. Madison Robertson (Research Coordinator, Centre for Studies in Aging and Health)** presented on the barriers to digital literacy for older adults. Key findings from a scoping review identified seven main barriers:

1. **Health Barriers:** Poor motor skills, visual/hearing difficulties, physical impairments (arthritis, cataracts), and cognitive impairments (memory loss).
2. **Support Network Barriers:** Lack of social support from family/friends; dependence on younger family members is not always feasible; negative interactions can discourage use.
3. **Convenience and Use Barriers:** Poor design/interface (small fonts, complex authentications); continuous updates causing confusion and loss of confidence.
4. **Knowledge and Information Barriers:** Gap in computer proficiency due to limited lifetime use; lack of awareness of available digital services.
5. **Perception/Attitude Barriers:** Concerns about online security/privacy; fear of scams; low self-efficacy ("too old to learn"); fear of social isolation or stigmatization from using assistive technologies; preference for traditional communication methods.
6. **Resource Barriers:** Limited access to devices/internet; poor internet speed (especially in rural areas); high costs of devices and services; absence of personalized training.
7. **Special Population Barriers:** Unique challenges for visually impaired, hearing impaired, those with chronic conditions, and older adults with disabilities.

**Strategies to mitigate barriers** include: Collaborative Learning (intergenerational programs, partnerships), Structured Content (gamification, hands-on activities), Technology-Facilitated Self-Learning (user-friendly designs, step-by-step guides), Tailored Interventions (personalized home-based training, user-driven content), Adaptive Tools (simplified interfaces, stylus pens, large keyboards), and Continuous Support (follow-up sessions, refresher courses).

**Ken Roy (General Manager, Connected Canadians)** presented on Connected Canadians, Canada's leading digital inclusion charity for adults aged 50+. Services include:
- **Tech Helpline:** Free one-on-one support pairing older adults with trained technology mentors (virtually or in-person). Over 550 mentors have been trained through a rigorous vetting process.
- **Digital Literacy Workshops:** 22 different topics covering online safety, banking, etc.
- **Device Distribution:** Partnering with organizations to distribute devices and cellular data access.
- **Organizational Volunteer Training:** Training staff at libraries, hospitals, and corporations (e.g., Rogers Communications trained 2,000 technicians).
- **Partnerships:** Works with organizations like TD (online banking curriculum), National Gallery of Canada (virtual art tours), and various senior-focused organizations.

**Q&A Discussion Highlights:**
- Connected Canadians has volunteers specializing in accessibility features for visually impaired and other disabilities.
- Connected Canadians has not directly worked with medical devices but has distributed smart speakers (Amazon Echo Show) for emergency communication.
- Research gaps exist for special populations like Indigenous populations on reserves lacking internet infrastructure, and for older adults aged 75+.
- Fear of strangers accessing computers is a significant barrier to overcome when encouraging older adults to sign up for digital literacy programs.
</summary>

<summary>
## What Is the Digital Divide? Meaning, Causes & Impact

This page from Syracuse University's iSchool provides a comprehensive overview of the digital divide—the gap between people who have meaningful access to digital technology and those who don't. It goes beyond device ownership to include quality of access, skills to use technology effectively, and ability to benefit from digital opportunities.

### Key Takeaways
- The digital divide describes gaps in who can access, use, and benefit from digital technology
- Economic factors, geography, education, and age all contribute to technology inequality
- Digital gaps affect education, employment, healthcare access, and social participation

### Types of Digital Divide
1. **Access Divide**: Disparities in who can connect to the internet and own devices. Rural communities face infrastructure gaps; cost is a major barrier (monthly bills of $50–$100). Some families rely on mobile-only internet.
2. **Skills Divide**: Differences in digital literacy—navigating technology effectively, safely, and productively. According to AARP research, 64% of adults over 50 feel technology is not designed with their age group in mind.
3. **Usage Divide**: How people use technology differently based on socioeconomic status. Higher-income users engage in more "capital-enhancing" activities; lower-income users often engage in more passive consumption.

### Causes
- **Economic factors**: Device costs ($200+) plus annual internet bills ($600–$1,200)
- **Geographic limitations**: Rural Americans are nearly 20 times more likely than urban residents to lack fixed broadband (USDA data)
- **Educational factors**: Under-resourced schools have outdated equipment and weaker tech curricula
- **Age-related gaps**: Older adults often lack confidence with digital tools
- **Infrastructure and policy limitations**

### Effects
- **Education**: Students without home internet struggle with homework, online resources, and remote learning
- **Employment**: Higher-wage workers are more likely to work remotely; lower-wage workers cannot (U.S. Census Bureau data)
- **Healthcare**: ~80% of providers offered telehealth in 2022, but older adults, rural residents, and low-income patients face greatest barriers (AMA)
- **Social participation**: Citizens without digital access face barriers to government services, banking, and civic engagement

### Bridging the Divide
Solutions include expanding broadband infrastructure (federal programs like BEAD), improving digital literacy through schools and libraries, policy solutions (subsidy programs, E-Rate funding), and support from private/nonprofit sectors (Microsoft's Airband Initiative, Google's Project Connect, EveryoneOn, PCs for People).

The page concludes that digital equity requires ongoing effort from schools, libraries, businesses, and governments, and that communities prioritizing digital inclusion see clear outcomes in education, employment, and healthcare.
</summary>

URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12263164

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a peer-reviewed research article (published in PMC, NIH-funded, 2025) examining how the COVID-19 pandemic's mandated closures of Adult Day Services (ADS) impacted dementia care dyads (persons with dementia and their informal caregivers). The study analyzed data from an NIH-funded interview-based investigation (N=43), focusing on a subsample of 13 informal caregivers whose care recipients attended ADS at the onset of COVID-19. The sample was predominantly female (92.3%), African-American (69.2%), adult children (53.8%), with a mean age of 56.6 and an average of 5.9 years caring for the person with dementia.

Four central themes emerged from the qualitative analysis:

1. **Struggle to meet needs of the person with dementia**: Caregivers were forced into round-the-clock care while balancing full-time employment and other obligations. Many lacked training to provide medical oversight previously handled by ADS.
2. **Physical and cognitive decline of the person with dementia**: Loss of regular physical activity, routine, socialization, and cognitive stimulation led to accelerated deterioration.
3. **Lack of time for self-care**: Caregivers reported exhaustion, isolation, and inability to meet their own basic needs due to loss of ADS respite.
4. **Adaptations by ADS and caregivers**: ADS centers implemented daily phone calls, virtual programming (Zoom), home delivery of medications and activity packets. Caregivers devised creative strategies like driving to provide stimulation.

The study concludes that the mandated closure of ADS sites exacerbated caregiving burden and deterioration in individuals with dementia. It recommends that policymakers consider the detrimental effects on vulnerable populations before closing community-based care services in future public health emergencies.
</summary>

We all were at home at the same time… I mean it was full-time care … within that full-time care I still had a full-time job… I have an 11-year-old son … so I was teacher, mom, daughter, caregiver, worker, supervisor, student, yeah, all those hats I wore…" - Tanya, "What has happened to her body in nine months since COVID is horrifying, horrifying!" - Emily on her mother's physical decline, "I'm [providing] 100 percent care. … I was exhausted. URL: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557971

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is Chapter 4 from the National Academies Press book "Social Isolation and Loneliness in Older Adults: Opportunities for the Health Care System" (2020), focusing on risk and protective factors for social isolation and loneliness in older adults. The chapter emphasizes that aging alone does not cause social isolation or loneliness, but people over 50 are more likely to experience risk factors.

**Physical Health Factors:** Roughly 60% of all adults and 80% of adults aged 65+ have at least one chronic disease, and 77% have at least two. Chronic diseases (cardiovascular disease, stroke, COPD, heart failure, chronic pain, HIV) can increase risk of social isolation and loneliness bidirectionally. Geriatric syndromes like frailty, functional impairment, urinary/fecal incontinence, and sensory impairments (hearing loss, visual impairment, dual sensory impairment) are significant risk factors.

**Psychological, Psychiatric, and Cognitive Factors:** Social isolation and loneliness are more common in older adults with depression and anxiety. The relationship is bidirectional. Dementia and cognitive impairment increase loneliness risk; one study found 33% of those with dementia reported loneliness vs. 22% without. Social withdrawal is a recognized feature of dementia.

**Social and Cultural Factors:** Social support networks, family relationships, and marriage quality affect loneliness risk. Single adults (unmarried, widowed, divorced) are more likely to experience loneliness. Friendships and neighbor relationships can buffer against loneliness. Caregivers are also at risk for social isolation and loneliness. Human-animal interaction research shows mixed results regarding benefits for loneliness.

**Disruptive Life Events:** Bereavement, illness, and retirement can alter interpersonal relations and increase isolation risk.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Explore Risk of Social Isolation - Age 65+ in the United States | AHR ---
URL: https://www.americashealthrankings.org/explore/measures/isolationrisk_sr_b/idl_sr_b

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from America's Health Rankings presents data on "Risk of Social Isolation - Age 65+" in the United States, based on U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey data (2020-2024). The measure is an index of social isolation risk factors among adults 65+ including living in poverty, living alone, being divorced/separated/widowed, never having married, having a disability, and having independent living difficulty.

Key data points:
- The national average for independent living difficulty among adults 65+ is 13.2%.
- **Top states (lowest risk):** South Dakota (9.6%), Vermont (9.6%), Maine (9.7%), North Dakota (9.8%), New Hampshire (9.9%).
- **Bottom states (highest risk):** Mississippi (16.2%), California (16.1%), Hawaii (15.4%), Alabama (15.4%), New York (15.1%).
- The overall index range: Utah (best) at 1, Mississippi (worst) at 100.

Nearly a quarter of U.S. adults 65+ are at risk for social isolation. Social isolation differs from loneliness—it is the objective absence of social relationships rather than the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connections.

**Health impacts:** Social isolation increases risk of mortality, dementia, coronary heart disease, and stroke. Healthcare costs of social isolation account for an estimated $6.7 billion in Medicare expenditures annually.

**Risk factors include:** living alone, having a disability or being homebound, living in poverty, race/ethnicity, immigration status, English proficiency, sexual orientation/gender identity.

**Interventions:** Technology-based interventions, expanded public transportation and public health collaboration, service-provision with volunteer intermediaries, and Medicare Advantage supplemental benefits (home-delivered meals, ride-sharing, companionship). Senior and community centers are highlighted as important for group interactions.

The data appears in America's Health Rankings Senior Report (published May 2026).
</summary>

"Across the United States, nearly a quarter of adults age 65 and older are at risk for social isolation.", "Social isolation differs from loneliness, which is the feeling of lacking meaningful social relationships, while social isolation addresses the objective lack of social relationships.", "The health care costs of social isolation are comparable to those of some chronic illnesses, accounting for an estimated $6.7 billion in Medicare expenditures annually.", "Interventions to reduce social isolation among older adults are most successful when they directly involve older adults rather than simply providing services or training.", "Life events such as retirement, loss of loved ones, and age-related mental and physical decline can make it difficult for older adults to maintain social connectedness."

--- SOURCE 2: The global prevalence and associated factors of loneliness ... ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-025-05304-x

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (April 2025) examining the global prevalence and associated factors of loneliness in older adults. A comprehensive search of six databases (Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, EMBASE, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar) from inception to March 2025 identified 126 studies involving 1,250,322 older adults (aged 60+).

**Key Findings:**
- **Global prevalence of loneliness: 27.6%** (95% CI: 25.5–29.8) — approximately one in four older adults
- **By continent:** North America highest (30.5%), followed by Asia (27.9%), Europe (27.2%), Oceania (25.7%), and Africa lowest (15.3%)
- **By gender:** Women (30.9%) had higher prevalence than men (24.2%)
- **By setting:** Institutionalized older adults (nursing homes, etc.) had 50.7% prevalence vs. community-dwelling
- Studies from 62 countries; US (18 studies), China (15), and Netherlands (8) contributed most
- Most common measurement tools: single-item questionnaire (67 studies), UCLA Loneliness Scale (35 studies), De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale (13 studies)

**Associated Factors (from 189 papers):**
- Strong positive associations: depression (52 studies), widowhood/being unmarried/divorced (24 studies), living alone (19 studies), poor health/well-being (17 studies), frailty (10 studies)
- Additional factors: cognitive impairment, institutionalization, hearing impairment, anxiety, sleep difficulties, social isolation, pain, falls
- Inverse associations: good quality of life, being married, higher cognitive function, better sleep quality

The authors note that loneliness is linked to depression, suicidal ideation, and mortality, and recommend that policymakers develop interventions to alleviate loneliness among older adults. Study limitations include restriction to English-language publications and reliance on single-item questionnaires in many studies.
</summary>

SUMMARY:

A national study published in JAMA in December 2024 shows that loneliness and isolation among older Americans (ages 50-80) have mostly returned to pre-pandemic rates, but over one-third still feel lonely and nearly as many feel isolated. **Key statistics:**
- In 2024, 33% of older adults felt lonely sometimes or often (vs 34% in 2018)
- In 2024, 29% felt isolated sometimes or often (vs 27% in 2018)

- Not working or on disability: 52% (up from 38% in 2018)

- Fair/poor mental health: 77% (slightly down from 79% in 2018)

This report from the Administration for Community Living (ACL) summarizes the 2018 highlights and accomplishments of Older Americans Act (OAA) Title III programs. Title III services account for the largest portion of OAA funding, supporting a national network of federal, state, and local agencies.

## Key Data Points (2018)

**AmeriCorps Seniors** is a United States government program run by the Corporation for National and Community Service (CNCS) that engages volunteers aged 55 and older to serve their communities. The program has over 200,000 volunteers nationwide.

**History:** Originally called Senior Corps, the program was formed in 1993 under President Bill Clinton when three constituent programs—Foster Grandparents, RSVP (Retired and Senior Volunteer Program), and Senior Companions—were merged under CNCS. On September 29, 2020, CNCS rebranded itself as AmeriCorps, and Senior Corps was rebranded as AmeriCorps Seniors.

Each of the three main programs has a unique history:
- **Foster Grandparents Program:** Piloted on August 28, 1965, to attract low-income individuals over 60 into community service. In the 1980s, First Lady Nancy Reagan championed the program.
- **Senior Companion Program:** Began in 1968 under the Department of Health, Education and Welfare and Administration on Aging, signed into law under President Richard Nixon in 1973.
- **RSVP:** Originated from private groups and government agencies, including the Community Service Society of New York on Staten Island (1965). Success led to an amendment to the Older Americans Act creating RSVP as a nationwide program in 1969.

**Programs:**
- **Foster Grandparents (55+):** Seniors interact with and support young children, providing emotional support to abuse victims, tutoring, mentoring, and caring for children with disabilities. Benefits include pre-service training, transportation reimbursement, annual physical, accident/liability insurance, and some income-eligible participants receive tax-free stipends.
- **RSVP (55+):** Flexible program allowing seniors to choose how and when to volunteer. Activities include job training, tutoring, building homes, immunization help, relief services, and a widespread telephone reassurance service. No stipend provided.
- **Senior Companions (55+):** Helps adults with disabilities or terminal illnesses (and their caregivers) live independently. Provides emotional/physical support, house chores, transportation, and companionship. Requires 5–40 hours/week. Includes training, transportation reimbursement, annual physical, meals, insurance, and income-eligible tax-free stipends.
