### Enjoy the SilverSneakers store!

# What Is SilverSneakers? What to Know and How to Get Started

## Here’s everything you need to know about this health and fitness program designed for older adults.

![senior woman doing a plank](https://www.silversneakers.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/SS_SilverSneakers_Questions_700x525.jpg)

Wouldn’t it be great if you could take fitness classes designed specifically for seniors and led by supportive instructors?

What if you could take those classes online from the comfort of your home? And get no-cost access to gyms and fitness locations in your area (and even nationwide!)?

If that sounds like the perfect program to help you get and [stay fit](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/lose-the-weight-keep-even-gain-the-muscle-your-3-step-plan/), we have awesome news for you.

If SilverSneakers is included in your [Medicare Advantage plan](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/important-facts-medicare-plan-open-enrollment/ ​), you can have all of that — at no additional cost to you.

To help you learn more and take advantage of SilverSneakers, we put together this handy guide to answer your questions. ([Click here to check your eligibility right away](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Eligibility/CheckEligibility).)

## Question #1: What Is SilverSneakers?

SilverSneakers is a health and fitness program designed for adults 65+ that’s included with many Medicare Advantage plans.

SilverSneakers members can:

The goal? To help you stay strong in body, mind, and spirit. Regular physical activity keeps your heart, brain, bones, muscles, and joints healthy.

If you have a chronic condition like [arthritis](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/joint-pain-and-osteoarthritis-the-silversneakers-guide/), diabetes, or [osteoporosis](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/osteoporosis-and-bone-health-what-older-adults-need-to-know/), safe exercise can help you feel better. Plus, [staying social](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/myths-about-loneliness-debunked-older-adults/) is vital to good health.

According to SilverSneakers members, it works. In fact, 95 percent of members rate their health as excellent, very good, or good. And 88 percent say SilverSneakers has improved their quality of life.

## Question #2: Is SilverSneakers Covered by Medicare Plans?

If you currently have a Medicare Advantage plan and you want to see if it includes SilverSneakers, you can [check your SilverSneakers eligibility instantly here](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Eligibility/CheckEligibility).

If you’re [new to Medicare](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/new-to-medicare-here-are-your-options/) or looking for health plans that include SilverSneakers, you can [find participating health plans here](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Eligibility/HealthPlans).

Not a member, or not age 65 yet? That’s OK. You can still create a [free online account](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Eligibility/StartHere) and enjoy hundreds of SilverSneakers On-Demand videos, health and fitness tips, and more!

## Question #3: Do I Need a SilverSneakers Card?

No. If you’re already a SilverSneakers member, you can [get your digital membership ID instantly here](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Eligibility/GetCard).

To make things even easier, download the SilverSneakers GO app (free, [iOS](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/silversneakers-go/id1410437380) and [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.tivityhealth.silversneakersgo)). You’ll be able to:

## Question #4: Is There an Age Requirement for SilverSneakers?

SilverSneakers is a health and fitness program designed for adults 65+ that’s included with many Medicare Advantage plans, but there’s no age requirement. If you have a Medicare Advantage plan, you can [check your SilverSneakers eligibility instantly here](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Eligibility/CheckEligibility).

## Question #5: Do You Have Online Classes?

Yes, and lots of them! If you’re a SilverSneakers member, you get access to both live online classes and prerecorded video workouts.

[SilverSneakers LIVE](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Search/OnlineClasses) offers full-length SilverSneakers classes daily live through Zoom. Classes range from 15 minutes to one hour. With hundreds of classes a week, there’s something for everyone.

You’ll find favorites such as SilverSneakers Classic, Circuit, Yoga, EnerChi and Total Body Strength. There’s also Zumba Gold, Cardio Mix, Walk Strong, Line Dancing, and many seated workouts.

Plus, you’ll find live wellness workshops on topics like stress, balance, nutrition, and pain management.

Classes and workshops occur multiple times throughout the day and are exclusive for SilverSneakers members. Learn more in our [guide to SilverSneakers LIVE](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/silversneakers-live-reasons-to-try/).

SilverSneakers On-Demand features hundreds of videos for SilverSneakers members only. You’ll find workout videos for cardio, strength training, and fall prevention.

You’ll also get nutrition videos, such as healthy eating habits for older adults and how to read food labels.

To get started, [log in to or create your online account](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Account/Login).

## Question #6: What Types of Exercise Classes Are Available, and Who Teaches Them?

You’ll find a variety of [fun exercise classes designed for](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Classes) all fitness levels and interests. Classes vary whether you’re doing them online or in person, but if available, you’ll find:

SilverSneakers classes are led by supportive instructors who are specially trained in senior fitness. They can help you learn how to do exercises safely and adapt exercises for your needs.

Learn more about [why SilverSneakers members love our classes](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/why-silversneakers-members-love-our-classes/) and [what SilverSneakers instructors know that other trainers don’t](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/5-things-silversneakers-instructors-know/).

## Question #7: What’s Included in a Gym Membership with SilverSneakers?

You’ll get a basic membership at any gym and participating location in the SilverSneakers network. Facilities, amenities, and classes vary by location, but if available, that generally means you can use:

It does not include extras like smoothies, massages, or personal training. If you choose to arrange and pay for those on your own, you certainly can.

Not a fan of the traditional gym? You might like [SilverSneakers Community classes](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Community), which are taught at recreation centers, local parks, and other neighborhood locations.

## Question #8: How Do I Find a Location or Class, and Can I Go to More Than One?

To find participating fitness locations or classes in the SilverSneakers network near you, use [our location tool](https://tools.silversneakers.com/LocationSearch), or download the SilverSneakers GO app (free, [iOS](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/silversneakers-go/id1410437380) and [Android](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.tivityhealth.silversneakersgo)).

We recommend that you check with locations directly to find out about their hours and class schedules.

And, yes! Some members find it hard to believe, but you can enroll in as many participating locations as you like, and use any location in the SilverSneakers network, at any time.

For example, you could use weights or exercise machines at one gym, swim in the pool at another, and take a SilverSneakers or Community class at your local rec center.

## Question #9: What’s the SilverSneakers Community Like?

Friendly. Supportive. Motivating. Fun. Like family. That’s how members often describe the SilverSneakers community.

What they all know: SilverSneakers is more than a fitness program, and often it’s the friendships that people make that keep them coming back. [Read what SilverSneakers members have to say about the program and our classes here](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/why-silversneakers-members-love-our-classes/).

Many SilverSneakers groups even plan social events outside of classes, like potlucks or outings around town. Or if they’re taking a SilverSneakers LIVE class, they’ll chat online before or after the workout.

This social support has real health benefits. SilverSneakers members who participate in group exercise are more active, feel healthier, and are [less likely to experience social isolation](https://www.silversneakers.com/blog/reconnect-isolation/) than non-members, according to a Massachusetts Institute of Technology AgeLab study.

Plus, you can stay connected with the SilverSneakers community on [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/silversneakers) and [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/silversneakers/).

## Question #10: Do You Sell Silver Sneakers—or Silver Slippers?

We don’t sell shoes of any kind, but we do offer SilverSneakers shirts, exercise bands, and bags at the [online SilverSneakers store](https://silversneakers.orders.com/store/home/).

## Question #11: I Have More Questions! Can You Help?

If you have questions about your SilverSneakers eligibility or membership, you can call us at 866-584-7389 or email us at [support@silversneakers.com](mailto:support@silversneakers.com).

## Activate Your FREE SilverSneakers Online Account

Get hundreds of free SilverSneakers On-Demand videos and stay in touch with us by [creating your free online account](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Eligibility/StartHere). You don’t have to be a SilverSneakers member to get on-demand workout videos, health and fitness tips from SilverSneakers, and more.

SilverSneakers members can go to thousands of nationwide gyms and fitness locations, plus take [SilverSneakers LIVE online classes](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Search/OnlineClasses) led by specially trained instructors and designed for all fitness levels and abilities – at no additional cost. If you have a Medicare Advantage plan, it may include SilverSneakers. [Check your eligibility here](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Eligibility/CheckEligibility).

Already a member? Get your SilverSneakers member ID, search for locations near you, and all the health and wellness resources you need by logging in to [your online member account here](https://tools.silversneakers.com/Account/Login).

## A 24/7 Lifeline for Older Adults and Caregivers Feeling Isolated, Overwhelmed, or Alone

## Call Us Anytime: [888.670.1360](tel:8886701360)

Loneliness, grief, and depression don’t keep business hours – and neither do we. Founded more than 50 years ago, Institute on Aging’s Friendship Line is the nation’s only accredited 24-hour toll-free emotional support line for older adults, seniors, caregivers, and adults with disabilities.

We’re here to do more than answer the phone. We connect with aging adults and their caregivers so they feel seen, heard, and understood during life’s most difficult moments. Whether you’re experiencing anxiety, loss, suicidal thoughts, or simply need someone to talk to, our trained staff and volunteers are here to listen, support, and help you feel less alone. Because everyone could use a friend.

To receive outbound calls from the Friendship Line, fill out the intake form.

[Get Started](#friendship-line-intake-form)

## When You Need Someone to Talk To, We’re Here

Life can feel overwhelming – especially as we age, cope with loss, or care for others. The Friendship Line is a **free, confidential helpline**, senior emotional support line in California, designed specifically for adults aged 60+ and adults living with disabilities.

**We’re here to support you when you are:**

* **Feeling lonely or disconnected from others**
* **Are living with depression, anxiety, or emotional distress**
* **Are grieving the loss of a loved one or friend**
* **Are caring for someone with dementia or serious illness**
* **Are having thoughts of suicide or self-harm**
* **Just need a kind, non-judgmental person who listens**

**You don’t have to be in crisis to call. Sometimes, just having someone to talk to makes all the difference.**

## How to Use the Friendship Line

Just call. No appointment. No application. No pressure.

## [English: 888.670.1360](tel:8886701360)

## [Cantonese: 888.670.2504](tel:8886702504)

## [Korean: 888.560.7684](tel:8885607684%20)

## [Mandarin: 888.670.2504](tel:8886702504%20)

## [Tagalog: 888.570.0867](tel:8885700867%20)

## [Vietnamese: 888.670.1361](tel:8886701361%20)

## [Russian: 888.560.7360](tel:8885607360)

## What the Friendship Line Offers

The Friendship Line was created to challenge the idea that aging means isolation, and to provide warm, personal advice without bureaucratic restraints. We offer connection to those who need emotional support and welcome them into our extended community.

* **24/7 Toll-Free Emotional Support** for older adults and adults with disabilities
* **Friendly conversation, active listening, and compassionate caregiver support across California**
* **Crisis intervention and suicide prevention**
* **Grief support** if you’re experiencing loss
* **Ongoing outreach calls** to individuals who request regular check-ins

Every call is answered by a trained team member – whether it’s 2 p.m. or 2 a.m. We’re here because we know connection saves lives.

## Friendship Line Program Services

The Friendship Line is more than just a phone call – it’s a comprehensive, culturally inclusive emotional support program rooted in dignity, compassion, and connection. If you or a loved one needs more support, we can connect you with additional resources through Institute on Aging’s integrated programs.

### Emotional Support in Multiple Languages

In addition to English, we also offer support in:

* **Spanish** – [Haga clic aquí para ver un folleto en Español](https://instituteo1stg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Friendship-Flier-Spanish-24_DSPA-1.pdf)

* **Mandarin** – [点击此处查看普通话传单](https://instituteo1stg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Friendship-Flier-Mandarin-24_D-SCH-formatted-1.pdf)
* **Tagalog** – [mag-click dito para sa isang flyer sa Tagalog](https://instituteo1stg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Friendship-Flier-Tagalog-24_D-TAG-1.pdf)
* **Vietnamese** – [nhấp vào đy để xem tờ rơi bằng tiếng Việt](https://instituteo1stg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Friendship-Flier-Vietnamese-24_D_VIE-1.pdf)
* **Korean** – [한국어 전단지를 보려면 여기를 클릭하세요](https://instituteo1stg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Friendship-Flier-Korean-24_D.pdf)
* **Russian** – [нажмите здесь, чтобы получить листовку на русском языке](https://instituteo1stg.wpenginepowered.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Friendship-Flier-Russian_D-1.pdf)

Our multilingual team is here for you!

### Who We Serve: Seniors, Adults with Disabilities, and Caregivers in California

* **Adults age 60+**
* **Adults living with disabilities of any age**
* **Caregivers seeking emotional support and guidance**

Whether you’re calling for yourself or someone you care about, you’ll find a supportive, judgment-free space with us.

## Center for Elderly Suicide Prevention and Grief Services (CESP)

## **Are you, or someone you know, experiencing grief or loss?**

The Institute on Aging’s Friendship Line offers free grief support through our Center for Elderly Suicide Prevention and Grief Services.

* **Virtual Grief and Bereavement Support Groups**
  + Safe, moderated spaces for adults navigating the loss of a spouse, partner, friend, or family member.
  + Open to individuals throughout California – join from the comfort of your home.
  + Led by trained facilitators specializing in elder grief and trauma recovery.
* **Grief and Bereavement Support is Offered in English.**

These support groups help combat isolation, promote healing, and create space for shared understanding. For more information, email [connect@ioaging.org](mailto:connect@ioaging.org), or call 415.750.4111 and ask about our grief services. Your inquiry will be handled in a confidential and sensitive manner.

## A Program With a Powerful Legacy

Founded in 1973 by Dr. Patrick Arbore, the Friendship Line was born as part of Institute on Aging’s commitment to one powerful truth:

**“Connection to others binds us to life.”**

Today, the Friendship Line responds to more than 11,000 calls every month, in eight different languages, providing comfort and support to aging adults throughout California. The line is accredited by the American Association of Suicidology and is part of IOA’s Center for Elderly Suicide Prevention and Grief-Related Services, one of California’s leading senior mental health services.

**Part of Institute on Aging’s Mission-Driven Approach**

As a nonprofit, Institute on Aging provides the Friendship Line free of charge, with no other agenda other than helping people feel less alone where and when it’s needed most. The Friendship Line isn’t a standalone service and reflects IOA’s deep commitment to emotional wellness and social connection across all stages of aging.

**This program serving the community is funded in part by:**

![](https://www.ioaging.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/logo-das-sf.webp)

![](https://www.ioaging.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/CDA-logo-stacked-white-1.png)

## Addressing the “Crisis of Loneliness and Isolation”

In 2023, U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy declared loneliness and social isolation a national “epidemic”. His report noted that the mortality impact of loneliness is equivalent to smoking 15 cigarettes a day – a greater risk than obesity or sedentary living. And this awareness keeps going – in 2024, San Mateo County became the first in the U.S. to declare loneliness a “public health emergency.”

The Friendship Line helps people forge life-changing connections. From a brief or more in-depth phone call, Friendship Line callers consistently report a more positive outlook following their interactions.

## Volunteer With Us

Want to make a difference in someone’s life – just by listening?  
Become a **Friendship Line Volunteer** and bring light to someone’s darkest day.

For volunteer or intern opportunities, contact: [flvolunteer@ioaging.org](mailto:flvolunteer@ioaging.org "mailto:flvolunteer@ioaging.org")

## Connection Can Be Life-Changing. Call Today.

If you or someone you know is struggling with loneliness, grief, or emotional distress, don’t wait. Pick up the phone. California’s only 24/7 senior emotional support line — the Friendship Line by Institute on Aging. Because no one should face aging – or caregiving – alone.

**24/7 Toll-Free in California:** **888.670.1360**

## RESOURCES FOR OLDER ADULTS

---

## MENTAL HEALTH AND SUICIDE PREVENTION: OLDER ADULTS

---

### AMERICAN FOUNDATION FOR SUICIDE PREVENTION

The Four D’s of Suicide Risk in Older Adults

Dr. Yeates Conwell, Director, Geriatric Psychiatry Program Director, Center for Study and Prevention of Suicide, University of Rochester Medical Center talks about the four D’s that contribute to suicide risk in older adults.

* <https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QcBzrY1WOfM>

---

### FRIENDSHIP LINE

The Institute on Aging’s 24-hour toll-free Friendship Line is the only accredited crisis line in the country for people aged 60 years and older, and adults living with disabilities. Knowing that older people do not contact traditional suicide prevention centers on a regular basis even if they are considering suicide, the Institute created the only program nationwide that reaches out to lonely, depressed, isolated, frail and/or suicidal older adults. Trained volunteers specialize in offering a caring ear and having a friendly conversation with depressed older adults.

The Friendship Line is both a crisis intervention hotline and a warmline for non-emergency emotional support calls. For the 24-hour toll-free FRIENDSHIP LINE call 1-800-971-0016.

* <https://www.ioaging.org/services/all-inclusive-health-care/friendship-line>

---

### CENTER FOR ELDERLY SUICIDE PREVENTION (CESP)

Provides counseling, referrals, grief support programs, and even well-being checks for tens of thousands of older and disabled adults in California and beyond. The Friendship Line is a national helpline. However, outreach and other services are available only in the San Francisco Bay area at this time. For more information, please visit the website or call the Institute on Aging at 1-415-750-4111.

* <https://www.ioaging.org/services/all-inclusive-health-care/psychological-services/center-for-elderly-suicide-prevention>

---

### MENTAL HEALTH AMERICA: Preventing Suicide in Older Adults

Provides a fact sheet identifying the signs and risks for suicide in the age group with links to information on Medicare coverage for mental health services.

* <https://www.mhanational.org/preventing-suicide-older-adults>

---

### HELPGUIDE.ORG

Helpguide’s mission is to help people understand, prevent and resolve many of life’s challenges by providing knowledge and hope. Their goal is to give individuals the information and encouragement they need to take charge of their health, well-being and make healthy choices. The website provides comprehensive information for mental and emotional health; family and relationships; healthy living; and seniors and aging.

* <https://www.helpguide.org/>

The Suicide Prevention page provides an understanding of suicide for all populations, including the higher risk factors for teens and older adults, dispels misconceptions, identifies the warning signs, and offers guidance on how to help.

* <https://www.helpguide.org/articles/suicide-prevention/suicide-prevention.htm>

---

### NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF MENTAL HEALTH “OLDER ADULTS AND MENTAL HEALTH”

Information, brochures, fact sheets, videos and links to federal resources for older adults and mental health.

* <https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/topics/older-adults-and-mental-health/index.shtml>

---

### NATIONAL COUNCIL ON AGING

Information to help seniors with behavioral/mental health issues, economic security, healthy living including falls management, nutrition, chronic disease management.

* <https://www.ncoa.org/>

---

### DRUGS.COM

Drugs.com is an independent medicine information website that aims “to empower patients with the knowledge to better manage their own healthcare and to improve consumer safety by assisting in the reduction of medication errors.”

Help Prevent Suicide in Older Adults: Provides education on suicide risks, warning signs, and guidance for helping an older adult receive the attention and care they need.

* [https://www.drugs.com/cg/help-prevent-suicide-in-older-adults.html](https://www.drugs.com/cg/help-prevent-suicide-in-older-adults.html )

---

## SERVICES FOR OLDER ADULTS

---

## SANTA CLARITA VALLEY

---

### SCV SENIOR CENTER

Services include Adult Day Program, the only licensed adult day care program in the Santa Clarita Valley that specializes in the care and activities for adults with Alzheimer’s disease, other types of dementia, post-stroke, Parkinson’s or other conditions requiring assistance and supervision. Other services include Care Management; Caregiver Support; In-home Care; Senior Access; a package of services designed to aid and assist low to moderate-income populations age 50 and older who reside in the city of Santa Clarita, and who may be at risk of homelessness and or institutionalization; Telephone Reassurance provides daily phone contact (Monday – Friday) with homebound individuals who live alone; Elderly Nutrition Program; Health & Wellness Education & Clinics; and a Handyworker Program. Located at 27180 Golden Valley Road, Santa Clarita. Call (661) 259-9444

* <https://myscvcoa.org/>

---

### COMFORT KEEPERS

Comfort Keepers provides award-winning in-home care for seniors and adults who need assistance at home. Comfort Keepers In-Home Care Services in Santa Clarita specializes in keeping seniors safe and independent in their own home, wherever that home may be. We've named our unique style of care Interactive Caregiving®, and it is built around the idea that meaningful interaction with seniors is key to helping them stay active and engaged.

Caregivers have one goal: enriching the lives of our clients and their families. We achieve this by maintaining their safety, well-being, and comfort as they continue to live independently. In-home care gives seniors freedom despite limited mobility, chronic conditions, and other age-related considerations.

We understand the struggle family members face when a loved one needs extra assistance in their home, and we’re here to help. Let our caregivers relieve this stress by providing professional home care services with a personal touch.

Call (661) 287-4200 to learn how our family can help your family navigate the process of aging and home care for an aging loved one in the Santa Clarita and North San Fernando Valleys.

* <https://www.comfortkeepers.com/offices/california/santa-clarita>

---

## GREATER LOS ANGELES

---

### LOS ANGELES COUNTY DEPARTMENT OF MENTAL HEALTH OLDER ADULT SYSTEMS OF CARE

Links to agencies that provide mental health services including screening and assessment, case management services, individual and family treatment, and crisis intervention services. 1-800-854-7771

* <https://dmh.lacounty.gov/our-services/older-adults/>

---

### COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT, AGING AND COMMUNITY SERVICES (WDACS)

This website contains descriptions of various programs available to help older adults and provides links to program providers. Older adults can learn how to access: Meals and nutrition programs; Support Services to promote and maintain independent living; Health Insurance Counseling; Legal Services Counseling and more.

Families can learn how to access ombudsman services, location services if a loved one goes missing, case management services, Adult Protective Services and more. Phone: (888) 211-0644. Phone for LA County Services: 211. Email: [[email protected]](/cdn-cgi/l/email-protection).

* [http://wdacs.lacounty.gov/](http://wdacs.lacounty.gov/	)

---

### LOS ANGELES COUNTY ADULT PROTECTIVE SERVICES

Adult Protective Services (APS) is a social services program provided by state and/or local governments nationwide serving older adults who are 60 years and older and adults with disabilities who need assistance. APS workers investigate cases of abuse, neglect or exploitation, working closely with a wide variety of allied professionals such as physicians, nurses, paramedics, firefighters and law enforcement officers.

Elder Abuse Hotline Call 1-877-477-3646 or 211. Lines are open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.

Long Term Care Related Reports Call 1-800-334-9473. Monday-Friday 8:30-5:30, or (800) 231-4024 after hours.

Non-emergency reports may be submitted online at the website below.

* <https://wdacs.lacounty.gov/services/older-dependent-adult-services/adult-protective-services-aps/>

---

### CALIFORNIA DEPARTMENT OF AGING

Administers programs that serve older adults, adults with disabilities, family caregivers, and residents in long-term care facilities throughout the State. These services are provided locally by the Area Agencies on Aging (AAA), Medi-Cal Community Based Adult Services (CBAS) centers, or other contracted agencies. available to those over 60 years of age, regardless of income level.

* <https://www.aging.ca.gov/>

---

### JEWISH FAMILY SERVICE LA

Mental health services include: individual and group counseling available in home, in community and via telehealth for to eligible individuals. Individuals with Medi-Cal, Medicare/Medi-Cal and low income and with no insurance are eligible. Individuals with a Medicare HMO are not eligible. Services are provided at 12821 Victory Boulevard North Hollywood, CA 91606. They are nonsectarian and available in English, Spanish, Russian, Farsi, and Korean.

A homeless prevention program is available to those residing in the Metro LA area and West LA area, age 55+ and is focused on those adults living with a hoarding disorder and/or at risk of becoming homeless as a result. In additional, JFSLA offers a Multipurpose Senior Services Program (MSSP), which is a nonsectarian state-funded program that provides a community-based alternative to nursing home care for frail older adults. MSSP provides and purchases services for eligible clients and their families that enable clients to remain in their homes. Nurses and social workers coordinate complete plans of care, arrange and purchase services which assist clients to remain at home safely and independently.

* <https://www.jfsla.org/page.aspx?pid=228>

---

### ELDERCARE LOCATOR

A public service of the U.S. Administration on Aging connecting you to services for older adults and their families. Learn more about support services, housing, elder rights, insurance and benefits, health and transportation. The website offers guidance and helpful resources or call 1-800-677-1116.

* <https://eldercare.acl.gov/Public/Index.aspx>

---

### MEALS ON WHEELS

Meals on Wheels is the only federally supported program designed specifically to meet the nutritional and social needs of seniors. Frequent in-home visits provide unique opportunities to meet nutritional needs, combat social isolation, address safety hazards and provide holistic care.

* <https://www.mealsonwheelsamerica.org/>

---

### A PLACE FOR MOM

A Place for Mom helps seniors and their families find senior care and housing based on their unique needs and budget. It is the largest senior living referral service in cities across the U.S. and Canada. A Place for Mom provides referrals to senior living communities within a network and is paid by those senior living communities and care providers so our service is provided to consumers at no charge. The website contains articles to help elders and family caregivers. Call (866) 750-5930.

* Connecting families to senior living - <https://www.aplaceformom.com/>

---

## RESOURCES FOR HEALTH LIVING

---

### AARP (AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF RETIRED PEOPLE)

U.S. based interest group whose stated mission is “to empower people to choose how they live as they age.”

* <http://www.aarp.org/>

---

### NATIONAL COUNCIL ON AGING

Empowering older adults to live healthier. Programs give older adults the knowledge and tools to prevent falls, manage chronic conditions and improve their lives.

* [http://www.ncoa.org/](http://www.ncoa.org/ )

---

### AmeriCorps Seniors

Volunteers age 55+ use the skills and talents they’ve learned over the years and develop new ones while serving their communities through Senior Corps programs, through its Foster Grandparent, Senior Companion, and RSVP programs enriching the lives of the volunteers and benefiting their communities.

* <https://www.nationalservice.gov/programs/senior-corps>

---

### EngAGED (THE NATIONAL RESOURCE CENTER FOR ENGAGING OLDER ADULTS)

Promotes and provides opportunities to improve the rates of social engagement in older adults because remaining socially engaged improves quality of life and is associated with better health.

* <https://www.engagingolderadults.org>

---

## RESOURCES FOR CAREGIVERS AND SENIOR FACILITIES

---

### CAREGIVER ACTION NETWORK

Caregiver Action Network (CAN) is the nation’s leading family caregiver organization working to improve the quality of life for more than 90 million Americans who care for loved ones with chronic condition, disabilities, disease, or the frailties of old age. CAN serves a broad spectrum of family caregivers ranging from the parents of children with significant health needs, to the families and friends of wounded soldiers; from a young couple dealing with a diagnosis of MS, to adult children caring for parents with Alzheimer’s disease. CAN is a non-profit organization providing education, peer support, and resources to family caregivers across the country free of charge. Caregiver Help Desk: (855) 227-3640

* <https://caregiveraction.org/>

---

### SENIORSMATTER.COM

SeniorsMatter.com is an online community dedicated through our virtual platforms to enhancing the knowledge, efficiency and effectiveness of senior caregivers by providing objective information, guidance, training and the latest developments in senior caregiving.

Article: Suicide Rates in the Elderly — Presents research, identifies possible causes, and recommendations for helping.

* <https://seniorsmatter.com/suicide-rates-in-the-elderly/>

---

### Resources for Senior Living Communities and Senior Centers

---

Information and articles regarding older adults and suicide including:

* PROMOTING EMOTIONAL HEALTH AND PREVENTING SUICIDE: A TOOLKIT FOR SENIOR CENTERS - <https://www.sprc.org/resources-programs/promoting-emotional-health-and-preventing-suicide-toolkit-senior-centers>
  
* PROGRAM TO ENCOURAGE ACTIVE, REWARDING LIVES (PEARLS) -intervention for adults and older adults with a depression or dysthymia diagnosis, aims to reduce symptoms of depression and suicidal ideation and improve quality of life, delivered in six to eight 50-minute sessions by a trained health or social service professional (e.g., social worker, nurse, case manager) in the client's home or other community-based setting. Sessions are initially held weekly and become less frequent over a four- to five-month period. - <https://www.sprc.org/resources-programs/program-encourage-active-rewarding-lives-pearls>

##### 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

- The [988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline](https://988lifeline.org/) (formerly known as the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline) offers 24/7 call, text and chat access to trained crisis counselors who can help people experiencing suicidal, substance use, and/or mental health crisis, or any other kind of emotional distress. People can also dial 988 if they are worried about a loved one who may need crisis support.

# The Value of the Friendship Line in Enhancing Mental Health for Seniors

## **Introduction: A Growing Crisis of Loneliness**

Loneliness and social isolation among older adults are public health challenges that profoundly affect mental and physical well-being. Research consistently demonstrates that these conditions are associated with adverse health outcomes, including increased risks of depression, cognitive decline, and mortality. Institute on Aging (IOA) has been at the forefront of addressing these challenges through the **Friendship Line**, a pioneering program offering emotional support and friendly conversation to seniors. [Founded in 1973](https://www.ioaging.org/services/friendship-line/) by Dr. Patrick Arbore, the Friendship Line operates as California’s largest warm line, answering over 11,000 inbound and outbound calls monthly and providing a vital connection for seniors facing loneliness.

The program’s effectiveness in combating loneliness is underscored by scientific research and the personal experiences of its participants. This white paper explores the critical role of the Friendship Line in improving the mental health of seniors, incorporating findings from a peer-reviewed study and insights from a co-author’s speech.

## **The Friendship Line: A Lifeline for Seniors**

Dr. Patrick Arbore founded the Friendship Line with the belief that “connection to others binds us to life.” This philosophy underpins the program’s mission to alleviate loneliness and provide emotional support for seniors who may be socially isolated or struggling with feelings of disconnection. Accredited by the American Association of Suicidology, the Friendship Line is a cornerstone of IOA’s Center for Elderly Suicide Prevention and Grief-Related Services.

Operating as a warm line rather than a hotline, the Friendship Line is unique in its dual functionality: it allows seniors to call for immediate emotional support while also enabling proactive outreach to individuals identified as at risk. Staffed by trained professionals and volunteers, the program ensures no call goes unanswered, offering an unparalleled sense of reliability and connection.

## **Scientific Validation: Evidence-Based Benefits**

A recent study published in the *[New York Academy of Sciences](https://nyaspubs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/nyas.15223)* journal, co-authored by IOA Vice President of Strategic Partnerships [Preston Burnes](https://www.linkedin.com/in/prestonb/), provides compelling evidence of the Friendship Line’s impact. The study enrolled 121 older adults identified as at risk for loneliness through a Medicare Advantage health plan and tracked their progress over six months. Key findings include:

* **Loneliness Reduction:** The percentage of participants reporting loneliness decreased from **46% to 28% (p<0.001)**.
* **Improved Mental Health:** Depression rates fell from **36% to 25% (p=0.07)**, and anxiety rates dropped from **63% to 43% (p=0.004)**.
* **Enhanced Quality of Life:** Participants experienced fewer unhealthy mental health days (14 to 8, p<0.001) and unhealthy physical health days (15 to 11, p<0.001).

These findings highlight the program’s ability to address both the subjective experience of loneliness and its tangible effects on mental and physical health.

Participants also expressed high satisfaction with the program, 75% felt the friendship line made them feel more socially connected. Many attributed improved mood and overall health to the consistent and empathetic phone calls. Notably, even those experiencing occasional loneliness found value in the Friendship Line, underscoring its broad applicability.

## **Understanding Loneliness and Social Isolation**

To appreciate the significance of the Friendship Line, it is essential to distinguish between loneliness and social isolation, as explained in a recent speech by Katrina A. Hough, the  lead author of the journal article:

* Social Isolation is an objective state defined by a lack of social interactions or relationships. It can be quantified by the number of interactions an individual has with others.
* Loneliness, on the other hand, is a subjective feeling of being disconnected or unfulfilled in social relationships. A person may feel lonely even when surrounded by others.

While related, these conditions have distinct implications for health. Loneliness is associated with heart disease, poor sleep, cognitive decline, and increased mortality, with its effects comparable to smoking 15 cigarettes a day. Social isolation also correlates with poor health outcomes, including disability and poorly controlled chronic conditions.

The Friendship Line addresses both loneliness and social isolation by fostering meaningful connections, thereby mitigating their harmful effects.

## **Why Talking Matters: The Power of Connection**

Hough further highlighted the mechanisms by which social connection promotes better health outcomes. Engaging in conversations and maintaining social ties:

1. **Enhances Cognitive Reserve:** Social interactions can bolster cognitive reserve, potentially delaying the onset of dementia by keeping the brain active and engaged.
2. **Reduces Stigma and Shame:** Many seniors with cognitive impairments or chronic illnesses withdraw socially due to feelings of embarrassment or shame. The Friendship Line provides a safe and judgment-free space to connect.
3. **Supports Caregivers:** Caregivers often experience loneliness and depression, which can be alleviated through support programs like the Friendship Line.

For seniors experiencing physical limitations, bereavement, or changes in living situations, having someone to talk to can significantly improve mental health and quality of life. The Friendship Line’s emphasis on proactive outreach ensures that even those who may not initiate contact receive the support they need.

## **Broader Implications: A Model for Social Prescribing**

IOA’s Friendship Line exemplifies the emerging concept of social prescribing, where healthcare providers connect patients with community resources to address non-medical determinants of health. Social prescribing recognizes that health is not merely the absence of disease but also the presence of social and emotional well-being.

As Hough noted, loneliness and social isolation are public health issues that demand systemic solutions. Programs like the Friendship Line, which seamlessly integrate with healthcare systems, demonstrate the potential for community-based interventions to improve health outcomes on a large scale.

## **Looking Ahead: Opportunities for Expansion**

The success of the Friendship Line underscores the need for continued investment in programs that address loneliness among seniors. Opportunities for expansion include:

* **Scaling the Model Nationwide:** By partnering with other organizations and healthcare providers, the Friendship Line’s model can be replicated across the country.
* **Leveraging Technology:** Integrating digital tools, such as video calls or app-based support, can enhance accessibility for tech-savvy seniors.
* **Collaborative Research:** Further studies can explore the long-term effects of telephone-based interventions and identify best practices for scaling similar programs.

## **Conclusion: A Lifeline That Saves Lives**

IOA’s Friendship Line is more than a phone call—it is a lifeline that provides hope, connection, and emotional support to seniors who might otherwise feel forgotten. Backed by scientific evidence and decades of success, the program stands as a model for addressing loneliness and enhancing mental health among older adults. As society grapples with the growing epidemic of loneliness, the Friendship Line offers a proven solution that binds us to life, one conversation at a time.

Join us in combating senior loneliness—call, donate, or volunteer today at [ioaging.org/friendship-line](https://www.ioaging.org/services/friendship-line/).

args.summary: This white paper from the Institute on Aging (IOA) highlights the Friendship Line, a pioneering warm line program founded in 1973 by Dr. Patrick Arbore to combat loneliness and social isolation among seniors. Operating as California's largest warm line, it handles over 11,000 calls monthly and provides emotional support through both inbound calls and proactive outreach. A peer-reviewed study published in the New York Academy of Sciences, co-authored by IOA's Preston Burnes and lead author Katrina A. Hough, enrolled 121 older adults at risk for loneliness over six months. Key findings include: loneliness reduction from 46% to 28% (p<0.001), depression rates falling from 36% to 25% (p=0.07), anxiety dropping from 63% to 43% (p=0.004), and unhealthy mental health days decreasing from 14 to 8 (p<0.001). 75% of participants felt more socially connected. The paper distinguishes between social isolation (objective lack of interactions) and loneliness (subjective feeling of disconnection), noting loneliness is as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. The Friendship Line addresses both by fostering meaningful connections and exemplifies the concept of social prescribing. Opportunities for expansion include scaling nationwide, leveraging technology, and further research.

Join us in Philadelphia for the 2026 Village to Village Network Conference, held in conjunction with the 2026 LeadingAge Annual Meeting! Don’t miss this chance to engage with thought leaders, share experiences, and shape the future of Villages!

### About the Village to Village Network

The Village to Village Network is a membership-based organization uniting Villages nationwide to exchange best practices and support the mission of helping older adults lead independent, healthy, and purposeful lives. Through expert guidance, resources, and advocacy, The Village to Village Network champions the Village model as a proven solution for fostering vibrant aging communities.

[LEARN MORE](https://www.vtvnetwork.org)

# Intergenerational Social Connections

While social isolation has long been identified as a concern for older adult populations, COVID-19 amplified the risk of it and awareness that we need increased attention to preventative efforts and interventions for both youth and older adults. The Intergenerational Social Connections (ISC) project builds on the Public Health Institute of Western Massachusetts' [Live Well Springfield Age-Friendly Initiative](/live-well-springfield), the [Youth Mental Health Roadmap for Western MA](/reports/ymh-roadmap), and the [Youth Mental Health Coalition](/youth-mental-health) to assess strategies, opportunities, and programming for social connection and social inclusion from an intergenerational perspective. Drawing on the Age-Friendly framework domain of Respect and Social Inclusion and the Youth Mental Health Roadmap, we are focusing on what supports, enhances, or creates challenges to intergenerational connection in Springfield.

## Goals

The goal of the ISC project is to foster stronger connections between generations—particularly youth (middle and high school students) and older adults (65+)—to address issues of social isolation and loneliness in Springfield, MA, through promoting intergenerational social connections, building upon existing community programs and partnerships, and addressing public health issues tied to loneliness and isolation.

Coalition Building

## Our Role

PHIWM is convening and leading this project in collaboration with members of the Springfield community. Year 1 will focus on conducting an assessment to better understand the needs and strengths in our community for intergenerational connections, as well as the interests and barriers faced by community residents, so that we can identify strategies to reduce loneliness in Springfield. In addition, we are building an Intergenerational Advisory Board, including representatives from groups convening older adults, members of the Youth Mental Health Coalition, and older adult and youth advisors. Years 2 and 3 will focus on the implementation of strategies identified in the assessment process.

The strategies being considered include: 

1. **Skill-building:** One generation teaches the other a particular skill
2. **Shared Activities:** Youth and older adults take part in a class, program, or activity together
3. **Mentoring:** Older adults and youth are matched one-to-one and build a relationship over time
4. **Built Environment:** Changes to the places we live, work, and play that encourage younger and older people to connect
5. **Communications:** A campaign to encourage social connection (e.g., on social media, posters, billboards, radio, etc.)

PHIWM will work with the Advisory Committee to create and execute an implementation plan.

![5 ways to increase social connection among young people and older adults](https://irp.cdn-website.com/8a359c3c/dms3rep/multi/opt/5+ways+to+increase+social+connection+among+young+people+and+older+adults-1920w.png)

## Partners

The Public Health Institute of Western Massachusetts intentionally involves youth and older adult resident advisors that represent the very age groups that this project is focused on. **Our Advisory Board**  includes these resident advisors and the following organizations: Baystate Health, Behavioral Health Network, City of Springfield, Community Music School of Springfield/Trust Transfer Project, Faith Based Health Alliance, Live Well Springfield, MLK Family Services, Mason Wright Senior Living, Treehouse Foundation, Youth Mental Health Coalition, UMASS Amherst Center for Community Living, and Urban League of Greater Springfield. 

**Experts** have also been invited to present to the Advisory Board about local intergenerational work already happening. This has been a tremendous learning opportunity. The following organizations have presented on their work: Treehouse Foundation, Springfield Dementia Friendly Coalition, Springfield Youth Health Survey, Mason Wright Senior Living, Faith Based Health Alliance, and Dr. Gloria DiFulvio’s work on intergenerational community engagement and storytelling at UMASS Amherst’s School of Public Health & Health Sciences. We will continue learning about loneliness and intergenerational work from these types of experts throughout the project. 

﻿

4. Built Environment (changes to places that encourage connection)

--- SOURCE 1: Social Isolation and Loneliness in Older Adults ---
URL: https://www.nationalacademies.org/projects/HMD-HSP-17-25/publication/25663

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine webpage details a completed consensus study (2020) on the health impacts of social isolation and loneliness in adults aged 50 and older, particularly among low-income, underserved, and vulnerable populations. The study was sponsored by the AARP Foundation.

Key findings: Approximately one-quarter of community-dwelling Americans aged 65+ are socially isolated, and social isolation presents a major risk for premature mortality comparable to high blood pressure, smoking, or obesity.

The committee, chaired by Dan G. Blazer II, was tasked with: 1) examining evidence linking social isolation/loneliness to poor health outcomes; 2) exploring effects on healthcare access and utilization; 3) making evidence-based recommendations for healthcare system interventions; and 4) examining translation and dissemination of findings to healthcare practitioners.

The resulting publication, 'Social Isolation and Loneliness in Older Adults: Opportunities for the Health Care System' (316 pages, ISBN 0-309-67100-0), provides recommendations for clinical settings to identify those suffering negative health impacts and target interventions to improve social conditions.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Approximately one-quarter of community-dwelling Americans aged 65 and older are considered to be socially isolated, and a significant proportion of adults in the United States report feeling lonely., A substantial body of evidence demonstrates that social isolation presents a major risk for premature mortality, comparable to other risk factors such as high blood pressure, smoking, or obesity., Social isolation and loneliness are serious yet underappreciated public health risks that affect a significant portion of the older adult population., As older adults are particularly high-volume and high-frequency users of the health care system, there is an opportunity for health care professionals to identify, prevent, and mitigate the adverse health impacts of social isolation and loneliness in older adults., Social Isolation and Loneliness in Older Adults considers clinical tools and methodologies, better education and training for the health care workforce, and dissemination and implementation that will be important for translating research into practice.
</key_excerpts>



--------------------------------------------------------------------------------


--- SOURCE 2: Summary - Social Isolation and Loneliness in Older Adults - NCBI Bookshelf ---
URL: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557972

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage is the Summary from the 2020 National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine consensus report "Social Isolation and Loneliness in Older Adults: Opportunities for the Health Care System." The report focuses on adults aged 50 and older, emphasizing that social isolation (objective lack of social contact) and loneliness (subjective feeling of being isolated) are serious public health risks. Approximately 24% of community-dwelling Americans aged 65+ are socially isolated, and 35% of adults 45+ (43% of those 60+) report feeling lonely.

The committee's charge was twofold: (1) summarize evidence on how social isolation and loneliness affect health and quality of life in older adults, particularly at-risk populations, and (2) identify opportunities for the health care system to help reduce adverse health impacts. The health care system is uniquely positioned because nearly all older adults interact with it, making it a key entry point for identifying and intervening with at-risk individuals.

KEY FINDINGS:
- Social isolation and loneliness are distinct phenomena; they are often not significantly correlated.
- More than four decades of research shows lacking social connection is associated with significantly increased risk for premature mortality from all causes—comparable to or greater than other well-established risk factors.
- Strong evidence links social isolation and loneliness to physical, cognitive, and psychological morbidity, health-related behaviors, and quality of life.

FIVE GOALS AND RECOMMENDATIONS:
1. **Develop a More Robust Evidence Base** – Fund research on social isolation/loneliness at levels reflecting their association with mortality; improve understanding of mechanisms, risk factors, and interventions.
2. **Translate Research into Health Care Practices** – Use validated tools to assess social isolation/loneliness in clinical settings; include social isolation in electronic health records.
3. **Improve Awareness** – Include measures in major health strategies/surveys; create public awareness campaigns.
4. **Strengthen Education and Training** – Incorporate social isolation/loneliness into health professions curricula and continuing education.
5. **Strengthen Ties Between Health Care and Community Networks** – Partner with social service providers; establish a national resource center to centralize evidence, training, and best practices.

The committee emphasizes that the health care system alone cannot solve these challenges but must connect with public health and social care communities. Key recommendations include funding research (NIH, CMS, PCORI), using validated assessment tools, including social isolation in EHRs, and creating a national resource center under HHS.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
Social isolation (the objective state of having few social relationships or infrequent social contact with others) and loneliness (a subjective feeling of being isolated) are serious yet underappreciated public health risks that affect a significant portion of the older adult population., Approximately one-quarter (24 percent) of community-dwelling Americans aged 65 and older are considered to be socially isolated, and a significant proportion of adults in the United States report feeling lonely (35 percent of adults aged 45 and older and 43 percent of adults aged 60 and older)., More than four decades of research has produced robust evidence that lacking social connection—and, particularly, scoring high on measures of social isolation—is associated with a significantly increased risk for premature mortality from all causes., Furthermore, there is some evidence that the magnitude of the effect of social connection on risk for mortality may be comparable to or greater than other well-established risk factors that are widely recognized and acted on by the public health and health care systems., The health care system has the potential to be a critical component of a much larger solution.
</key_excerpts>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the National Council on Aging (NCOA) discusses social isolation and loneliness among older adults. Key points include:

- Social isolation (objectively few relationships) differs from loneliness (subjective feeling of disconnection), though they often co-occur.
- Nearly one-fourth of adults 65+ are socially isolated; over 20% of U.S. adults identify as lonely, isolated, or both.
- Risk factors include living alone, losing loved ones, chronic illness, hearing loss, and COVID-19 impacts on long-term care residents.
- Loneliness can increase mortality risk by 50%—higher than air pollution, obesity, or excessive alcohol use—and is linked to high blood pressure, heart disease, cognitive decline, Alzheimer's, and depression.
- Disconnection follows a U-shaped curve across life, with high loneliness in young adulthood and later life.
- Technology can supplement (not replace) in-person connection, with more tools being designed for older adults.
- Multigenerational friendships (nearly 40% of adults have a close friend 15+ years apart) offer unique benefits like broadening perspectives and providing role models.

URL: https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/loneliness-and-social-isolation/loneliness-and-social-isolation-tips-staying-connected

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the National Institute on Aging (NIA) addresses loneliness and social isolation among older adults, providing definitions, health risks, and strategies for staying connected.

**Key definitions:** Loneliness is the distressing feeling of being alone or separated, while social isolation is the lack of social contacts and having few people to interact with regularly. Older adults face higher risks due to changes in health (hearing, vision, memory loss), disability, mobility issues, and loss of family/friends.

**Health risks:** Social isolation and loneliness are associated with higher risks for high blood pressure, heart disease, obesity, weakened immune function, anxiety, depression, cognitive decline, dementia (including Alzheimer's), and death. People experiencing these may also exercise less, drink more alcohol, smoke, and sleep poorly. Chronic loneliness can trigger stress responses leading to chronic inflammation and reduced immunity.

**Risk factors:** Loss of mobility, vision/hearing problems, psychological challenges, lack of purpose, financial struggles, living alone, lack of transportation, major life changes (death of a loved one, retirement), separation from friends/family, caregiving responsibilities, living in rural/unsafe areas, discrimination, and language barriers.

**Strategies for staying connected:** Find enjoyable activities or hobbies, schedule daily contact with family/friends (in-person, phone, video, email, social media), use communication technologies, consider adopting a pet, stay physically active (150 minutes of moderate activity weekly), connect with neighbors, join faith-based organizations, explore local community centers and senior centers, and volunteer.

**Special guidance for those with dementia living alone:** Identify a trusted person for regular visits and emergency contact, learn about community-based support services, stay connected via technology, and join support groups or memory cafés.

**Resources provided:** Eldercare Locator (800-677-1116), NIA ADEAR Center (800-438-4380), AmeriCorps Seniors, AARP, Family Caregiver Alliance, Meals on Wheels America, and others.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 6: Association of social isolation, loneliness and risk of cardiovascular diseases: Meta-analysis of cohort studies ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12462301

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This meta-analysis, published in BMC Public Health (2025) by Wang et al., examines the association between social isolation, loneliness, and risk of cardiovascular diseases (CVD). The study included 6 cohort studies with 5,253,128 participants, with follow-up periods ranging from 4 to 11.3 years, published between 1996 and 2022. All studies were of high quality (NOS score ≥ 7). --- SOURCE 2: Social Isolation and Loneliness in Older Adults: Review and Commentary of a National Academies Report ---
URL: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7437541

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article, published in the American Journal of Geriatric Psychiatry (August 2020), provides a comprehensive review of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine (NASEM) consensus committee report on Social Isolation and Loneliness (SI/L) in older adults, authored by committee members Nancy J. Donovan and Dan Blazer. The report was commissioned by the AARP Foundation in 2018 and released in February 2020 as the COVID-19 pandemic was emerging.

**Key Definitions:** Social isolation is the objective lack of social contacts, while loneliness is the subjective feeling of being isolated. They are distinct—socially isolated persons may not feel lonely, and socially connected persons may feel lonely.

**Epidemiology:** Prior to COVID-19, 24% of U.S. adults aged 65+ (7.7 million people) were socially isolated, and 4% were severely isolated. 43% of Americans aged 60+ reported feeling lonely. Older socially isolated adults tend to be among the oldest old, unmarried, male, with low education and income.

**Health Consequences:** SI/L are associated with a 50% increased risk of dementia, 30% increased risk of coronary artery disease or stroke, and 26% increased risk of all-cause mortality. The excess mortality risk from social isolation rivals that of obesity and smoking. SI/L are also linked to depression, anxiety, suicidal ideation, and reduced quality of life.

**Mechanisms:** Three categories of mediators link SI/L to health outcomes: behavioral (poorer health behaviors, sleep disruption), psychological (heightened stress response), and biological (cardiovascular, neuroendocrine, and inflammatory pathway dysregulation, including elevated blood pressure, cortisol dysregulation, and increased inflammatory markers).

**Interventions:** The report reviewed 92 published interventions. Most effective approaches specifically targeted socially isolated or lonely individuals, had a sound theoretical basis, used multileveled approaches, and involved active participant engagement. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and mindfulness-based approaches showed promise. Tele-delivered behavioral activation interventions for homebound older adults demonstrated improvements in social interaction and loneliness. No pharmacologic interventions are currently evidenced for reducing SI/L.

**Healthcare System Role:** The committee developed five goals: (1) develop stronger evidence on assessment and intervention, (2) translate research into practice, (3-4) improve awareness and training, and (5) strengthen ties between healthcare and community networks. The report emphasized the importance of screening for SI/L using validated measures (e.g., Berkman-Syme Social Network Index, UCLA Loneliness Scale) and integrating these into electronic health records.

**Technology:** Technological applications range from video-conferencing to advanced AI and virtual reality, though questions of accessibility, acceptability, cost, and privacy remain.
</summary>

# A 50-state survey study of thoughts of suicide and social isolation among older adults in the United States

## Background & Methods
This study analyzed data from 6 waves of a 50-state non-probability internet-based survey conducted between February and December 2021 (The COVID States Project). The sample included 16,164 respondents aged 65 and older (mean age 70.9, SD 5.0; 61.4% female; 86.8% White, 6.7% Black, 2.2% Hispanic, 2.0% Asian). The study used the PHQ-9 to assess depressive symptoms and thoughts of suicide (item 9), and multiple measures of social connectedness including household size, face-to-face interactions, social support (emotional, financial, caregiving, employment), and loneliness. Multiple logistic regression and generalized random forests were used for analysis.

## Key Findings
- **Prevalence**: 7.1% of older adults (1,144 respondents) reported thoughts of suicide at least several days in the prior 2-week period; 2.4% reported such symptoms more than half the time.
- **Living alone**: 25.6% lived alone, but living alone was NOT associated with greater risk of suicidality. In fact, living in larger households (3+ additional members) was associated with higher odds of thoughts of suicide (adjusted OR 1.73, 95% CI 1.28–2.33).
- **Social support**: Lack of social supports was strongly associated with thoughts of suicide. The largest effect was for lack of emotional support (adjusted OR 2.60, 95% CI 2.09–3.23), followed by lack of health/caregiving support (OR 2.24), financial support (OR 1.69), and employment support (OR 1.54).
- **Loneliness**: Greater loneliness scores were significantly associated with suicidality (adjusted OR 1.75, 95% CI 1.64–1.87).
- **Heterogeneity**: Effects varied across sociodemographic groups. The association between emotional support and thoughts of suicide was strongest among "younger-old" adults (65-74) compared to those 75+, and among those in higher-income households and larger households.

## Conclusions
Thoughts of suicide are common among older adults in the US and are associated with lack of social support and loneliness, but not with living alone. Emotional social support was the strongest predictor. The findings highlight the need for targeted psychosocial interventions that modify social risk factors for suicidality in this vulnerable population. The study was conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, which may have influenced results.

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review

## Overview
This meta-analysis, published in *PLoS Medicine* (July 27, 2010), investigates the extent to which social relationships influence mortality risk. The study was conducted by Julianne Holt-Lunstad, Timothy B. Smith, and J. Bradley Layton.

## Key Findings
- **Across 148 studies (308,849 participants)**, the random effects weighted average effect size was **OR = 1.50 (95% CI 1.42 to 1.59)**, indicating a **50% increased likelihood of survival** for participants with stronger social relationships.
- This finding remained consistent across age, sex, initial health status, cause of death, and follow-up period.
- Significant differences were found across the type of social measurement evaluated (p<0.001):
  - Strongest association: complex measures of social integration (OR = 1.91; 95% CI 1.63 to 2.23)
  - Lowest: binary indicators of residential status (living alone vs. with others) (OR = 1.19; 95% CI 0.99 to 1.44)

## Context
- The authors note that social relationships in industrialized societies are decreasing (three-fold increase in Americans reporting no close confidant over the past two decades).
- The influence of social relationships on mortality risk is **comparable with well-established risk factors** such as smoking, alcohol consumption, and exceeds the influence of physical inactivity and obesity.

## Methods
- Studies from January 1900 to January 2007 were identified via multiple electronic databases.
- 148 prospective studies were included, with participants from North America (51%), Europe (37%), Asia (11%), and Australia (1%).
- Average participant age at intake: 63.9 years; 49% female, 51% male.
- Average follow-up: 7.5 years (range: 3 months to 58 years).
- Three major components of social relationships were evaluated: (a) degree of integration in social networks, (b) received social support, and (c) perceived social support.

## Conclusions
The authors conclude that the influence of social relationships on risk for mortality is comparable with well-established risk factors for mortality. They recommend that physicians, health professionals, educators, and the media acknowledge social relationships as a significant factor affecting health outcomes.

--- SOURCE 1: Correlates of Loneliness and Social Isolation among Older Adults during the COVID-19 Outbreak: A Comprehensive Assessment from a National United States Sample ---
URL: https://www.mdpi.com/2308-3417/9/4/96

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in Geriatrics (2024), examines correlates of loneliness and social isolation among U.S. older adults during the COVID-19 outbreak using data from the 2020 National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS), a nationally representative sample of 3,257 respondents aged 65+ (representing 26,229,876 older adults). The study used weighted multiple logistic regression models to analyze sociodemographic, health, social support, and community correlates of three outcomes: loneliness during COVID-19, higher loneliness compared to pre-pandemic, and social isolation.

Key findings: About 35.2% reported loneliness during the outbreak, 21.9% reported higher loneliness than before COVID-19, and 32.8% were socially isolated. 

**Loneliness correlates** (increased odds): female gender (86% higher), college education (82% higher), physical activity (53% higher), depression (187% higher), anxiety (173% higher), and functional limitations (66% higher). Protective factors: being married (49% lower odds), having one child (30% lower), good sleep quality (82% lower), and being Black (35% lower odds compared to White).

**Higher pandemic loneliness correlates** (increased odds): female (103% higher), college degree (148% higher), physical activity (38% higher), anxiety (92% higher), and virtual communication access (64% higher). Protective: being married (32% lower), having one child (37% lower), employment (52% lower), Black (35% lower), and good sleep quality (68% lower).

**Social isolation correlates** (increased odds): higher age (3% per year), Black (45% higher), Hispanic (76% higher), children in household (one child: 47% higher; two+: 148% higher), and metropolitan residence (42% higher). Protective: physical activity (37% lower), higher income (48% lower), virtual communication access (34% lower), and transportation access (65% lower).

The study found that many correlates for loneliness and social isolation were mutually exclusive or had opposing directional relationships, underscoring the need to examine both constructs separately. The authors recommend multifaceted interventions spanning individual, community, and societal levels to address the social disconnection epidemic among older adults.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This study, published in JAMA on December 9, 2024, characterizes loneliness and social isolation among US adults aged 50-80 using data from the University of Michigan National Poll on Healthy Aging across six time points (October 2018, June 2020, January 2021, January 2022, January 2023, and March 2024). Loneliness is defined as the subjective feeling of being alone, while social isolation is the objective lack of connections to family, friends, or community. The authors note that while the pandemic disrupted social connections, rates were substantial both before and after the early pandemic. Limitations include possible recall bias, self-reported data, and non-longitudinal design. The authors recommend clinicians consider screening older adults for loneliness and social isolation, much like routinely asking about diet and exercise.

This is a transcript of a webinar titled "Barriers to digital literacy for older adults: Bridging the Digital Divide," co-hosted by Elder Abuse Prevention Ontario and the Ontario Age-Friendly Communities Outreach Program on March 24, 2025.

**Presentations:**

**Dr. Madison Robertson (Research Coordinator, Centre for Studies in Aging and Health)** presented on the barriers to digital literacy for older adults. Key findings from a scoping review identified seven main barriers:

1. **Health Barriers:** Poor motor skills, visual/hearing difficulties, physical impairments (arthritis, cataracts), and cognitive impairments (memory loss).
2. **Support Network Barriers:** Lack of social support from family/friends; dependence on younger family members is not always feasible; negative interactions can discourage use.
3. **Convenience and Use Barriers:** Poor design/interface (small fonts, complex authentications); continuous updates causing confusion and loss of confidence.
4. **Knowledge and Information Barriers:** Gap in computer proficiency due to limited lifetime use; lack of awareness of available digital services.
5. **Perception/Attitude Barriers:** Concerns about online security/privacy; fear of scams; low self-efficacy ("too old to learn"); fear of social isolation or stigmatization from using assistive technologies; preference for traditional communication methods.
6. **Resource Barriers:** Limited access to devices/internet; poor internet speed (especially in rural areas); high costs of devices and services; absence of personalized training.
7. **Special Population Barriers:** Unique challenges for visually impaired, hearing impaired, those with chronic conditions, and older adults with disabilities.

**Strategies to mitigate barriers** include: Collaborative Learning (intergenerational programs, partnerships), Structured Content (gamification, hands-on activities), Technology-Facilitated Self-Learning (user-friendly designs, step-by-step guides), Tailored Interventions (personalized home-based training, user-driven content), Adaptive Tools (simplified interfaces, stylus pens, large keyboards), and Continuous Support (follow-up sessions, refresher courses).

- **Tech Helpline:** Free one-on-one support pairing older adults with trained technology mentors (virtually or in-person). Over 550 mentors have been trained through a rigorous vetting process.

- Connected Canadians has volunteers specializing in accessibility features for visually impaired and other disabilities.
- Connected Canadians has not directly worked with medical devices but has distributed smart speakers (Amazon Echo Show) for emergency communication.
- Research gaps exist for special populations like Indigenous populations on reserves lacking internet infrastructure, and for older adults aged 75+.
- Fear of strangers accessing computers is a significant barrier to overcome when encouraging older adults to sign up for digital literacy programs.

--- SOURCE 10: What Is the Digital Divide? Meaning, Causes & Impact ---
URL: https://ischool.syracuse.edu/what-is-the-digital-divide

SUMMARY:
<summary>
## What Is the Digital Divide? Meaning, Causes & Impact

This page from Syracuse University's iSchool provides a comprehensive overview of the digital divide—the gap between people who have meaningful access to digital technology and those who don't. It goes beyond device ownership to include quality of access, skills to use technology effectively, and ability to benefit from digital opportunities.

### Key Takeaways
- The digital divide describes gaps in who can access, use, and benefit from digital technology
- Economic factors, geography, education, and age all contribute to technology inequality
- Digital gaps affect education, employment, healthcare access, and social participation

### Types of Digital Divide
1. **Access Divide**: Disparities in who can connect to the internet and own devices. Rural communities face infrastructure gaps; cost is a major barrier (monthly bills of $50–$100). Some families rely on mobile-only internet.
2. **Skills Divide**: Differences in digital literacy—navigating technology effectively, safely, and productively. According to AARP research, 64% of adults over 50 feel technology is not designed with their age group in mind.
3. **Usage Divide**: How people use technology differently based on socioeconomic status. Higher-income users engage in more "capital-enhancing" activities; lower-income users often engage in more passive consumption.

### Causes
- **Economic factors**: Device costs ($200+) plus annual internet bills ($600–$1,200)
- **Geographic limitations**: Rural Americans are nearly 20 times more likely than urban residents to lack fixed broadband (USDA data)
- **Educational factors**: Under-resourced schools have outdated equipment and weaker tech curricula
- **Age-related gaps**: Older adults often lack confidence with digital tools
- **Infrastructure and policy limitations**

### Effects
- **Education**: Students without home internet struggle with homework, online resources, and remote learning
- **Employment**: Higher-wage workers are more likely to work remotely; lower-wage workers cannot (U.S. Census Bureau data)
- **Healthcare**: ~80% of providers offered telehealth in 2022, but older adults, rural residents, and low-income patients face greatest barriers (AMA)
- **Social participation**: Citizens without digital access face barriers to government services, banking, and civic engagement

### Bridging the Divide
Solutions include expanding broadband infrastructure (federal programs like BEAD), improving digital literacy through schools and libraries, policy solutions (subsidy programs, E-Rate funding), and support from private/nonprofit sectors (Microsoft's Airband Initiative, Google's Project Connect, EveryoneOn, PCs for People).

The page concludes that digital equity requires ongoing effort from schools, libraries, businesses, and governments, and that communities prioritizing digital inclusion see clear outcomes in education, employment, and healthcare.
</summary>

<summary>

The study analyzed data from an NIH-funded interview-based investigation (N=43), focusing on a subsample of 13 informal caregivers whose care recipients attended ADS at the onset of COVID-19. 1. **Struggle to meet needs of the person with dementia**: Caregivers were forced into round-the-clock care while balancing full-time employment and other obligations. Many lacked training to provide medical oversight previously handled by ADS.
2. **Physical and cognitive decline of the person with dementia**: Loss of regular physical activity, routine, socialization, and cognitive stimulation led to accelerated deterioration.

SUMMARY:
<summary>

- Unintentional injuries are the 8th leading cause of death among older adults (previously 7th, shifted during COVID-19).
- Falls and motor vehicle crashes are the leading causes of unintentional injury deaths and most TBI-related hospitalizations/deaths in older adults.

- In 2022, nearly 50 million licensed drivers were ages 65+ (1 in 5 drivers). The number of older adult drivers has increased 40% in the past decade.
- Over 9,100 older adults died in traffic crashes in 2022; each day, 25 older adults die and over 550 are injured in motor vehicle crashes.
- TBI death rates among older adults increased about 22% in the last 10 years. In 2021, there were nearly 70,000 TBI-related deaths in the U.S.
- Older adults have the highest rates of TBI-related hospitalizations and deaths and take longer to recover from TBIs.
- Social connectedness improves physical, emotional, and overall wellbeing in older adults, while social isolation and loneliness increase risk of negative health outcomes.

The page also references the "Still Going Strong" initiative, which offers tips and resources for older adults, caregivers, and healthcare providers to help older adults stay injury-free and independent.
