args.summary:
This is the official webpage for California Volunteers' **Neighbor-to-Neighbor** program, a network designed to strengthen communities through social connections. The initiative encourages neighbors to know each other to improve community health, well-being, and disaster resilience.

**Key elements:**
- **"Meet 6 Neighbors" challenge**: Connects neighbors to build healthier, more resilient communities. Knowing at least six neighbors is associated with improved health and well-being.
- **Disaster preparedness**: Encourages checking on neighbors (especially elderly/high-risk), exchanging contact info, and signing up for alerts at ready.ca.gov.
- **Local Partners**: Includes City of Richmond, San Francisco, San Mateo County, San Jose, Long Beach, Riverside, Kern County, Nevada City, Paradise Recreation & Parks District, and Cupertino.
- **Partner Spotlights**: Highlights community-driven initiatives including (1) Paradise Recreation & Parks District's fire resilience work post-2018 Camp Fire (Good Fire Weekend with tribal groups and prescribed burning), (2) San Francisco's partnership with Community Living Campaign for intergenerational connections, and (3) City of Riverside's resident-led Blue Zones initiative in the Arlanza neighborhood focusing on volunteerism, public health, and sustainability.
- **Call to action**: "When the fire broke out, I was able to help my elderly neighbors. They trusted us because they knew us."

# Eldercare Locator

![](https://www.usaging.org/content_images/e201753d-c230-45a8-81d1-3de64b1ba81c(1).jpg)

  
 **Connecting Older Adults to Critical Local Resources**  
   
 Launched in 1991, the **[Eldercare Locator](https://eldercare.acl.gov/home)** is the only national information and referral resource to provide support to consumers across the spectrum of issues affecting older Americans. The Locator was established and is funded by the U.S. Administration on Aging, part of the [**U.S**](https://acl.gov/)**[Administration for Community Living](https://acl.gov/)**, and is administered by USAging.    
    
 Through its National Call Center (800.677.1116), which operates Monday through Friday from 8:00 AM to 9:00 PM ET, and website (www.eldercare.acl.gov), the Locator is a trusted gateway for older adults and people with disabilities searching for information and resources vital to their well-being and independence.   
    
 The Locator receives about 400,000 requests for assistance annually on a wide range of topics including transportation, housing, benefits eligibility and home and community-based services. Certified Information Specialists refer the majority of inquiries to more than 600 Area Agencies on Aging and nearly 300 Title VI Native American Aging Programs that provide vital services and supports in virtually every community in America; referrals are also made to federal/state agencies and nonprofits.  
   
 **Raising Public Awareness of Major Issues Affecting Older Adults**  
   
 The Eldercare Locator also educates the public about some of the most important issues affecting older adults in the U.S. By developing and distributing consumer brochures on such high-profile topics as **[combatting isolation and loneliness](https://www.usaging.org/Files/Isolation%20BrochureFINAL.pdf)**, **[transitioning to a non-driving future](https://www.nadtc.org/wp-content/uploads/GivingUpTheKeys_Final_508_AcrobatXI.pdf)** and **[strengthening brain health](https://www.usaging.org/files/BrainHealth(1).pdf)** through its annual Home for the Holidays Campaign, the Locator plays a vital role in stimulating a national conversation about these serious issues.

# Services for Older Adults Living at Home

# Services for Older Adults Living at Home

There are many types of services available to help meet the [long-term care](/health/long-term-care/what-long-term-care) needs of an older person living at home. Family members and friends may be able to help with some personal and household tasks. But you might want to hire professionals to assist with others. The ideas and resources below can help you find the services you need.

## Home health care services

Home health care services may be available to help older people with many aspects of health care, such as medications, wound care, medical equipment, and physical therapy. The provider may come for a few hours each day or stay 24/7.

Home health care services may include in-home nursing care to help a person recover from surgery, an accident, or an illness. If the person just left the hospital and still needs nursing care at home for a short time, the hospital can help arrange for a home health aide. In-home health services can also help manage long-lasting (chronic) conditions such as diabetes, for example, by testing a person’s blood sugar or giving insulin through a pump.

![An older man and his wife talk to a home health care provider](/sites/default/files/inline-images/iStock-161843047-inline.jpg)**What to know about costs:**

* Home health services charge by the hour.
* Medicare has limited coverage of home health service costs. The services must be short-term and provided by agencies certified by Medicare.
* Medicaid also provides coverage for home health service costs, but these benefits vary by state.
* Most private health insurance plans do not cover these costs.
* You must pay all costs not covered by Medicare, Medicaid, or private insurance.

To find a home health care service, ask your doctor or other health care professional about good options in your area. You can also ask friends or neighbors for referrals.

* ### Home health care services: Do your research!

  Get as much information as you can about a service before you sign an agreement. [This online tool](http://www.medicare.gov/care-compare) can help you find and compare Medicare-certified home health agencies.

  It’s always a good idea to check references before hiring a particular person or company. If possible, check for any complaints filed against a company with state and local agencies that regulate health services. Or contact the [Better Business Bureau](https://www.bbb.org/) in your area.

  See [Worksheet: Questions To Ask Before Hiring a Care Provider](/sites/default/files/2023-04/worksheet-questions-hiring-care-provider.pdf) (PDF, 141K) for considerations when choosing a home care service.

## Help with everyday activities

Does the older adult need help with chores, such as housecleaning, yard work, grocery shopping, or laundry? Some grocery and drug stores will take orders over the phone or online and deliver the items to a person’s home, and someone you know may have a housekeeper or gardener to recommend. Laundry and dry-cleaning services that pick up and deliver clothes are another option.![Home health aide helps an older man put on his coat](/sites/default/files/inline-images/iStock-1444971960-inline.jpg)

Older adults may also need help with personal care. This includes everyday activities, also called “activities of daily living,” such as bathing, dressing, grooming, using the toilet, eating, and moving around — for example, getting out of bed and into a chair. To provide support for personal care, a relative, friend, or trained aide could help for a short time each day.

Some older adults, especially people who live alone, simply need someone to check on them. You can ask family, neighbors, or nearby friends to drop by on a regular basis to make sure the older person has everything they need.

### Friendly visitor and senior companion services

Some organizations have volunteers who regularly pay short visits (less than two hours) to older adults. The volunteer can provide support, assistance, and companionship.

**What to know about costs:**

* Volunteer services are available at no cost. You can also get this type of service from home health agencies for a fee.
* Medicare, Medicaid, and private health insurance generally do not cover these services. Some long-term care insurance plans help pay for companion visits.

Nearby senior centers and your state or local government can help connect you with volunteers near where you live.

* ![Cover of Caregiver's Handbook publication](/sites/default/files/styles/convert_to_avif/public/2023-10/NIA_Caregivers_Guide_Cover_600x400_150dpi.jpg.avif?itok=O5HXfgYj)

  ### The Caregiver’s Handbook

  Explore this guide to getting started with caregiving, finding support, and taking care of yourself.

  [Download the PDF](https://order.nia.nih.gov/publication/caregivers-handbook)

## Nutrition, food, and meal services

Maybe you’re worried that an older person isn’t eating nutritious meals or is eating alone too often. You might suggest they share cooking duties with a friend or have a potluck dinner with a group of neighbors. Find out if their religious community or a local senior center serves meals. Is it hard for the person to get out? Plan to bring them a healthy meal a few times a week, ask a neighbor or friend to help out, or consider a meal delivery program.

Meal delivery programs bring healthy, nutritious meals to a person’s home on a daily or weekly basis. Many of these services offer options for special diets and can handle dietary restrictions. However, the delivery staff do not assist with making meals at home or feeding the person.

**What to know about costs:**

* In some cases, a person must qualify for the service based on certain guidelines. These can include age, mobility, and economic need.
* Medicare does not generally cover meal delivery services, although under certain circumstances, it will provide this benefit for a short time. Medicaid may pay for some meal delivery services if the person is eligible.
* Some meal delivery services do not require payment. Others charge a fee or accept donations.

To find a meal delivery service in your area, contact [Meals on Wheels America](http://www.mealsonwheelsamerica.org) online or by calling 888-998-6325. Some local governments provide low- or no-cost meals to older adults. Call or check their websites for details. Your health care provider or local senior center may also be able to recommend a service.

Additionally, there are many subscription services that deliver ready-to-eat meals and meal kits. These can be arranged online and generally involve a regular weekly or monthly charge.

## Money management

If the older adult needs help with tasks such as paying bills and filling out health insurance forms, you or a trusted relative could lend a hand. Trained volunteers, financial counselors, and other professionals can also help. Just make sure you get a referral from a trustworthy source, such as your local Area Agency on Aging.

If the older adult uses a computer, you could help them pay their bills online through the websites of service providers or their bank. Some regular bills, such as utilities and rent or mortgage payments, can be paid automatically from a person’s bank account each month.

Ask the person to consider providing someone they trust with legal permission to discuss their financial matters with others. One way to do this is through a power of attorney, which allows a trusted relative or friend to make financial decisions on their behalf. That person could help deal with creditors, pay bills from the older person’s bank account, or find out about Social Security or Medicare benefits.

For more information, visit the [Consumer Financial Protection Bureau](http://www.consumerfinance.gov) online or call 855-411-2372.

## Transportation services

If an older person can no longer drive, neighbors or volunteers may be able to help take them to the doctor’s office or run errands, such as grocery shopping. Transportation services can also help. They drive people to and from medical appointments, shopping centers, and other places in the community. ![Older man getting into the back seat of a car](/sites/default/files/inline-images/iStock-1159638229-inline.jpg)

Various state and local agencies, nonprofit organizations, and companies offer transportation services for older adults. Some senior housing complexes and community groups also offer rides. Public transit agencies often have discounted fares and other services for older adults and people with disabilities. Many communities also have taxis, ride-sharing services, and other transportation resources available. If needed, you can request a vehicle that will accommodate a wheelchair, walker, or electric scooter.

**What to know about costs:**

* Some transportation services are free. These include programs from state and local governments and some nonprofit organizations.
* Other services, such as taxis, car services, and ride-sharing companies, charge a fee for transportation. Some offer discounts for older adults.
* For people who do not have access to a ride, Medicaid provides transportation for emergency medical care and for doctor’s appointments. Medicare provides transportation via ambulance for health care emergencies and limited nonemergencies (such as a ride to a dialysis facility).

## Emergency medical alert systems

If an older person lives alone, you might be concerned they will become sick, fall, or get lost when there’s no one around to help. Services such as an emergency medical alert system, fall monitor, or GPS tracking device can help lower these risks.

Emergency medical alert systems respond to medical and other emergencies via an electronic monitor that a person wears. The monitor alerts emergency personnel when a person becomes lost, falls, or needs urgent medical assistance.

However, emergency medical alert systems won’t be useful in every kind of emergency. They must be set up correctly and worn by the older adult, and the batteries need to be charged or replaced as recommended. These services can’t replace regular check-ins by family, friends, and other caregivers.

**What to know about costs:**

* Emergency medical alert systems typically charge a fee to get started, followed by a monthly service fee. The costs vary based on the company, available features, and coverage area.
* Medicare will not pay for emergency medical alert systems, but Medicaid and other programs may provide coverage.
* Some private health care insurance plans cover emergency medical alert systems. Some long-term care insurance plans also pay a portion of the costs.
* You must pay all costs not covered by private health insurance or government programs.

## Help for caregivers

Caring for an older adult can be rewarding, but it can also be demanding, difficult, and stressful. To get support, talk to a trusted family member or friend, or seek counseling from a mental health professional. Join an online or in-person support group for caregivers. These are people who will know what you’re going through and may have suggestions or advice.

It’s important to take a break if you need it. You can ask another family member or friend to step in, hire an aide to come for a few hours a week, or sign up the older person for an adult day care program.

### Respite care

[Respite services](/health/caregiving/what-respite-care) provide short-term care for an older adult at home, in a health care facility, or at an adult day care center. The care may last anywhere from a few hours to several weeks at a time. These services provide regular caregivers with a break to rest, travel, or spend time with other family and friends.

**What to know about costs:**

* Respite services charge by the hour or by the number of days or weeks that services are provided.
* For a person receiving hospice care, Medicare will cover most of the cost for up to five consecutive days of respite care in a hospital or skilled nursing facility. Medicaid also may provide payment assistance.
* Most private health insurance plans do not cover these costs. Some long-term care insurance plans may help pay for respite care.
* You must pay all costs not covered by private insurance or government programs.

To search for respite care programs in your area, visit the [ARCH National Respite Locator](https://archrespite.org/caregiver-resources/respitelocator/) or call 703-256-2084.

### Adult day care servicesOlder adults enjoy breakfast together at a facility

Adult day care services can provide a much-needed break for caregivers at home. These programs provide a safe environment for older adults with trained staff in a nearby facility. An adult day care center may offer social activities, exercise, meals, personal care, and basic health care services. Some will provide transportation — the facility may pick up the person, take them to day care, and then return the person home.

**What to know about costs:**

* Adult day care tends to be less expensive than in-home or nursing home care. Charges can be hourly or by the day.
* Medicare will not pay for adult day care, but Medicaid and other government programs may provide coverage.
* Most private health insurance plans don’t cover the costs of adult day care. Some long-term care insurance plans pay a portion of the costs.
* You must pay all costs not covered by a government program or private insurance.

To find an adult day care center in your area, contact the [National Adult Day Services Association](http://www.nadsa.org) online or by calling 877-745-1440.

## Other professional services

These professionals also provide services that can help older adults and their caregivers.

### Geriatric care managers

A geriatric care manager, also called an aging life care expert, is usually a licensed nurse or social worker who specializes in geriatrics (health care for older adults). Geriatric care managers work with older adults and their families to identify needs, make a care plan, and find services in the community. They can be especially helpful when a caregiver lives far away.

Geriatric care managers can:

* Discuss difficult topics and complex issues
* Make home visits and suggest services
* Address emotional concerns and provide support
* Make short- and long-term plans
* Evaluate in-home care needs
* Coordinate medical services
* Refer to other care specialists
* Evaluate potential living arrangements
* Provide stress relief to caregivers

**What to know about costs:**

* The cost of an initial evaluation varies and may be expensive.
* Geriatric care managers charge by the hour.
* Medicare and Medicaid do not pay for this service.
* Most private health insurance plans don’t cover these costs. Long-term care insurance may pay for some of the costs: Check the plan to see if it includes coverage.
* Most people must pay for some or all of this service themselves.

There are several ways to locate a geriatric care manager. Your doctor or other health care provider may be able to provide a recommendation. Or contact the [Aging Life Care Association](http://www.aginglifecare.org) online or by calling 520-881-8008. Additionally, you can contact a support group for diseases related to aging. These groups may be able to recommend geriatric care managers who have assisted others in your area.

* ### Choosing a geriatric care manager

  When interviewing a geriatric care manager, you might want to ask:

  + Are you a licensed geriatric care manager?
  + How long have you been providing care management services?
  + Are you available for emergencies around the clock?
  + Does your company also provide home care services?
  + How will you communicate information to me?
  + What are your fees? Will you provide information on fees in writing prior to starting services?
  + Can you provide references?

### Mental health professionals

Counselors can help older adults and caregivers deal with stress they may be feeling. They can help you understand your feelings, such as anger, sadness, or feeling out of control and overwhelmed. Counselors can also help develop plans for unexpected or sudden events.

Professionals who provide mental health counseling include psychologists, therapists, and social workers, among others. Counseling can occur in-person at an office, at a person’s home, or in a community setting. Virtual counseling sessions, which take place remotely on a computer or smartphone, are becoming more common.

**What to know about costs:**

* Professional mental health counselors charge by the hour. Rates vary widely.
* Medicare or Medicaid may cover some of the costs.
* Some private health insurance companies will cover some of the costs.
* You must pay all costs not covered by Medicare, Medicaid, or private health insurance.

Check with your health insurance provider to find out which counselors and services are in your plan’s network. Then ask your doctor, local family service agency, or community mental health agency for referrals to counselors who participate with your insurance plan.

### You may also be interested in

* Reading more about [aging in place](/health/aging-place/aging-place-growing-older-home), or growing older at home
* Finding tips for [getting your affairs in order](/health/advance-care-planning/getting-your-affairs-order-advance-care-planning)

args.summary:
This National Institute on Aging (NIA) webpage provides comprehensive information about services available to help older adults living at home, covering various types of care and support options.

**Home Health Care Services:** In-home nursing care for medication management, wound care, physical therapy, and chronic condition management. Costs are charged by the hour; Medicare has limited short-term coverage, Medicaid varies by state, and most private insurance doesn't cover these costs.

**Help with Everyday Activities:** Includes assistance with chores (housecleaning, yard work, grocery shopping) and personal care (bathing, dressing, grooming, using the toilet, eating, moving around). Friendly visitor and senior companion services are available from volunteers at no cost or from home health agencies for a fee.

**Nutrition, Food, and Meal Services:** Meal delivery programs like Meals on Wheels (888-998-6325) bring healthy meals to homes. Costs vary—some are free, others charge fees or accept donations. Medicare generally doesn't cover these, though limited exceptions exist.

**Money Management:** Assistance with paying bills, filling out insurance forms, and setting up automatic payments. Power of attorney arrangements allow trusted individuals to make financial decisions.

**Transportation Services:** Various state/local agencies, nonprofits, and companies offer rides for medical appointments and errands. Some services are free; others charge fees. Medicaid provides transportation for emergency care and doctor's appointments.

**Emergency Medical Alert Systems:** Electronic monitors that alert emergency personnel when someone falls, becomes lost, or needs urgent medical assistance. Typically charge startup and monthly fees; Medicare generally doesn't pay for these.

**Help for Caregivers:** Respite care provides short-term breaks (hours to weeks) for caregivers, available at home, in facilities, or at adult day care centers. Adult day care services offer a safe environment with social activities, exercise, meals, and basic health care.

**Other Professional Services:** Geriatric care managers (licensed nurses or social workers) help identify needs and coordinate care; they charge by the hour and are not covered by Medicare/Medicaid. Mental health professionals (psychologists, therapists, social workers) provide counseling for stress management.

The page includes cost information for each service type, contact information for Eldercare Locator (800-677-1116), Medicaid (877-267-2323), Medicare (800-633-4227), and specific organizations for finding services.

# How to launch and grow telephone reassurance services

Practical tips and lessons learned for setting up a successful volunteer telephone reassurance program for seniors.

## Introduction

Programs like telephone reassurance are a great way to engage volunteers and have been shown to [positively impact](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamapsychiatry/fullarticle/2776786) loneliness, depression, and anxiety for participants.

Many older people experience isolation and loneliness, a problem exacerbated further during COVID-19. Over a quarter of people over age 60 live alone, according to a [Pew Research Survey](https://www.pewresearch.org/fact-tank/2020/03/10/older-people-are-more-likely-to-live-alone-in-the-u-s-than-elsewhere-in-the-world/). And 43 percent of people over 60 reported feeling lonely before COVID-19, according to another study in [JAMA Internal Medicine](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/1188033). As people live longer and apart from friends and family, loneliness will continue to become a growing a public health crisis.

Talking on the phone with a friendly caller has become an appealing option to combat feelings of loneliness and isolation. At Mon Ami, we have helped communities across the country scale support to older adults, enabling millions of call minutes that address isolation and loneliness. Here we share some practical tips and lessons for how to launch a new program or grow an existing one.

## Examples of Telephone Reassurance Programs

There are already a number of nationwide and local telephone reassurance programs for older adults, like the [AARP Friendly Voices Program](https://aarpcommunityconnections.org/friendly-voices/) where any older adult can request a one-time call from an AARP volunteer. There are also industry-specific programs, like the Motion Picture and Television Fund’s Daily Call Sheet which matches volunteers with older adults in the entertainment industry.

SAGE, a national nonprofit serving LGBT elders and [partner](https://www.sageusa.org/news-posts/sage-launches-sageconnect-to-combat-social-isolation-for-lgbt-elders/) of Mon Ami’s, created an innovative program called [SAGEConnect](https://www.sageusa.org/sageconnect/) to address isolation and build connection within the LGBT community. Through SAGEConnect, older adults connect once a week or more with the same volunteer over the phone to talk, check-in, and just be with one another.

Many local chapters of the federal Retired Senior Volunteers Program (RSVP) have recruited and trained older volunteers to provide telephone reassurance calls to those experiencing isolation in the community. The RSVP of Lehigh, Northampton, and Carbon Counties in Pennsylvania, for example, partnered with its county’s Department of Aging and Adult Services to deliver regular friendly calls to local seniors through a joint program called [Senior CHAT](https://www.rsvpoflnc.org/seniorchat/).

Despite these existing programs, many millions of older adults present a need for more community-based telephone reassurance programs that can match locally and culturally - things that go a long way in creating a truly successful match. If your organization or program works with older adults in any way, consider creating a friendly caller program for your local community to support one another in a time of need.

## Choose a goal for your program

Think through the needs of your client base and the role that you believe your organization’s volunteers can play. There should be a clear purpose communicated to volunteers and to clients regarding the purpose of these telephone calls. This will inform how you conduct training for volunteers and what information you might need to collect after a phone call. Consider how different goals may conflict with one another in the delivery of your program. Choosing a single, clearly articulated goal will help align everyone involved towards successful execution of your program. Typically, programs choose to align around one of two overarching goals:

* 1. **To promote social connection and combat loneliness**: With this goal, programs are looking to help build meaningful connections between participants to address isolation and loneliness. The calls might be longer and between the same two people to promote consistency and relationship-building.
* 1. **To conduct a wellness check-in:** With this goal, programs are primarily looking to make sure seniors are ok and not in immediate harm. The calls tend to be shorter in length with a structured format.

## Structuring your telephone reassurance program

Start by writing down the main questions of who, what, when, where that you’ll need to create the shape of your telephone reassurance program. Here are some things to consider.

## Recruiting clients

Typically, identifying and recruiting participants for a telephone reassurance program is the most time consuming and challenging step in the process. Many programs report taking 6 months or longer to recruit the first clients because it takes time to build trust and form partnerships that offer positive referrals. Remember, it is unlikely at least in the beginning for clients to sign up themselves. Instead, most programs receive 80% of their new clients through referrals from local partners like Meals on Wheels, Area Agency on Aging, doctors’ offices, etc.

Here are some places to start or expand your recruiting efforts:

* **Your existing organization:** If you are starting a program out of an existing organization, you may already have participants in mind. Otherwise, consider reaching out across your organization to identify clients who may benefit from an additional service like telephone reassurance
* **Local referral partners**: Identify agencies in your area that serve a similar population. This could be Area Agencies on Aging, Meals on Wheels, senior centers, United Way chapters, faith-based organizations, or other service organizations. Educate them about your new service, and give them a way to easily make a referral, whether it’s through an online form or a simple email template. Check in regularly to remind them of your program and report success stories back to them where you can.
* **State representative offices**: Your local representative may have a good pulse on who in the community is in need of your services. They receive a high call volume and can refer individuals who they think may be a good fit.
* **Local media**: Is there a local or regional publication that your target audience reads or watches? Your audience could be the individuals themselves or their family, friends, and caregivers. Consider placing an ad in a local newspaper or reach out to the news desk to pitch a story about your program.
* **Bulk mailing lists:** In some cases, programs have found it useful to purchase a bulk mailing list of addresses that target their audience with postcards or flyers mailed to their home.

When talking to prospective clients and creating outreach materials, there are a few best practices:

Do’s and Donts

## Recruiting and training volunteers

Through the right channels, you will likely find many people who are eager to volunteer for your telephone reassurance program. The benefits of volunteering are many: it’s a fantastic way to connect with others, build relationships, give back to the community, and incredibly easy to do.

Set up a volunteer application to collect the information you’ll need to make matches. At a minimum, you’ll need names and phone numbers, but you may choose to ask about location, language, interests, hobbies, age, or other demographic details to make more compatible matches. Consider creating an online application, rather than a paper application, to eliminate the need to mail applications and to ease the management process. Once you’ve recruited your volunteers, consider what basic training they’ll need to be successful in their calls. This might include phone etiquette [guidelines](/advice/tips-for-a-successful-call) like how to introduce themselves, appropriate times to call, or how to manage differences in opinion. Your training might also include the steps for how they schedule, log, and keep track of any of their calls.

## Scheduling and tracking calls

Once you have participants in your program, you’ll need a system to match people and keep track of who is calling whom, when, and how often. You may choose for your team to make the matches, or you may send new call requests to volunteers and allow them to express interest and sign up.

* Make matches between volunteers and clients
* Notify volunteers of new call requests, and allow them to view details of the request and sign up to be matched
* Mask phone numbers through a central designated phone system so that volunteers and clients don’t need to share personal contact information with each other
* Automatically track calls made between volunteers and clients, without volunteers needing to submit a call log or time sheet
* Collect feedback and notes about calls and see a history of client well-being and concerns

## Consider privacy and security measures

Especially when working with seniors, privacy and security are a big concern for both volunteers and clients. You should consider integrating a background check process into your volunteer onboarding. At a minimum, it should include federal and county level criminal searches and sex offender searches.

In addition, take precautions to protect personal information of both seniors and volunteers when creating a match. You may choose to only provide first names when sharing the details of a match. When volunteers are making phone calls, they will likely be using their own phones, and so caller-ID blocking or other security measures are recommended.

## Measuring success

Consider the goals you set in step 1. Whatever goals you have set for your program will drive the way you measure the success of your program. If your goal was to build meaningful connections, collect data on the frequency of notes shared from seniors or your volunteers. You can even build specific questions for your feedback surveys asking “how successful was [your organization] at building meaningful connections?”

Depending on the goal you set for your program, customize your assessment to measure that goal. In addition, it’s important to track growth and retention for your program as these are implicit indicators of the experience for both the people you serve and the volunteers that support your organization. Many of our partner organizations use the [UCLA 3-question Loneliness Survey](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2394670/) to measure client impact over time, whereas others have crafted their own satisfaction surveys or partnered with research institutes and academic institutions to analyze the impact of their programs. You can also contract a third party to complete a phone survey of satisfaction and impact, or can even train your volunteers to complete such a survey.

Check out our article on “How to evaluate telephone reassurance programs” for more information.

## Telephone Reassurance Starter Kit

From our experience launching telephone reassurance programs across the country, we’ve compiled a starter kit for organizations that are looking to kick start their telephone reassurance program. Our telephone reassurance starter kit includes:

* Recruitment flyer templates
* Sample volunteer guidelines for participation
* Ideas for how to recruit participates of the program
* General best practices and tips for running the program

[Download the starter kit here.](https://docs.google.com/document/d/e/2PACX-1vTJt9OwZj9-4766PHpXqLOTHJP7LXKaUA2tJM2bHxgg_39nBQ4OGwNa3pguO9zEArs599nJwj5PGG0G/pub)

## Keep reading

1. **Promote social connection and combat loneliness** – longer calls between same matched pairs to build relationships
2. **Conduct wellness check-ins** – shorter, structured calls focused on safety

## Key Guidance
- **Recruiting clients is the hardest part**, often taking 6+ months; 80% of new clients come through referrals from partners like Meals on Wheels, Area Agencies on Aging, and doctors' offices
- Other recruitment channels: existing organizations, state representative offices, local media, bulk mailing lists
- **Volunteer recruitment**: collect applications with names, phone numbers, location, language, interests for better matching; provide training on phone etiquette
- **Scheduling and tracking**: need a system for matching, notifying volunteers, masking phone numbers, tracking calls, and collecting feedback
- **Privacy and security**: background checks (federal, county, sex offender), caller-ID blocking, limiting personal information shared
- **Measuring success**: use tools like the UCLA 3-question Loneliness Survey, tailored satisfaction surveys, or third-party assessments

The article also offers a downloadable Telephone Reassurance Starter Kit with recruitment flyer templates, volunteer guidelines, and best practices.

# Telephone Reassurance Programs

# Telephone Reassurance Programs

## **What is a Telephone Reassurance Program?**

Telephone Reassurance Programs—also known as Friendly Caller, Phone-a-Friend, Outreach Calls, or Check-in Calls—connect individuals in need with regular, caring phone conversations. These programs primarily support:

* Older Adults/Seniors
* Homebound individuals
* People with disabilities or persistent mental illnesses

Volunteers or staff make scheduled outgoing calls to enrolled clients, offering friendly chats and wellness checks. Calls may occur daily, weekly, or several times per week, providing comfort, social connection, and safety monitoring. Some programs include safety tasks, such as confirming medication adherence or checking for illness or falls, and may request wellness checks if clients do not answer.

## **Why Are Telephone Reassurance Programs Needed?**

Social isolation is a significant public health issue, especially for older adults. It is linked to higher risks of high blood pressure, heart disease, obesity, anxiety, depression, dementia, and increased suicide risk. Research shows that loneliness and isolation can worsen health outcomes and that many healthcare providers do not adequately screen for depression among seniors.

A 2012 poll by the John A. Hartford Foundation found that nearly 1 in 3 of survey participants over age 65 assumed that depression was a normal and expected part of the aging process (it is not). The poll also found that physicians and other professionals in regular contact with seniors did not effectively screen for depression or provide adequate communication and follow-up regarding mental health care. Social isolation and the associated depression can place an individual at higher risk of death by suicide. Studies show that people aged 45-64 and 65 and older have the highest rates of suicide among all age groups.

Telephone Reassurance Programs help reduce isolation and its associated health risks. Trained volunteers and staff can recognize signs of depression and connect participants with resources, potentially preventing suicide. These programs also support older adults in aging in place and maintaining independence.

## **What Agencies Operate Telephone Reassurance Programs?**

A variety of organizations run Telephone Reassurance Programs, including:

* Aging and Disability Resource Centers
* Departments of Aging
* Area Agencies on Aging
* Mental health organizations
* Crisis centers and warmlines

While some programs operate nationwide, local programs are often preferred for their ability to address community-specific needs and coordinate care among local agencies.

## **Key Needs of Telephone Reassurance Programs?**

Organizations operating these programs require tools to:

* Recruit, Train, and Manage Volunteers and Staff
* Maintain volunteer/staff shift schedules
* Enable remote work
* Enroll and manage client information
* Create and manage call schedules
* Document call notes and data
* Assess for depression, suicide, and health risks
* Connect clients with resources and referrals
* Conduct satisfaction surveys and collect outcome data
* Generate reports for funders and stakeholders

## **How iCarol Can Help**

iCarol software supports Telephone Reassurance Programs by enabling organizations to:

* Accept volunteer/staff applications online
* Manage volunteer/staff records and training
* Enroll clients via online intake forms
* Schedule shifts and calls
* Enable remote work and calling
* Maintain client records
* Create and follow call schedules
* Document calls and connect clients with resources via email or SMS
* Communicate through 2-way texting
* Share data securely with partner organizations
* And more

--- SOURCE 1: Explore Risk of Social Isolation - Age 65+ in the United States | AHR ---
URL: https://www.americashealthrankings.org/explore/measures/isolationrisk_sr_b/idl_sr_b

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from America's Health Rankings presents data on "Risk of Social Isolation - Age 65+" in the United States, based on U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey data (2020-2024). The measure is an index of social isolation risk factors among adults 65+ including living in poverty, living alone, being divorced/separated/widowed, never having married, having a disability, and having independent living difficulty.

Key data points:
- The national average for independent living difficulty among adults 65+ is 13.2%.
- **Top states (lowest risk):** South Dakota (9.6%), Vermont (9.6%), Maine (9.7%), North Dakota (9.8%), New Hampshire (9.9%).
- **Bottom states (highest risk):** Mississippi (16.2%), California (16.1%), Hawaii (15.4%), Alabama (15.4%), New York (15.1%).
- The overall index range: Utah (best) at 1, Mississippi (worst) at 100.

Nearly a quarter of U.S. adults 65+ are at risk for social isolation. Social isolation differs from loneliness—it is the objective absence of social relationships rather than the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connections.

**Health impacts:** Social isolation increases risk of mortality, dementia, coronary heart disease, and stroke. Healthcare costs of social isolation account for an estimated $6.7 billion in Medicare expenditures annually.

**Risk factors include:** living alone, having a disability or being homebound, living in poverty, race/ethnicity, immigration status, English proficiency, sexual orientation/gender identity.

**Interventions:** Technology-based interventions, expanded public transportation and public health collaboration, service-provision with volunteer intermediaries, and Medicare Advantage supplemental benefits (home-delivered meals, ride-sharing, companionship). Senior and community centers are highlighted as important for group interactions.

The data appears in America's Health Rankings Senior Report (published May 2026).
</summary>

"Across the United States, nearly a quarter of adults age 65 and older are at risk for social isolation.", "Social isolation differs from loneliness, which is the feeling of lacking meaningful social relationships, while social isolation addresses the objective lack of social relationships.", "The health care costs of social isolation are comparable to those of some chronic illnesses, accounting for an estimated $6.7 billion in Medicare expenditures annually.", "Interventions to reduce social isolation among older adults are most successful when they directly involve older adults rather than simply providing services or training.", "Life events such as retirement, loss of loved ones, and age-related mental and physical decline can make it difficult for older adults to maintain social connectedness."

--- SOURCE 2: The global prevalence and associated factors of loneliness ... ---
URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-025-05304-x

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (April 2025) examining the global prevalence and associated factors of loneliness in older adults. A comprehensive search of six databases (Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, EMBASE, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar) from inception to March 2025 identified 126 studies involving 1,250,322 older adults (aged 60+).

**Key Findings:**
- **Global prevalence of loneliness: 27.6%** (95% CI: 25.5–29.8) — approximately one in four older adults
- **By continent:** North America highest (30.5%), followed by Asia (27.9%), Europe (27.2%), Oceania (25.7%), and Africa lowest (15.3%)
- **By gender:** Women (30.9%) had higher prevalence than men (24.2%)
- **By setting:** Institutionalized older adults (nursing homes, etc.) had 50.7% prevalence vs. community-dwelling
- Studies from 62 countries; US (18 studies), China (15), and Netherlands (8) contributed most
- Most common measurement tools: single-item questionnaire (67 studies), UCLA Loneliness Scale (35 studies), De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale (13 studies)

**Associated Factors (from 189 papers):**
- Strong positive associations: depression (52 studies), widowhood/being unmarried/divorced (24 studies), living alone (19 studies), poor health/well-being (17 studies), frailty (10 studies)
- Additional factors: cognitive impairment, institutionalization, hearing impairment, anxiety, sleep difficulties, social isolation, pain, falls
- Inverse associations: good quality of life, being married, higher cognitive function, better sleep quality

The authors note that loneliness is linked to depression, suicidal ideation, and mortality, and recommend that policymakers develop interventions to alleviate loneliness among older adults. Study limitations include restriction to English-language publications and reliance on single-item questionnaires in many studies.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 3: 1 in 3 older adults still experience loneliness and isolation ---
URL: https://www.michiganmedicine.org/health-lab/1-3-older-adults-still-experience-loneliness-and-isolation

SUMMARY:
<summary>
A national study published in JAMA in December 2024 shows that loneliness and isolation among older Americans (ages 50-80) have mostly returned to pre-pandemic rates, but over one-third still feel lonely and nearly as many feel isolated. The University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation analyzed six years of data from the National Poll on Healthy Aging.

**Key statistics:**
- In 2024, 33% of older adults felt lonely sometimes or often (vs 34% in 2018)
- In 2024, 29% felt isolated sometimes or often (vs 27% in 2018)
- Peak loneliness during early COVID-19 was 42%; peak isolation was 56%

**Highest loneliness rates in 2024 (most vulnerable groups):**
- Fair/poor mental health: 75% (74% in 2018)
- Fair/poor physical health: 53% (up from 50% in 2018)
- Not working or on disability: 52% (up from 38% in 2018)

**Highest isolation rates in 2024:**
- Fair/poor mental health: 77% (slightly down from 79% in 2018)
- Fair/poor physical health: 52% (up from 43% in 2018)
- Not working or on disability: 50% (up from 36% in 2018)

Adults ages 50-64 were more likely to feel lonely or isolated than those 65-80. Those with household incomes below $60,000 and those living alone also had higher rates. The study builds on the U.S. Surgeon General's 2023 advisory on social connection. Lead author Preeti Malani noted that while the return to pre-pandemic rates "might seem like great news... that baseline was not good, and it was especially bad for some groups of older adults."
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"At the surface, this might seem like great news, that we're back to where we were before COVID-19 struck. But that baseline was not good, and it was especially bad for some groups of older adults, who continue to have very high rates of loneliness and social isolation," said Preeti Malani, M.D., MSJ, the study's lead author.,"These trends make it clear: clinicians should see loneliness and isolation as a key factor in their patients' lives, especially those with serious physical or mental health conditions," said poll director Jeffrey Kullgren, M.D., M.P.H., M.S.,"One of the biggest differences now is that we have greater recognition of the impact of loneliness and isolation on health especially as we age."

# Older Americans Act Title III Programs: 2018 Summary of Highlights and Accomplishments

## Overview
This report from the Administration for Community Living (ACL) summarizes the 2018 highlights and accomplishments of Older Americans Act (OAA) Title III programs. Enacted in 1965, the OAA created the foundation for a comprehensive system of services enabling older adults to live independently. Title III services account for the largest portion of OAA funding, supporting a national network of federal, state, and local agencies.

## Key Data Points (2018)
- **56 state agencies**, **1,050 local agencies**, and **11,212 senior centers** were funded
- **Over 10.8 million older persons** received Title III services
- **Over 196,000 caregivers** serving older adults were supported
- **147 million** home-delivered meals provided
- **74 million** congregate meals provided
- **20 million** rides to medical appointments, grocery stores, and other activities
- **21 million hours** of homemaker services
- **89-96%** of service recipients noted services helped them stay in their homes
- The majority of service recipients rated services as excellent, very good, or good

## Demographic Context
By 2030, 73 million people (1 in 5) in the U.S. will be 65 or older. Between 2020-2030, the number of people 85+ is projected to rise by 35%. The OAA targets those with greatest economic or social need, particularly low-income and minority persons, older individuals with limited English proficiency, and those in rural areas.

## OAA Title III Service Categories
- **Part B**: Supportive services and senior centers (case management, transportation, homemaker services, legal assistance, adult day care, etc.)
- **Part C**: Nutrition services (congregate meals, home-delivered meals, nutrition counseling and education)
- **Part D**: Evidence-based prevention and health promotion services
- **Part E**: National Family Caregiver Support Program (counseling, support groups, respite services)

## Funding and Administration
- ACL is the primary federal agency administering OAA programs
- Funds flow from federal → state units on aging (56 SUAs) → area agencies on aging (629 AAAs) → local service providers
- In 2020, the Supporting Older Americans Act (SOAA) reauthorized the OAA for 5 years with a 7% increase in initial year funding and 6% annually thereafter
- COVID-19 supplemental appropriations included $480M for nutrition programs and $100M for caregiver support

## Historical Context
The OAA was signed into law on July 14, 1965. Key milestones include the establishment of AAAs in 1973, the creation of the National Family Caregiver Support Program in 2000, and the establishment of ACL in 2012.

The OAA, passed in 1965, aims to help older Americans maintain independence and dignity in a home environment. It is administered by the Administration on Aging, which funds State Units on Aging and Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) to deliver services tailored to each state's needs.

**Eligibility:** Participants must be 60+ and in greatest social or economic need. There is no means-testing; voluntary contributions are encouraged. Notably, immigrants ineligible for other federal benefits under PRWORA can still receive OAA services. Eligibility does not depend on work history or Social Security quarters.

**Title III Programs (the core of the article):**

- **Title III-B (Supportive Services):** Priority services include legal assistance, transportation, outreach, case management, and in-home services (homemaker/home health aides, chore maintenance). Special provisions exist for "Frail Older Americans" (those unable to perform 2+ ADLs) and those with Alzheimer's disease.
- **Title III-C (Nutrition/Meals):** Provides at least one meal per day, five days a week to senior centers and homes. Meals meet federal dietary guidelines, and modified meals (low-fat, low-sodium) are available. Spouses of participants and disabled individuals under 65 in senior housing are also eligible.
- **Title III-D (Disease Prevention & Health Promotion):** Funds health screening, education, and counseling at senior centers, congregate meal sites, or via home-delivered meals. Priority is given to medically underserved areas.
- **Title III-E (National Family Caregiver Support Program):** Provides caregivers with information, counseling, training, respite care, and supplemental services.

**Conclusion:** OAA programs can fill gaps for Medicare/Medicaid beneficiaries and those otherwise ineligible. Local services can be found by contacting a local AAA, State Office on Aging, or the national elder care locator (1-800-677-1116).
</summary>

**AmeriCorps Seniors** is a United States government program run by the Corporation for National and Community Service (CNCS) that engages volunteers aged 55 and older to serve their communities. The program has over 200,000 volunteers nationwide.

- **Senior Companions (55+):** Helps adults with disabilities or terminal illnesses (and their caregivers) live independently. URL: https://brevy.com/caregiver/aaa-vs-adrc-vs-eldercare-locator

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This guide from Brevy (published July 16, 2026, last verified July 16, 2026) explains the three main federal "front doors" for getting help with an aging parent: the Eldercare Locator, the Area Agency on Aging (AAA), and the Aging and Disability Resource Center (ADRC). All three are free to contact and often overlap or are the same office.

**Eldercare Locator:** A nationwide public service of the Administration for Community Living (ACL) that connects families to their local aging services. It does NOT deliver services but routes callers to the right local agency. Reach it at 1-800-677-1116 (Mon-Fri, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. ET) or eldercare.acl.gov.

**Area Agency on Aging (AAA):** The local state-designated agency that actually delivers services under the Older Americans Act—meals, transportation, caregiver support, benefits counseling. Each state designates one AAA per planning and service area (city, county, or multi-county district). Local names vary (e.g., "Council on Aging").

**ADRC (Aging and Disability Resource Center):** A broader state single entry point serving older adults, people with disabilities (any age), veterans, and families at all income levels. It is part of the federal No Wrong Door system and is designed for screening conversations about long-term care and Medicaid.

**Which to use:**
- Don't know your local agency → Start with Eldercare Locator
- Need immediate services (meals, transport, caregiver break) → Call AAA directly
- Weighing long-term care, Medicaid, or disability supports → Ask for ADRC

**Eligibility & Cost:** Contacting any is free. Older Americans Act services require age 60+ (no income test/means test). ADRC serves all ages and income levels. Voluntary contributions may be requested but cannot be required, and services cannot be denied for refusal to contribute.

**Key takeaway:** The three doors are complementary, not competing. Any will move you toward the same local network. The FAQ section clarifies that the Eldercare Locator is not the same as an AAA, and that some states may brand ADRCs differently ("access point" or "no wrong door" system).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Friendly Calling and Visiting Quantitative Pilot Study ---
URL: https://www.mealsonwheelsamerica.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/report_friendly-calling-and-visiting-quantitative-pilot-study_11-8-24.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This November 2024 report by Meals on Wheels America, funded by Caesars Foundation and evaluated by Dr. Matthew Lee Smith, presents findings from a quantitative pilot study assessing the effectiveness of Friendly Calling and Friendly Visiting social connection programs for older adults.

**Background & Purpose:** Social isolation was declared a national epidemic by the U.S. Surgeon General in 2023. The Meals on Wheels network prioritized addressing this issue. Ten Meals on Wheels organizations participated in a pilot to explore scaling social connection programs and demonstrate efficacy in reducing disconnectedness.

**Methods (2023 Pilot):** The pilot included four standardized components: (1) ServTracker database hub, (2) CallHub HIPAA-compliant social call software, (3) TimeSlips communication and engagement training ("Beautiful Questions"), and (4) the Upstream Social Interaction Risk Scale (U-SIRS-13) for consistent evaluation. Staff/volunteers were trained and clients assessed at baseline and three-month follow-up.

**Findings:** 
- Of 539 unique clients recruited, 475 received friendly calls and 64 received friendly visits. 109 clients had matched baseline and three-month follow-up data.
- At baseline, over 82% of clients were at risk for social disconnectedness. Highest risk items: "I miss having people around me" (80.7%), "I feel isolated from others" (77.1%), "I lack companionship" (75.2%).
- On average, clients reported statistically significant reductions in social disconnectedness from baseline to three-month follow-up (t=3.17, P=0.002). About 53% of clients reported lower scores at follow-up.
- Friendly calling clients significantly reduced disconnectedness (t=3.25, P=0.004; 56% improved). Friendly visiting clients showed no significant difference (t=0.61, P=0.550; 39% improved).
- Significant improvements were observed in clients' ability to "find companionship when I want it" (24% reduction) and being "content with my friendships and relationships" (19% reduction).
- Higher baseline risk was associated with fewer social calls and less call time.
- Clients averaged 78.3 years old; 76.1% lived alone; 52.3% worried about money for basic needs.

**Process Evaluation:** 367 staff/volunteers were trained. Of ~18,383 clients deemed eligible, 13.1% (2,405) were approached, and 684 agreed to participate. Key barriers: difficulty reaching clients, client refusal, hearing/cognitive impairments, stigma, volunteer shortages, language barriers, and competing activities.

**Limitations:** High staff turnover (4 of 10 programs), significant data gaps (only 109 of 539 clients had complete data), missing sociodemographic info, and challenges engaging socially disconnected clients weakened statistical power.

**Conclusion:** The pilot validates that Meals on Wheels social connection programs effectively increase social connectedness. Despite administrative challenges, clients reported tangible improvements in companionship and relationship satisfaction. Recommendations include thorough staff/volunteer onboarding, robust technical support, and adherence to data collection protocols for future scaling.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
Meals on Wheels America is a nonprofit organization that supports a nationwide network of community-based programs providing meals, friendly visits, and safety checks to help seniors maintain independence. The site highlights a growing crisis: nearly 14 million older Americans struggle with hunger each year, and demand for services far exceeds available funding. The organization's network serves 244 million meals annually to 2.6 million seniors, with over 50 years of proven impact. URL: https://www.ioaging.org/aging/the-value-of-the-friendship-line-in-enhancing-mental-health-for-seniors

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This white paper from the Institute on Aging (IOA) highlights the Friendship Line, a pioneering warm line program founded in 1973 by Dr. Patrick Arbore to combat loneliness and social isolation among seniors. Operating as California's largest warm line, it handles over 11,000 calls monthly and provides emotional support through both inbound calls and proactive outreach. A peer-reviewed study published in the New York Academy of Sciences, co-authored by IOA's Preston Burnes and lead author Katrina A. Hough, enrolled 121 older adults at risk for loneliness over six months. Key findings include: loneliness reduction from 46% to 28% (p<0.001), depression rates falling from 36% to 25% (p=0.07), anxiety dropping from 63% to 43% (p=0.004), and unhealthy mental health days decreasing from 14 to 8 (p<0.001). 75% of participants felt more socially connected. The paper distinguishes between social isolation (objective lack of interactions) and loneliness (subjective feeling of disconnection), noting loneliness is as harmful as smoking 15 cigarettes a day. The Friendship Line addresses both by fostering meaningful connections and exemplifies the concept of social prescribing. Opportunities for expansion include scaling nationwide, leveraging technology, and further research.
</summary>

**Goals:** Foster stronger intergenerational connections to reduce isolation and loneliness, build upon existing community programs, and address public health issues tied to loneliness.

1. Skill-building (one generation teaches another)
2. Shared Activities (classes/programs together)
3. Mentoring (one-to-one relationships over time)
4. Built Environment (changes to places that encourage connection)

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The National Council on Aging (NCOA) article explores how intergenerational connections can help ease loneliness in older adults. It distinguishes between social isolation (few social connections) and loneliness (perception of being alone causing distress), noting they are distinct phenomena. According to a 2023 University of Michigan National Poll on Healthy Aging, 34% of adults aged 50-80 reported feeling isolated from others, and 37% reported lacking companionship in the past year.

Causes of social isolation include chronic diseases, dementia, mobility challenges, sensory impairment, depression, poverty, lack of transportation, and rural location. Social isolation is linked to a 29% higher all-cause mortality risk and a 25% greater risk for cancer mortality. It is also associated with high blood pressure, heart disease, weakened immune system, dementia, functional decline, and mental health issues like depression and suicidal ideation.

The article highlights Lori's Hands, a nonprofit that pairs college students with older adults and people with chronic illness for weekly visits. Students provide practical support (grocery shopping, housework) while clients share life experience. The program offers mutual benefits: students improve career readiness, communication skills, and empathy, while clients experience measurably lower loneliness levels with longer program participation. Lori's Hands has expanded to new chapters and offers training to organizations wanting to start similar programs.

Additional strategies to overcome social isolation include cognitive behavioral therapy, support groups, and senior centers (nearly 11,000 facilities nationwide serving 1 million older adults).
</summary>

--- SOURCE 4: Loneliness and Social Isolation — Tips for Staying Connected ---
URL: https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/loneliness-and-social-isolation/loneliness-and-social-isolation-tips-staying-connected

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from the National Institute on Aging (NIA) addresses loneliness and social isolation among older adults, providing definitions, health risks, and strategies for staying connected.

**Key definitions:** Loneliness is the distressing feeling of being alone or separated, while social isolation is the lack of social contacts and having few people to interact with regularly. Older adults face higher risks due to changes in health (hearing, vision, memory loss), disability, mobility issues, and loss of family/friends.

**Health risks:** Social isolation and loneliness are associated with higher risks for high blood pressure, heart disease, obesity, weakened immune function, anxiety, depression, cognitive decline, dementia (including Alzheimer's), and death. People experiencing these may also exercise less, drink more alcohol, smoke, and sleep poorly. Chronic loneliness can trigger stress responses leading to chronic inflammation and reduced immunity.

**Risk factors:** Loss of mobility, vision/hearing problems, psychological challenges, lack of purpose, financial struggles, living alone, lack of transportation, major life changes (death of a loved one, retirement), separation from friends/family, caregiving responsibilities, living in rural/unsafe areas, discrimination, and language barriers.

**Strategies for staying connected:** Find enjoyable activities or hobbies, schedule daily contact with family/friends (in-person, phone, video, email, social media), use communication technologies, consider adopting a pet, stay physically active (150 minutes of moderate activity weekly), connect with neighbors, join faith-based organizations, explore local community centers and senior centers, and volunteer.

**Special guidance for those with dementia living alone:** Identify a trusted person for regular visits and emergency contact, learn about community-based support services, stay connected via technology, and join support groups or memory cafés.

**Resources provided:** Eldercare Locator (800-677-1116), NIA ADEAR Center (800-438-4380), AmeriCorps Seniors, AARP, Family Caregiver Alliance, Meals on Wheels America, and others.
</summary>

- Christian theology recognizes humans as created for relationship (imago Dei), and faith communities provide social infrastructure that can mitigate isolation.

--- SOURCE 18: Services for Older Adults Living at Home | National Institute on Aging ---
URL: https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/caregiving/services-older-adults-living-home

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This National Institute on Aging (NIA) webpage provides comprehensive information about services available to help older adults living at home, covering various types of care and support options.

**Home Health Care Services:** In-home nursing care for medication management, wound care, physical therapy, and chronic condition management. Costs are charged by the hour; Medicare has limited short-term coverage, Medicaid varies by state, and most private insurance doesn't cover these costs.

**Help with Everyday Activities:** Includes assistance with chores (housecleaning, yard work, grocery shopping) and personal care (bathing, dressing, grooming, using the toilet, eating, moving around). Friendly visitor and senior companion services are available from volunteers at no cost or from home health agencies for a fee.

**Nutrition, Food, and Meal Services:** Meal delivery programs like Meals on Wheels (888-998-6325) bring healthy meals to homes. Costs vary—some are free, others charge fees or accept donations. Medicare generally doesn't cover these, though limited exceptions exist.

**Money Management:** Assistance with paying bills, filling out insurance forms, and setting up automatic payments. Power of attorney arrangements allow trusted individuals to make financial decisions.

**Transportation Services:** Various state/local agencies, nonprofits, and companies offer rides for medical appointments and errands. Some services are free; others charge fees. Medicaid provides transportation for emergency care and doctor's appointments.

**Emergency Medical Alert Systems:** Electronic monitors that alert emergency personnel when someone falls, becomes lost, or needs urgent medical assistance. Typically charge startup and monthly fees; Medicare generally doesn't pay for these.

--- SOURCE 1: Explore Risk of Social Isolation - Age 65+ in the United States | AHR ---
URL: https://www.americashealthrankings.org/explore/measures/isolationrisk_sr_b/idl_sr_b

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from America's Health Rankings presents data on "Risk of Social Isolation - Age 65+" in the United States, based on U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey data (2020-2024). The measure is an index of social isolation risk factors among adults 65+ including living in poverty, living alone, being divorced/separated/widowed, never having married, having a disability, and having independent living difficulty.

Key data points:
- The national average for independent living difficulty among adults 65+ is 13.2%.
- **Top states (lowest risk):** South Dakota (9.6%), Vermont (9.6%), Maine (9.7%), North Dakota (9.8%), New Hampshire (9.9%).
- **Bottom states (highest risk):** Mississippi (16.2%), California (16.1%), Hawaii (15.4%), Alabama (15.4%), New York (15.1%).
- The overall index range: Utah (best) at 1, Mississippi (worst) at 100.

Nearly a quarter of U.S. adults 65+ are at risk for social isolation. Social isolation differs from loneliness—it is the objective absence of social relationships rather than the subjective feeling of lacking meaningful connections.

**Health impacts:** Social isolation increases risk of mortality, dementia, coronary heart disease, and stroke. Healthcare costs of social isolation account for an estimated $6.7 billion in Medicare expenditures annually.

**Risk factors include:** living alone, having a disability or being homebound, living in poverty, race/ethnicity, immigration status, English proficiency, sexual orientation/gender identity.

**Interventions:** Technology-based interventions, expanded public transportation and public health collaboration, service-provision with volunteer intermediaries, and Medicare Advantage supplemental benefits (home-delivered meals, ride-sharing, companionship). Senior and community centers are highlighted as important for group interactions.

The data appears in America's Health Rankings Senior Report (published May 2026).
</summary>

URL: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-025-05304-x

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This is a systematic review and meta-analysis published in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (April 2025) examining the global prevalence and associated factors of loneliness in older adults. A comprehensive search of six databases (Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, EMBASE, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar) from inception to March 2025 identified 126 studies involving 1,250,322 older adults (aged 60+).

**Key Findings:**
- **Global prevalence of loneliness: 27.6%** (95% CI: 25.5–29.8) — approximately one in four older adults
- **By continent:** North America highest (30.5%), followed by Asia (27.9%), Europe (27.2%), Oceania (25.7%), and Africa lowest (15.3%)
- **By gender:** Women (30.9%) had higher prevalence than men (24.2%)
- **By setting:** Institutionalized older adults (nursing homes, etc.) had 50.7% prevalence vs. community-dwelling
- Studies from 62 countries; US (18 studies), China (15), and Netherlands (8) contributed most
- Most common measurement tools: single-item questionnaire (67 studies), UCLA Loneliness Scale (35 studies), De Jong Gierveld Loneliness Scale (13 studies)

**Associated Factors (from 189 papers):**
- Strong positive associations: depression (52 studies), widowhood/being unmarried/divorced (24 studies), living alone (19 studies), poor health/well-being (17 studies), frailty (10 studies)
- Additional factors: cognitive impairment, institutionalization, hearing impairment, anxiety, sleep difficulties, social isolation, pain, falls
- Inverse associations: good quality of life, being married, higher cognitive function, better sleep quality

The authors note that loneliness is linked to depression, suicidal ideation, and mortality, and recommend that policymakers develop interventions to alleviate loneliness among older adults. Study limitations include restriction to English-language publications and reliance on single-item questionnaires in many studies.
</summary>

A national study published in JAMA in December 2024 shows that loneliness and isolation among older Americans (ages 50-80) have mostly returned to pre-pandemic rates, but over one-third still feel lonely and nearly as many feel isolated. The University of Michigan Institute for Healthcare Policy and Innovation analyzed six years of data from the National Poll on Healthy Aging.

**Key statistics:**

- In 2024, 29% felt isolated sometimes or often (vs 27% in 2018)

- Not working or on disability: 52% (up from 38% in 2018)

This report from the Administration for Community Living (ACL) summarizes the 2018 highlights and accomplishments of Older Americans Act (OAA) Title III programs. - **Over 196,000 caregivers** serving older adults were supported
- **147 million** home-delivered meals provided

## Demographic Context
By 2030, 73 million people (1 in 5) in the U.S. will be 65 or older. Between 2020-2030, the number of people 85+ is projected to rise by 35%. The OAA targets those with greatest economic or social need, particularly low-income and minority persons, older individuals with limited English proficiency, and those in rural areas.

## OAA Title III Service Categories
- **Part B**: Supportive services and senior centers (case management, transportation, homemaker services, legal assistance, adult day care, etc.)
- **Part C**: Nutrition services (congregate meals, home-delivered meals, nutrition counseling and education)
- **Part D**: Evidence-based prevention and health promotion services
- **Part E**: National Family Caregiver Support Program (counseling, support groups, respite services)

## Funding and Administration
- ACL is the primary federal agency administering OAA programs
- Funds flow from federal → state units on aging (56 SUAs) → area agencies on aging (629 AAAs) → local service providers

- COVID-19 supplemental appropriations included $480M for nutrition programs and $100M for caregiver support

## Historical Context
The OAA was signed into law on July 14, 1965. Key milestones include the establishment of AAAs in 1973, the creation of the National Family Caregiver Support Program in 2000, and the establishment of ACL in 2012.

The OAA, passed in 1965, aims to help older Americans maintain independence and dignity in a home environment. It is administered by the Administration on Aging, which funds State Units on Aging and Area Agencies on Aging (AAAs) to deliver services tailored to each state's needs.

- **Title III-E (National Family Caregiver Support Program):** Provides caregivers with information, counseling, training, respite care, and supplemental services.

--- SOURCE 11: AmeriCorps Seniors - Wikipedia ---

SUMMARY:
<summary>
**AmeriCorps Seniors** is a United States government program run by the Corporation for National and Community Service (CNCS) that engages volunteers aged 55 and older to serve their communities. The program has over 200,000 volunteers nationwide.

**History:** Originally called Senior Corps, the program was formed in 1993 under President Bill Clinton when three constituent programs—Foster Grandparents, RSVP (Retired and Senior Volunteer Program), and Senior Companions—were merged under CNCS. On September 29, 2020, CNCS rebranded itself as AmeriCorps, and Senior Corps was rebranded as AmeriCorps Seniors.

Each of the three main programs has a unique history:
- **Foster Grandparents Program:** Piloted on August 28, 1965, to attract low-income individuals over 60 into community service. In the 1980s, First Lady Nancy Reagan championed the program.
- **Senior Companion Program:** Began in 1968 under the Department of Health, Education and Welfare and Administration on Aging, signed into law under President Richard Nixon in 1973.
- **RSVP:** Originated from private groups and government agencies, including the Community Service Society of New York on Staten Island (1965). Success led to an amendment to the Older Americans Act creating RSVP as a nationwide program in 1969.

**Programs:**
- **Foster Grandparents (55+):** Seniors interact with and support young children, providing emotional support to abuse victims, tutoring, mentoring, and caring for children with disabilities. Benefits include pre-service training, transportation reimbursement, annual physical, accident/liability insurance, and some income-eligible participants receive tax-free stipends.
- **RSVP (55+):** Flexible program allowing seniors to choose how and when to volunteer. Activities include job training, tutoring, building homes, immunization help, relief services, and a widespread telephone reassurance service. No stipend provided.
- **Senior Companions (55+):** Helps adults with disabilities or terminal illnesses (and their caregivers) live independently. Provides emotional/physical support, house chores, transportation, and companionship. Requires 5–40 hours/week. Includes training, transportation reimbursement, annual physical, meals, insurance, and income-eligible tax-free stipends.
</summary>

This guide from Brevy (published July 16, 2026, last verified July 16, 2026) explains the three main federal "front doors" for getting help with an aging parent: the Eldercare Locator, the Area Agency on Aging (AAA), and the Aging and Disability Resource Center (ADRC). All three are free to contact and often overlap or are the same office.

**Eldercare Locator:** A nationwide public service of the Administration for Community Living (ACL) that connects families to their local aging services. It does NOT deliver services but routes callers to the right local agency. Reach it at 1-800-677-1116 (Mon-Fri, 8 a.m. to 9 p.m. ET) or eldercare.acl.gov.

**Area Agency on Aging (AAA):** The local state-designated agency that actually delivers services under the Older Americans Act—meals, transportation, caregiver support, benefits counseling. Each state designates one AAA per planning and service area (city, county, or multi-county district). Local names vary (e.g., "Council on Aging").

**ADRC (Aging and Disability Resource Center):** A broader state single entry point serving older adults, people with disabilities (any age), veterans, and families at all income levels. It is part of the federal No Wrong Door system and is designed for screening conversations about long-term care and Medicaid.

**Which to use:**
- Don't know your local agency → Start with Eldercare Locator
- Need immediate services (meals, transport, caregiver break) → Call AAA directly
- Weighing long-term care, Medicaid, or disability supports → Ask for ADRC

**Eligibility & Cost:** Contacting any is free. Older Americans Act services require age 60+ (no income test/means test). ADRC serves all ages and income levels. Voluntary contributions may be requested but cannot be required, and services cannot be denied for refusal to contribute.

**Key takeaway:** The three doors are complementary, not competing. Any will move you toward the same local network. The FAQ section clarifies that the Eldercare Locator is not the same as an AAA, and that some states may brand ADRCs differently ("access point" or "no wrong door" system).
